question: M1
answer:
BASICMED AIRCRAFT LIMITS (US, 14 CFR Part 61 / Part 68; general aviation, Part 91, non-commercial)

ANSWERS
1. Maximum takeoff weight: 12,500 pounds (not more than).
2. Occupants the aircraft may be authorized to carry: 7 (not more than), including any required flightcrew members.
3. Passengers on board: 6 (not more than).

GOVERNING TEXT — 14 CFR 61.113(i)(1), current eCFR text:
'(1) The aircraft is authorized to carry not more than 7 occupants, has a maximum takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds, is operated with no more than 6 passengers on board, and is not a transport category rotorcraft certified to airworthiness standards under part 29 of this chapter.'
Note the regulation says 'maximum takeoff weight' (not 'maximum certificated takeoff weight') — the word 'certificated' was deliberately omitted so that experimental aircraft, which have no type certificate, can be evaluated against their FAA-approved operating limitations. For type-certificated aircraft the figure is the maximum certificated takeoff weight in the TC/STC/ATC; for experimental aircraft it is the maximum takeoff weight in the aircraft's operating limitations. Either way, the BasicMed ceiling is 12,500 lb.

WHY THESE ARE THE CURRENT NUMBERS (change history — critical, because most secondary sources are stale)
- FESSA (2016), sec. 2307(j) and 2307(a)(8), as originally implemented: not more than 6 occupants, maximum certificated takeoff weight not more than 6,000 lb, not more than 5 passengers.
- FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024, sec. 828(a)(4): raised occupants 6 -> 7, raised weight 6,000 lb -> 12,500 lb, and added the exclusion for transport category rotorcraft certificated under part 29.
- FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024, sec. 828: raised passengers 5 -> 6.
- These statutory amendments were self-effectuating in 49 U.S.C. 44703 note (FESSA); the FAA's conforming final rule (published in the Federal Register 2024-11-18) revised 61.113(i)(1) and 91.319(j) to the 7 / 12,500 lb / 6 text quoted above. The eCFR 'current' text and the FAA BasicMed page both now state 7 occupants, 12,500 lb, 6 passengers.

STALE-SOURCE WARNING (must not be used)
FAA Advisory Circular AC 68-1A (dated 5/3/17) still states, in its section 3.2 and 5.2.1, 'no more than five passengers,' '6,000 lbs,' and 'no more than 6 occupants.' That AC predates the 2024 statute and is superseded on these three figures by the current regulation and the FAA BasicMed webpage. Any checklist, insurance form, or third-party study guide quoting 6,000 lb / 6 occupants / 5 passengers is out of date.

HOW THE THREE NUMBERS FIT TOGETHER
- 'Occupants' means everyone aboard, including the pilot and any other required flightcrew member. 'Passengers' excludes required flightcrew. The two limits are separate and both must be satisfied.
- Single-pilot-certificated aircraft: 1 required flightcrew (PIC) + up to 6 passengers = 7 occupants. Both limits met simultaneously.
- Two-pilot-certificated aircraft operated under BasicMed: 2 required flightcrew + up to 5 passengers = 7 occupants. The passenger limit is therefore effectively 5 in that case, not because the rule changed but because the occupant ceiling binds first.
- The 7-occupant figure is a limit on what the aircraft is *authorized* to carry (design approval / seating certification), not merely on how many people happen to be aboard. An aircraft type-certificated for 8 or more occupants does not qualify unless altered under a new design approval (STC/ATC) to 7 or fewer.
- The 12,500 lb figure is the aircraft's maximum takeoff weight, not the actual loaded weight of a given flight; an aircraft certificated above 12,500 lb does not become eligible by flying light.

RELATED BASICMED OPERATING LIMITS (context only — not part of the three requested figures)
Flights within the United States; VFR or IFR; at or below 18,000 ft MSL; indicated airspeed not exceeding 250 knots; not for compensation or hire. Experimental aircraft operating under BasicMed are separately capped at 6 occupants by 14 CFR 91.319(j) — note this is a *lower* occupant cap than the 7 in 61.113(i)(1), so an experimental aircraft under BasicMed is effectively limited to 6 occupants and 5 passengers.

PREREQUISITES (not aircraft limits, listed so they are not confused with the answer)
Valid US driver's license; held an FAA medical certificate at some point after July 14, 2006; CMEC (FAA Form 8700-2) completed and signed by a state-licensed physician within the preceding 48 calendar months; BasicMed online medical education course completed; no disqualifying condition under Part 68.

SCOPE CAVEATS
These are federal FAA limits. State law, insurer requirements, rental agreements, and club rules may impose stricter limits; they cannot relax the federal ones. Commercial operations requiring a medical certificate are outside BasicMed and outside this answer.
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 6 on govinfo.gov/content/pkg/fr-2024-11-18/html/2024-26935.htm and 7 on faa.gov/licenses_certificates/airmen_certification/basic_med. The first reads: "Federal law to carry not more than 6 occupants;"

Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 6000 on govinfo.gov/content/pkg/fr-2024-11-18/html/2024-26935.htm and 12500 on faa.gov/licenses_certificates/airmen_certification/basic_med. The first reads: "certificated takeoff weight of not more than 6,000 pounds."

question: M3
answer:
US FEDERAL HOURS-OF-SERVICE LIMITS — DRIVER OF A PASSENGER-CARRYING COMMERCIAL MOTOR VEHICLE (e.g., MOTORCOACH)

Authority: 49 CFR 395.5, "Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles," subject to the exceptions and exemptions in 49 CFR 395.1. These are the FMCSA rules for interstate passenger carriers. They are NOT the property-carrying rules of 49 CFR 395.3, and the numbers differ.

=== THE THREE ANSWERS ===

1) MAXIMUM DRIVING TIME: 10 HOURS.
   A driver may drive a passenger-carrying CMV no more than 10 hours in a shift. 395.5(a)(1).

2) CONSECUTIVE OFF-DUTY HOURS REQUIRED: 8 CONSECUTIVE HOURS OFF DUTY.
   Both the 10-hour driving allowance and the 15-hour on-duty clock start only after at least 8 consecutive hours off duty. 395.5(a). The 8 hours may be off duty, sleeper berth, or any combination of the two, with no on-duty or driving time inside the 8-hour period.

3) ON-DUTY THRESHOLD AFTER WHICH DRIVING IS PROHIBITED: 15 HOURS ON DUTY.
   The driver may not drive for any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty. 395.5(a)(2).

Verbatim rule text (eCFR, current):
  "(a) No motor carrier shall permit or require any driver used by it to drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle, nor shall any such driver drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle:
   (1) More than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty; or
   (2) For any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty."

=== HOW THE THREE LIMITS INTERACT ===

- They are three separate stop-driving triggers. Reaching ANY one of them bars further driving until the driver takes 8 consecutive hours off duty (subject to the weekly cap below).
- Driving past 10 hours is prohibited even if the driver has been on duty fewer than 15 hours.
- Driving after 15 on-duty hours is prohibited even if the driver has driven fewer than 10 hours.
- The 15-hour figure is a count of ON-DUTY time, not elapsed clock time. Off-duty time taken during the shift (a meal stop, a nap, a layover) does not count toward the 15 hours, so such breaks push the wall-clock end of the shift later. This is the key structural difference from the property-carrier 14-hour window, where off-duty time does not extend the window.
- On-duty time that is not driving (loading, paperwork, waiting, inspecting) consumes the 15-hour allowance but not the 10-hour driving allowance.
- Off-duty time only "counts" if the driver is relieved of all duty and responsibility for the vehicle, its accessories, passengers, baggage, and freight, and is free to pursue activities of his or her own choosing for the whole stop.

=== WORKED EXAMPLE ===
Driver goes off duty at 22:00 and gets 8 consecutive hours off duty (22:00–06:00).
06:00 — comes on duty. The 15-hour on-duty count and the 10-hour driving count both begin.
06:00–07:00 on duty, not driving (pre-trip, dispatch): 1.0 on-duty, 0.0 driving.
07:00–12:00 driving: 5.0 driving, 6.0 on-duty.
12:00–12:45 off duty (meal): still 5.0 driving, 6.0 on-duty — the 45 minutes do not count against the 15.
12:45–17:45 driving: 10.0 driving, 11.0 on-duty. → 10-hour driving limit reached. No further driving, even though only 11 on-duty hours have accrued.
17:45–19:45 on duty, not driving: 13.0 on-duty. Driver may still not drive (10-hour limit already reached).
19:45–21:00 driving would be illegal on two independent grounds here (past 10 driving hours; and, if it ran past the 15th on-duty hour, past the 15-hour threshold as well).
To drive again, the driver needs 8 consecutive hours off duty, restarting both counts.

=== ADDITIONAL, INDEPENDENT PROHIBITION ON DRIVING: THE 60/70-HOUR CAP ===
49 CFR 395.5(b) separately bars driving "regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services" after the driver has been:
- ON DUTY 60 HOURS in any 7 consecutive days, if the employing motor carrier does not operate CMVs every day of the week; or
- ON DUTY 70 HOURS in any period of 8 consecutive days, if the employing motor carrier operates CMVs every day of the week.
This cap is not one of the three questions asked, but it independently stops the driver from driving and must be tracked alongside them. Notes:
- All on-duty time counts, including work for other employers, whether or not they are motor carriers.
- Section 395.5(b) contains no 34-hour restart. Relief comes only when enough hours age out of the 7- or 8-day window that the driver is back below 60/70 (the FMCSA passenger guide states this expressly: the driver "will not be able to drive again until you have dropped below 60 hours for a 7-consecutive-day period" / "below 70 hours for an 8-consecutive-day period"). The 34-hour restart belongs to the property-carrying rule, 395.3(c). Do not assume it here absent a specific exemption.

=== WHAT DOES NOT APPLY TO THIS DRIVER (common errors) ===
- 11-hour driving limit, 10 consecutive hours off duty, 14-hour window, 30-minute break after 8 cumulative driving hours, and the 34-hour restart: all property-carrying (49 CFR 395.3), not applicable to passenger-carrying operations.
- A 30-minute driving break is not required of passenger-carrier drivers under 395.5.
- The short-haul exception in 395.1(e)(1) (150 air-mile radius, 14-hour duty period) exempts the driver from the record-of-duty-status and related requirements only; it does not raise the 10-hour or 15-hour limits in 395.5.

=== QUALIFICATIONS THAT COULD CHANGE THESE NUMBERS ===
- Sleeper-berth split, 395.1(g)(3): a driver of a passenger-carrying CMV equipped with a sleeper berth may accumulate the equivalent of the 8 consecutive off-duty hours using two sleeper-berth rest periods, if the four conditions of 395.1(g)(3)(i)-(iv) are met. The full text of those four conditions was not in the source passages; confirm them before relying on a split. The equivalent rest total remains 8 hours — it is not a 10-hour split.
- Adverse driving conditions, 395.1(b): may permit a limited extension of driving/duty time to finish the run when the driver unexpectedly encounters adverse conditions and cannot safely complete the run within the limits. Confirm the current scope and the exact extension before relying on it; the standard answer above assumes no such exception.
- Intrastate-only operations: a state's intrastate HOS rules may differ from 395.5. The answers above are the federal interstate rule.
- Carrier policy or a customer/charter contract may impose stricter limits than the federal rule; the stricter limit governs the driver's actual obligation.
- Alaska has separate provisions in Part 395 for certain operations; verify if any part of the run is in Alaska.

=== ENFORCEMENT CONTEXT ===
395.5(a) binds both sides: "No motor carrier shall permit or require any driver used by it to drive ... nor shall any such driver drive." A violation is attributable to the driver and to the carrier, and driving past the 15-hour threshold or the 10-hour driving limit is a common out-of-service trigger. The three figures above (10 / 8 / 15) should be the ones embedded in dispatch software, trip-planning templates, and driver training materials for this operation.

=== ONE-LINE ANSWER ===
A passenger-carrying CMV driver may drive up to 10 hours after 8 consecutive hours off duty, and may not drive after being on duty 15 hours following those 8 consecutive hours off duty — with an additional bar on driving after 60 hours on duty in 7 consecutive days, or 70 hours on duty in 8 consecutive days if the carrier operates CMVs every day of the week (49 CFR 395.5).
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 15 on ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-b/chapter-iii/subchapter-b/part-395 and 10 on ecfr.gov/current/title-49/section-395.5. The first reads: "(i) More than 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off-duty;"

question: M5
answer:
# Flight Attendant Rest After a Scheduled Duty Period of 14 Hours or Less — 14 CFR Part 135

## Answer

| Question | Answer | Authority |
|---|---|---|
| Minimum rest owed after a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less | **9 consecutive hours** | 14 CFR § 135.273(b)(2) |
| Lowest level to which that rest may be reduced | **8 consecutive hours**, conditioned on a subsequent rest of at least 10 consecutive hours | 14 CFR § 135.273(b)(3) |

## Governing rule and why this rule applies to an on-demand operator

§ 135.273 is the flight-attendant duty/rest rule, and it applies across the whole part. § 135.263(e) states: "Section 135.273 prescribes duty period limitations and rest requirements for flight attendants in all operations conducted under this part." That is dispositive for the operation-type question: an on-demand charter operator flying under Subpart E (§ 135.267) is not carved out of § 135.273. Subpart F's flight-time sections (135.265/267/269) govern *flightcrew*; § 135.273 governs *flight attendants* in every operation under Part 135.

## The operative text

**§ 135.273(b)(1)** — baseline duty limit:

> "Except as provided in paragraphs (b)(4), (b)(5), and (b)(6) of this section, no certificate holder may assign a flight attendant to a scheduled duty period of more than 14 hours."

**§ 135.273(b)(2)** — the rest owed:

> "Except as provided in paragraph (b)(3) of this section, a flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less as provided under paragraph (b)(1) of this section must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 9 consecutive hours. This rest period must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period."

**§ 135.273(b)(3)** — the permitted reduction:

> "The rest period required under paragraph (b)(2) of this section may be scheduled or reduced to 8 consecutive hours if the flight attendant is provided a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours; this subsequent rest period must be scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period and must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period."

**§ 135.273(b)(10) and (b)(11)** — the hard edges:

> "(10) No certificate holder may assign a flight attendant any duty period with the certificate holder unless the flight attendant has had at least the minimum rest required under this section."
> "(11) No certificate holder may assign a flight attendant to perform any duty with the certificate holder during any required rest period."

## Conditions attached to the 8-hour reduction — all four must be satisfied

1. **Floor.** 8 consecutive hours is the absolute floor. § 135.273(b)(3) authorizes reduction "to 8 consecutive hours" and no lower. There is no unforeseen-circumstances or in-flight-rest escape from this floor for flight attendants (unlike the flightcrew exceedance relief in § 135.267(e), which is keyed to flight *time* exceedances, not flight-attendant rest).
2. **Compensating rest of at least 10 consecutive hours** must actually be provided — not merely planned.
3. **Timing of the compensating rest:** it must be *scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period*. The clock runs from the **beginning** of the reduced rest, not its end and not the start of the next duty period.
4. **Placement:** both the reduced rest and the compensating rest must fall *between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period*.

Consecutive means consecutive: the 9 (or 8) hours and the 10 hours are unbroken. § 135.273(b)(11) forbids assigning the flight attendant any duty during a required rest period, so the block cannot be interrupted by a phone call, a repositioning leg, or training.

## Worked timeline

Scheduled duty period 07:00–21:00 (14.0 hours, at the (b)(1) ceiling). Rest begins 21:30 after post-flight duties.

- **Full rest (default):** 21:30 → 06:30 next day = 9 consecutive hours. Earliest next duty 06:30.
- **Reduced rest:** 21:30 → 05:30 next day = 8 consecutive hours. Earliest next duty 05:30, **provided** a subsequent rest of at least 10 consecutive hours is scheduled to begin no later than 21:30 the following day (24 hours after 21:30, the start of the reduced rest) and that rest falls between the end of the following duty period and the start of the one after it.

## What this answer is not

- **Not the flightcrew numbers.** §§ 135.265/135.267/135.269 rest figures (e.g., the 10 consecutive hours in § 135.267(d) for on-demand flightcrew, and the 8/9/10-hour reduction ladder in § 135.267(c)) apply to pilots, not flight attendants, unless the operator makes the election below.
- **Not the long-duty numbers.** Paragraphs (b)(4) through (b)(8) address scheduled duty periods exceeding 14 hours and are not reached by this question. In particular, the "reduce to 10 consecutive hours / compensate with 14 consecutive hours" pair in (b)(8), and the 14-hour cap in (b)(9) that rides with that reduction, belong to that longer-duty regime and must not be applied to a ≤14-hour duty period.
- **No reduction for unforeseen circumstances.** § 135.273 contains no counterpart to § 135.267(e)'s exceedance-relief rest ladder. If the duty period runs past 14 hours, the answer is no longer (b)(2)/(b)(3) — it is the (b)(4)–(b)(6) analysis, which is outside this question.

## Election that would change the answer (§ 135.273(c))

A certificate holder may instead apply the *flightcrew* flight-time and rest rules to its flight attendants for all operations under the part, but only if it establishes written procedures that (i) apply to all flight attendants used in its operation, (ii) incorporate the Subpart F flightcrew requirements as appropriate to the operation (in-flight rest facilities not required), (iii) add one flight attendant to the minimum complement for each flightcrew member above the type-certificate minimum assigned under Subpart F, and (iv) are approved by the Administrator and described or referenced in the certificate holder's operations specifications. Absent such an approved, ops-spec-referenced election, the 9/8 answer above governs. If the election *is* in place, the applicable rest is the § 135.267 figure — 10 consecutive hours within the 24 hours preceding planned completion of the assignment — and the reduction ladder would be § 135.267(c)'s, not § 135.273(b)(3)'s.

## Compliance verification checklist for the operator

1. Confirm no § 135.273(c) election appears in the ops specs. If one does, this memo's 9/8 answer does not apply; use the Subpart F figures.
2. Confirm the individual is a flight attendant within the meaning of § 135.273(a) rather than a flightcrew member; if the person is a pilot performing flight-attendant duties, the flightcrew rules govern.
3. Build the rest computation from *scheduled* duty period length (report to release), per (b)(1)/(b)(2); confirm no deadhead or positioning time is being used to inflate the rest block.
4. Log every 8-hour reduction with the paired 10-hour compensating rest, its scheduled start time, and evidence that the start was within 24 hours of the beginning of the reduced rest.
5. Confirm no duty of any kind — including training, administrative work, or positioning — is assigned during a required rest period, per (b)(11).
6. Check any CBA or company manual for a stricter rest minimum; a stricter contractual minimum controls operationally even though the regulation permits 8.
7. Re-verify the rule text against the current eCFR before publication; the citations above are taken from the eCFR text fetched for this analysis (§ 135.273, current as of the fetch date).

The first reads: "(1) A rest required under paragraph (b)(1) of this section may be scheduled for or reduced to a minimum of 8 hours if the flight crewmember is given a rest period of at least 10 hours that must begin no later than 24 hours after the commenc"

# HTTP/2 current specification and its obsoleted RFCs

As-of date for the status statements below: 2026-11-16 (the date the cited RFC Editor / IETF Datatracker pages were retrieved).

## Answer 1 — Current specification of HTTP/2

**RFC 9113, "HTTP/2"** (June 2022), Standards Track, Proposed Standard. Editors: M. Thomson (Mozilla) and C. Benfield (Apple Inc.). Was `draft-ietf-httpbis-http2bis` (HTTPBIS WG). ISSN 2070-1721.

Supporting statements from the authoritative records:
- RFC Editor page for RFC 9113: "RFC 9113: HTTP/2 ... June 2022 ... Proposed Standard".
- RFC Editor page for RFC 7540 (the previous specification) carries the status banner: "This RFC is now obsolete, see RFC 9113." This is the direct evidence that 9113, not 7540, is the current specification.
- Datatracker record for RFC 9113: "RFC 9113 ... Proposed Standard ... June 2022".

Note on maturity: RFC 9113 is a **Proposed Standard**, not an Internet Standard. "Current specification" here means "the RFC that presently specifies HTTP/2", which is 9113; it does not imply Internet Standard maturity.

## Answer 2 — RFCs obsoleted by RFC 9113

RFC 9113 obsoletes exactly two RFCs:

| Obsoleted RFC | Title | Nature of the superseded document |
|---|---|---|
| **RFC 7540** | Hypertext Transfer Protocol Version 2 (HTTP/2) | The original HTTP/2 specification (May 2015; Belshe, Peon, Thomson, Ed.). Superseded in full by RFC 9113. |
| **RFC 8740** | Using TLS 1.3 with HTTP/2 | TLS 1.3 profile for HTTP/2; its content was folded into RFC 9113 (see RFC 9113 Appendix B: "Use of TLS 1.3 was defined based on [RFC8740], which this document obsoletes"). |

Evidence (three independent statements in the primary sources, all in agreement):
1. RFC 9113 document header: `Obsoletes: 7540, 8740`.
2. RFC 9113 abstract: "This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740."
3. Datatracker metadata for RFC 9113: "Obsoletes RFC 8740, RFC 7540".

Provenance caveat: the titles for RFC 7540 and RFC 8740 are the IETF record titles. RFC 7540's title is confirmed verbatim in the fetched RFC Editor page ("RFC 7540: Hypertext Transfer Protocol Version 2 (HTTP/2)"); RFC 8740's title is not quoted in the fetched passages and is supplied from the IETF RFC record — the *number* (8740), which is what the answer turns on, is directly evidenced in all three statements above.

## Citation-ready form

> The current specification of HTTP/2 is RFC 9113 ("HTTP/2", June 2022). It obsoletes RFC 7540 ("Hypertext Transfer Protocol Version 2 (HTTP/2)") and RFC 8740 ("Using TLS 1.3 with HTTP/2").

## Disambiguations a reader will likely need

1. **Obsoletes vs. updates.** These are distinct metadata relations and must not be conflated. RFC 7540's own status banner says both things: "This RFC is now obsolete, see RFC 9113" *and* "This RFC was updated, see RFC 8740." So RFC 8740 was an *update* to RFC 7540, and then RFC 9113 *obsoleted both of them*. Anyone compiling the list from an "Updates" field would produce the wrong set.
2. **What is *not* obsoleted.** RFC 9113's obsoletes header lists only 7540 and 8740. Companion documents such as RFC 7541 (HPACK header compression) do not appear in that header and are therefore not obsoleted by RFC 9113; likewise, RFC 9113 is explicitly "an alternative to, but does not obsolete, the HTTP/1.1 message syntax" (RFC 7540 carried the same statement), and RFC 9113 retains references to RFC 7540 for the deprecated priority scheme semantics (Appendix B). "Obsoletes 7540" is therefore a document-level supersession, not an erasure of every concept RFC 7540 introduced.
3. **Deprecated-but-retained content.** Appendix B of RFC 9113 records that the RFC 7540 priority scheme is deprecated, that the PRIORITY frame and HEADERS priority fields are retained in format only, and that the HTTP/1.1 Upgrade mechanism (and the HTTP2-Settings header field, marked "obsoleted" in Section 11.1) is removed. A reader who needs "what still applies from 7540" must read Appendix B, not just the obsoletes line.
4. **Errata.** RFC 9113 has a published errata page (rfc-editor.org/inline-errata/rfc9113.html). Errata do not change the document's status or its obsoletes list; they are recorded corrections to the text. Nothing in the retrieved records indicates RFC 9113 has itself been obsoleted or replaced, so it remains the current specification as of the as-of date above.
5. **Time sensitivity.** This answer is a snapshot. If a future HTTP/2 revision is published, RFC 9113's status banner will change to point at it (as RFC 7540's now points at RFC 9113). Re-verify against rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113 and datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9113 before relying on this in a document with a long life.

question: M9
answer:
# UK statutory minimum wage rates effective 1 April 2026

## 1. Direct answers

| Ask | Band | Statutory name | Hourly rate from 1 April 2026 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Workers aged 21 and over | National Living Wage (NLW) | **£12.71** |
| 2 | Workers aged 18 to 20 | National Minimum Wage — 18-20 Year Old Rate | **£10.85** |

Both are gross hourly rates in pounds sterling, before tax and National Insurance, applying UK-wide (England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland — the NMW/NLW is a single UK-wide statutory floor with no devolved variation).

## 2. Effective date and legal basis

- The rates take effect on **1 April 2026**, the standard annual uprating date, and replace the rates that applied from 1 April 2025 (£12.21 for 21+, £10.00 for 18-20).
- Legal instrument: the National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026, **SI 2026/357**, which amend the National Minimum Wage Regulations 2015 (SI 2015/621) and come into force on 1 April 2026. The Explanatory Note states:
  - reg. 2(2): national living wage for workers aged 21 or over increased **from £12.21 to £12.71 per hour** (reg. 4 of the 2015 Regulations);
  - reg. 2(3)(a): national minimum wage for workers aged 18 or over but not yet 21 increased **from £10.00 to £10.85 per hour** (reg. 4A(1)(b) of the 2015 Regulations).
- Policy chain: the Low Pay Commission (LPC) submitted its recommendations to the Government on 27 October 2025; the Government accepted them in full and announced the new rates at the Autumn Budget on 26 November 2025; the LPC published its advice on 26 November 2025 and its impact report on 1 April 2026.

## 3. Full rate card for 1 April 2026 (context — only rows 1 and 2 answer the asks)

| NMW rate from April 2026 | Rate | Annual increase (£) | Annual increase (%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| National Living Wage (21 and over) | **£12.71** | £0.50 | 4.1 |
| 18-20 Year Old Rate | **£10.85** | £0.85 | 8.5 |
| 16-17 Year Old Rate | £8.00 | £0.45 | 6.0 |
| Apprentice Rate | £8.00 | £0.45 | 6.0 |
| Accommodation Offset (daily, not hourly) | £11.10 | £0.44 | 4.1 |

Age-threshold history relevant to interpreting the question: NLW covered 25+ before April 2021, 23+ from April 2021, and **21+ from April 2024** — so "21 and over" is the correct band for April 2026. The apprentice rate is a separate band (under 19, or 19+ in the first year of an apprenticeship); an apprentice aged 21 who has completed the first year is entitled to the 21+ NLW of £12.71, not the apprentice rate.

## 4. Verification checks performed

1. **Cross-source agreement (4 independent sources):** gov.uk NMW rates page ('April 2026' row: 21 and over £12.71; 18 to 20 £10.85); LPC report *The National Minimum Wage in 2026* (same two figures); gov.uk *Minimum wage rates for 2026* (LPC advice, published 26 Nov 2025: same two figures); SI 2026/357 Explanatory Note (same two figures, with prior-year baselines). No source in the grounding gives a different April 2026 value.
2. **Arithmetic consistency:** 12.21 + 0.50 = 12.71 ✓; 0.50 ÷ 12.21 = 4.095% ≈ 4.1% ✓. 10.00 + 0.85 = 10.85 ✓; 0.85 ÷ 10.00 = 8.5% ✓. 7.55 + 0.45 = 8.00 ✓; 0.45 ÷ 7.55 = 5.96% ≈ 6.0% ✓.
3. **Date-bound check (the main trap):** the gov.uk rates page also shows an 'April 2027' row (£13.21 / £11.27 / £8.31 / £8.31) and an 'April 2025 to March 2026' row (£12.21 / £10.00 / £7.55 / £7.55). Neither is the answer to an April-2026 question; only the 'April 2026' row is used here, and £13.21 and £12.21 are explicitly excluded from the answers above.
4. **Band-existence check:** the LPC report notes the Government's stated policy is eventually to remove the 18-20 Year Old Rate, but for April 2026 the band is still in force at £10.85 (confirmed by the SI, which amends reg. 4A(1)(b) rather than repealing it). So the question's premise holds for the period asked about.

## 5. Scope, assumptions and exclusions

- **Statutory rates, not the voluntary Real Living Wage.** These are the statutory NLW/NMW under the National Minimum Wage Act 1998 and the 2015 Regulations. The Living Wage Foundation's voluntary 'Real Living Wage' is a different, non-statutory benchmark and is not reported here (no grounded figure for it was available, and it is out of scope of the question).
- **'From April 2026' interpreted as the rates in force from 1 April 2026** — the annual uprating date. There is no mid-year change in the grounding.
- **Gross hourly pay**, not take-home pay; no modelling of tax, NI, pension contributions or salary sacrifice.
- **Compliance mechanics excluded.** What counts as 'working time' for NMW purposes (travel, training, sleep-in shifts, uniforms, deductions, accommodation offset against pay) is a separate question from the headline rate and is not addressed here.
- **No devolved-nation differences** apply to the rate itself.

## 6. How a reviewer re-verifies in two minutes

1. Open gov.uk/national-minimum-wage-rates and read the 'April 2026' row: 21 and over = £12.71; 18 to 20 = £10.85.
2. Open gov.uk/government/publications/minimum-wage-rates-for-2026 (LPC advice, 26 Nov 2025) and confirm the same two figures in its table.
3. Open legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2026/357/note/made and confirm the Explanatory Note's £12.21 → £12.71 and £10.00 → £10.85 wording.

question: M11
answer:
Governing provision: 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1), '150 air-mile radius driver' (current eCFR text, verified against the 2024 govinfo printed CFR). This is the short-haul exception that exempts a qualifying driver from the records-of-duty-status requirements of 395.8 and the ELD requirements of 395.11.

Requested limits:

1. Radius: 150 air miles. The driver must operate within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location. The regulation expresses the unit as air miles and supplies the parenthetical conversion '(172.6 statute miles).' The compliance answer should preserve 'air miles' rather than silently substituting statute miles.

2. Release time: 14 consecutive hours. The driver must return to the work reporting location and be released from work within 14 consecutive hours. This is a maximum duty-period requirement; it is not the 11-hour driving limit and not the separate 14-hour driving window in 395.3.

Both figures apply to the 395.1(e)(1) short-haul exception for property-carrying and passenger-carrying drivers. The distinction between property and passenger operation affects the required off-duty separation: at least 10 consecutive hours off duty for a property-carrying CMV driver, and at least 8 consecutive hours off duty for a passenger-carrying CMV driver, separating each 14 hours on duty.

Companion conditions that determine whether the exception is actually available:
- The driver, except a driver-salesperson, must return to the work reporting location and be released from work within 14 consecutive hours.
- The motor carrier must maintain and retain for 6 months accurate and true time records showing the time the driver reports for duty each day, total hours on duty each day, time released from duty each day, and for drivers used for the first time or intermittently, total time for the preceding 7 days under 395.8(j)(2).
- If the driver exceeds the 150 air-mile radius or is not released within 14 consecutive hours, the exception is lost for that day and a record of duty status is required.
- The separate non-CDL property-carrying exception in 395.1(e)(2) also uses a 150 air-mile radius but has different hour mechanics (14-hour and 16-hour driving cutoffs on 5 and 2 days of a 7-day period); it is not the answer to the general short-haul/RDOS exception asked about here.

Short answer: 150 air miles; 14 consecutive hours.

question: M1
answer:
BASICMED (US) AIRCRAFT LIMITS — CURRENT LAW

Governing authority: 14 CFR § 61.113(i)(1), as amended to implement § 828 ('Expansion of BasicMed') of the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024, Public Law 118-63. The expanded limits apply to operations on or after 12 November 2024. Source of record used here: FAA Notice N 8000.386 (dated 11/14/24), § 5.a, and the FAA BasicMed program page (faa.gov/licenses_certificates/airmen_certification/basic_med).

=== THE THREE LIMITS (answers) ===

1. Maximum takeoff weight: 12,500 lb maximum certificated takeoff weight (MTOW).
2. Occupants: the aircraft may be authorized to carry no more than 7 occupants.
3. Passengers: no more than 6 passengers on board.

Verbatim from FAA Notice N 8000.386, ¶ 5.a(2): 'Per PL 118-63, Section 828, Expansion of BasicMed, the following aircraft limitations will apply on or after November 12, 2024: • The aircraft is authorized to carry no more than seven occupants, • The aircraft has an MTOW of no more than 12,500 pounds, and • The aircraft is operated with no more than six passengers on board.'

Verbatim from the FAA BasicMed page: 'Any aircraft authorized under federal law to carry not more than 7 occupants / Has a maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds / Operating Requirements / Carries not more than six passengers.'

=== HOW THE THREE NUMBERS RELATE (so the limits are applied correctly) ===

- 'Occupants' includes the pilot and any other required flightcrew members. It is a property of the aircraft's authorization (type certificate, STC, amended TC, or experimental operating limitations) — not of who actually shows up.
- 'Passengers' is an operational count for the specific flight and excludes required flightcrew.
- Consequence: with a single-pilot-certificated aircraft, the pilot plus 6 passengers = 7 occupants, which is the maximum case. With an aircraft type certificated for two required pilots, 2 crew + 6 passengers = 8 occupants would exceed the 7-occupant authorization, so the effective passenger count becomes 5. General rule: passengers allowed = min(6, 7 − number of required flightcrew).
- The 12,500 lb figure is the certificated MTOW (the number on the type certificate data sheet / design approval), not the actual takeoff weight on a given day. An aircraft certificated above the limit cannot be brought into compliance by loading it light.

=== CARVE-OUT TO FLAG ===

The 12,500 lb increase excludes transport category helicopters, per the FAA's announcement of the rule change ('Increase the maximum aircraft takeoff weight to 12,500 lbs. from 6,000 lbs., excluding transport category helicopters'). For a transport category helicopter, the applicable BasicMed MTOW limit remains 6,000 lb. If the specific aircraft is a transport category rotorcraft, substitute 6,000 lb for the weight answer above; the occupant (7) and passenger (6) limits are unchanged.

=== STALE-SOURCE WARNING (important) ===

AC 68-1A (dated 5/3/17) and the July/August 2017 FAA Safety Briefing still state the pre-amendment limits: 6,000 lb MTOW, 6 occupants, 5 passengers (e.g., AC 68-1A ¶ 3.2: 'Fly with no more than five passengers... maximum certificated takeoff weight of no more than 6,000 lbs... authorized to carry no more than 6 occupants'). Those figures were correct from 2017 until 11 November 2024 and are now superseded. Do not cite the AC for the numeric limits without checking for its revision; cite § 61.113(i)(1) as amended and Notice N 8000.386.

=== SURROUNDING BASICMED OPERATING LIMITS (context, not part of the three answers) ===

Per § 61.113(i)(2) and the FAA BasicMed page, the flight must be conducted:
- at or below 18,000 ft MSL;
- within the United States, or within another country in which BasicMed is authorized;
- at an indicated airspeed not exceeding 250 knots;
- under VFR or IFR (day or night);
- not for compensation or hire.

Note that the operating limitations attach to the whole flight: a pilot operating under BasicMed may not act as PIC at any point on a flight that exceeds them, even if another pilot on board holds a medical certificate.

=== EXPERIMENTAL / NON-TYPE-CERTIFICATED AIRCRAFT ===

For experimental aircraft, the occupant ceiling is set by § 91.319(j) in addition to the operating limitations issued with the aircraft. AC 68-1A ¶ 5.1.1 describes § 91.319(j) as prohibiting operation under BasicMed carrying more than six occupants — that text predates the 2024 expansion and should be verified against the current § 91.319(j) before being relied on. The safe statement for an experimental aircraft is: it must be authorized (by its operating limitations) for no more than 7 occupants, must not exceed 12,500 lb MTOW, and the flight may carry no more than 6 passengers.

=== COMPARISON ANCHORS ===

- Sport pilot: 1 passenger, 1,320 lb (or 1,430 lb for seaplanes/gliders under the light-sport definition), max 87 kt (or 120 kt clean VH). Not the same regime as BasicMed.
- Third-class medical: no BasicMed-style aircraft weight/occupant/passenger limits and no 18,000 ft / 250 kt / US-only restriction; those limits exist only when exercising BasicMed privileges.

=== ONE-LINE ANSWER ===

Under BasicMed as in force today, a pilot may fly an aircraft with a maximum certificated takeoff weight of 12,500 lb or less, authorized to carry no more than 7 occupants, with no more than 6 passengers on board (transport category helicopters remain limited to 6,000 lb).

question: M3
answer:
HOURS OF SERVICE — PASSENGER-CARRYING COMMERCIAL MOTOR VEHICLE (MOTORCOACH), US INTERSTATE OPERATION
Governing rule: 49 CFR 395.5 (passenger-carrying), subject to the exceptions and exemptions in 49 CFR 395.1.

============================================================
1. ANSWERS
============================================================

| # | Question | Answer | Basis |
|---|----------|--------|-------|
| 1 | How many hours may the driver drive? | 10 hours | 395.5(a)(1) — may not drive more than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty |
| 2 | After how many consecutive hours off duty? | 8 consecutive hours off duty | 395.5(a)(1) and (a)(2) — both the 10-hour and 15-hour limits run from '8 consecutive hours off duty' |
| 3 | After how many hours on duty may the driver no longer drive? | 15 hours on duty | 395.5(a)(2) — no driving for any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty |

Plain statement: A motorcoach driver must take 8 consecutive hours off duty, may then drive no more than 10 hours, and may not drive at all once 15 hours of on-duty time have elapsed since the end of that 8-hour off-duty period — whichever limit is reached first.

============================================================
2. REGULATORY TEXT RELIED ON
============================================================

49 CFR 395.5 (eCFR / govinfo CFR-2025-title49-vol5, as fetched):

  'Subject to the exceptions and exemptions in Sec. 395.1:
   (a) No motor carrier shall permit or require any driver used by it to drive a
   passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle, nor shall any such driver drive a
   passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle:
     (1) More than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty; or
     (2) For any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive
     hours off duty.
   (b) ... for any period after -
     (1) Having been on duty 60 hours in any 7 consecutive days if the employing
     motor carrier does not operate commercial motor vehicles every day of the week; or
     (2) Having been on duty 70 hours in any period of 8 consecutive days if the
     employing motor carrier operates commercial motor vehicles every day of the week.'
   [70 FR 50073, Aug. 25, 2005]

FMCSA, 'Hours of Service for Motor Carriers of Passengers' (carrier-safety page, as fetched), restates the same three figures: 'More than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty'; 'For any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty'; and the 60-in-7 / 70-in-8 on-duty caps.
FMCSA Motor Carrier Safety Planner 6.4.3 (as fetched) restates: '8 consecutive hours off duty prior to starting a shift'; '10-Hour Limit'; '15-Hour Limit'; '60 and 70-Hour Limits.'

============================================================
3. CORRECTION OF A PLAN-PHASE ASSUMPTION (must be fixed before publication)
============================================================
The plan context states, as an assumption, 'driving permitted after 10 consecutive hours off duty.' That is the PROPERTY-carrying rule (49 CFR 395.3(a)(2): 11 hours driving within a 14-hour window after 10 consecutive hours off duty). It is NOT the passenger-carrying rule. Every primary and secondary source fetched for passenger-carrying vehicles says 8 consecutive hours off duty and a 15-hour on-duty window.
  Wrong: 10 consecutive off-duty hours, 11-hour drive limit, 14-hour window.
  Right: 8 consecutive off-duty hours, 10-hour drive limit, 15-hour on-duty window (49 CFR 395.5).
Do not carry the property-carrier figures into a motorcoach answer; the two are different subsections of Part 395 and the difference is 2 hours of off-duty time and 1 hour of driving.

============================================================
4. HOW THE THREE LIMITS INTERACT
============================================================
- One 8-hour off-duty period starts both clocks: the 10-hour driving allowance and the 15-hour on-duty window.
- The 15-hour window is a wall clock on on-duty time, not on driving time. Once 15 hours of on-duty time have elapsed since the end of the 8-hour off-duty period, driving is prohibited even if fewer than 10 hours of driving have been used. The remaining driving hours are simply lost.
- Driving is capped at 10 hours regardless of how much window remains; a driver who reaches 10 driving hours at hour 9 of the window also stops.
- Non-driving on-duty work (loading, inspections, paperwork, passenger assistance, a second job of any kind) consumes window time without consuming driving time, which is how a driver can hit 15 hours with driving hours left over.
- Both limits reset only when 8 consecutive hours off duty are completed.

Worked example (arithmetic verified):
  06:00  on duty; 8 consecutive hours off duty completed just before 06:00
  06:00-09:00  driving            3.0 h  (driving 3.0 / window 3.0)
  09:00-11:00  on duty, not driving 2.0 h (driving 3.0 / window 5.0)
  11:00-14:00  driving            3.0 h  (driving 6.0 / window 8.0)
  14:00-18:00  on duty, not driving 4.0 h (driving 6.0 / window 12.0)
  18:00-20:00  driving            2.0 h  (driving 8.0 / window 14.0)
  21:00  on-duty window expires (06:00 + 15 h). Driving prohibited from 21:00
         onward even though 2.0 of the 10 driving hours remain unused.
  21:00  start 8 consecutive hours off duty -> may drive again at 05:00 next day
         (21:00 + 8 h = 05:00).
  Checks: driving 3+3+2 = 8 <= 10 OK; on-duty total by 20:00 = 14 <= 15 OK;
  reset interval = 8 h = the stated off-duty requirement OK.

============================================================
5. ADDITIONAL LIMITS THAT BIND (reported for completeness)
============================================================
- Weekly on-duty cap (395.5(b)): 60 hours on duty in any 7 consecutive days if the carrier does not operate CMVs every day of the week; 70 hours on duty in any 8 consecutive days if the carrier operates CMVs every day of the week. No driving after the cap is reached, regardless of the 10- and 15-hour status.
- Multiple-employer drivers: all on-duty time for every carrier, and all compensated work for any employer, counts toward the 60/70 totals (395.8(j) and FMCSA passenger guidance).
- Record of duty status / ELD: drivers required to keep RODS are generally subject to the ELD rule; the FMCSA passenger page lists narrow ELD exceptions (e.g., RODS required no more than 8 days in any 30-day period).

============================================================
6. WHAT CHANGES THE NUMBERS, AND WHAT DOES NOT
============================================================
CHANGES THE NUMBERS:
- Alaska: 49 CFR 395.1(b)(1)-(3) substitutes different limits for CMV operation in Alaska (for property-carrying: 15 h driving after 10 consecutive hours off duty, no driving after 20 hours on duty, 70/7 and 80/8 on-duty caps; adverse driving conditions allow completing the run, followed by 10 consecutive hours off duty for property-carrying and 8 consecutive hours for passenger-carrying drivers). If the motorcoach operates in Alaska, that section must be applied instead.
- Adverse driving conditions, 395.1(b)(2): the 10-hour and 15-hour limits do not apply while completing the run in adverse conditions; the weekly 60/70 caps still apply; the driver must then take 8 consecutive hours off duty before driving again.
- Intrastate operation within a single state: state law governs and may differ from Part 395. This answer assumes interstate operation.
- Short-haul / 150 air-mile exception, 395.1(e): for passenger-carrying operations this relieves the record-of-duty-status requirement (within 150 air miles of the normal work reporting location and released within 14 consecutive hours); it is a paperwork/ELD relief, not a licence to exceed the 10/8/15 limits.
- Split sleeper berth, 395.1(g)(3): a driver in a sleeper-berth-equipped passenger-carrying CMV may accumulate the equivalent of 8 consecutive hours off duty using two rest periods meeting the four conditions of 395.1(g)(3)(i)-(iv). The exact arithmetic must be modelled in the carrier's ELD configuration; the underlying requirement being satisfied is still 8 hours.

DOES NOT CHANGE THE NUMBERS:
- The property-carrier 11-hour/14-hour/10-consecutive-hour rules do not apply to passenger-carrying vehicles.
- The 30-minute break requirement (395.3(a)(3)(ii)) is a property-carrying provision; passenger-carrying drivers have no equivalent break rule under 395.5.
- The 34-hour restart: 395.5 contains no restart paragraph, and the restart in 395.3(c) is written for property-carrying operations. Do not present a 34-hour restart as a passenger-carrier entitlement; the 60/70-hour totals roll off day by day on the 7/8-consecutive-day basis. Treat any carrier practice of applying a 34-hour reset to motorcoach drivers as a policy choice to be confirmed with counsel or FMCSA guidance, not as a regulatory right.

============================================================
7. VERIFICATION CHECKLIST (log/ELD audit procedure)
============================================================
Run these deterministic checks on any 24-hour-plus duty cycle for a passenger-carrying driver:
1. OFF-DUTY RESET: locate each qualifying 8-consecutive-hour off-duty (or 395.1(g)(3)-equivalent) interval. FAIL if driving occurs without a preceding qualifying 8-hour interval.
2. DRIVE CAP: sum driving time between consecutive qualifying 8-hour intervals. FAIL if sum > 10.0 h.
3. WINDOW CAP: elapsed time from start of on-duty (after the qualifying 8-hour interval) to last driving segment. FAIL if any driving occurs at or after the 15th hour.
4. INTERACTION: FAIL any cycle where driving time <= 10 h but driving occurs past hour 15, or where window < 15 h but driving > 10 h.
5. WEEKLY CAP: rolling 7-day on-duty sum vs 60 h (carrier not operating every day) or rolling 8-day sum vs 70 h (carrier operating every day). FAIL on exceedance.
6. NON-DRIVING ON-DUTY TIME: confirm on-duty-not-driving entries (inspections, loading, passenger assistance, second employment) are captured; missing entries systematically overstate available window.
7. JURISDICTION: confirm the vehicle did not operate in Alaska (395.1(b)) and that operation is interstate; if either is false, re-evaluate against the applicable rule set.
8. DOCUMENTATION: confirm RODS/ELD status and any 395.1(e) short-haul relief is properly claimed.

============================================================
8. SCOPE NOTE
============================================================
These figures are the federal interstate limits for passenger-carrying CMVs under 49 CFR 395.5. They assume the driver is not covered by an exemption in 395.1 and is not operating in Alaska. A state-only (intrastate) motorcoach operation may be governed by different state limits and must be checked separately against that state's statute or regulation.
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 10 on ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-b/chapter-iii/subchapter-b/part-395/subpart-a/section-395.5 and 15 on ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-b/chapter-iii/subchapter-b/part-395/subpart-a. The first reads: "(1) More than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty;"

Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 10 on ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-b/chapter-iii/subchapter-b/part-395/subpart-a and 8 on ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-b/chapter-iii/part-395. The first reads: "(A) More than 15 hours following 10 consecutive hours off-duty;"

question: M5
answer:
# Flight attendant rest after a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less — 14 CFR Part 135

## 1. Short answers

| Ask | Answer | Authority |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Rest required after a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less | **at least 9 consecutive hours** | 14 CFR 135.273(b)(2) |
| 2. Rest may be reduced to | **8 consecutive hours**, but only if a subsequent rest period of **at least 10 consecutive hours** is given, beginning **no later than 24 hours** after the beginning of the reduced rest period | 14 CFR 135.273(b)(3) |

Both figures are consecutive-hour blocks that must fall between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.

## 2. The rule text relied on

14 CFR 135.273(b) — Flight attendant requirements (quoted as fetched from eCFR / GovInfo, current title 14):

> (1) Except as provided in paragraphs (b)(4), (b)(5), and (b)(6) of this section, no certificate holder may assign a flight attendant to a scheduled duty period of more than 14 hours.
>
> (2) Except as provided in paragraph (b)(3) of this section, a flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less as provided under paragraph (b)(1) of this section must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 9 consecutive hours. This rest period must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.
>
> (3) The rest period required under paragraph (b)(2) of this section may be scheduled or reduced to 8 consecutive hours if the flight attendant is provided a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours; this subsequent rest period must be scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period and must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.
>
> (10) No certificate holder may assign a flight attendant any duty period with the certificate holder unless the flight attendant has had at least the minimum rest required under this section.
>
> (11) No certificate holder may assign a flight attendant to perform any duty with the certificate holder during any required rest period.

Related provisions that must be applied alongside, not instead of, the 9/8 figures:

- **135.273(b)(13):** each certificate holder must relieve each flight attendant engaged in air transportation from all further duty for **at least 24 consecutive hours during any 7 consecutive calendar days**. Reduced rest under (b)(3) does not displace this.
- **135.273(b)(14):** a flight attendant is not considered scheduled for duty in excess of the duty-period limitations if the flights were scheduled and normally terminate within the limitations but, due to circumstances beyond the control of the certificate holder (e.g., adverse weather), were not at departure expected to reach their destination within the scheduled time.
- **135.273(c):** the alternative compliance election — see section 6, which is the only condition that changes the answers.

## 3. How to apply it — decision procedure

1. **Establish that the person is a flight attendant under the certificate.** 135.273 is the flight attendant rule; it is not keyed to scheduled vs. on-demand, so an on-demand charter operator using cabin crew is inside it. (Pilot/flight-crewmember rest for non-scheduled operations sits in 135.267; do not apply 135.267's 10-hour figure to a flight attendant unless the (c) election in section 6 has been made.)
2. **Determine the *scheduled* duty period length (report-to-release), not the actual.** (b)(2) and (b)(3) are keyed to the scheduled duty period. Apply (b)(14) if the actual exceeded the schedule for reasons beyond the certificate holder's control.
3. **If the scheduled duty period is 14.0 hours or less → schedule at least 9 consecutive hours of rest** between completion of that duty period and the start of the next one. Fourteen hours exactly is inside this row; the text says "14 hours or less."
4. **If you want to shorten it → you may go to 8 consecutive hours only**, and only by also scheduling the compensatory rest: at least 10 consecutive hours, starting no later than 24 hours after the start of the reduced rest, located between completion of the scheduled duty period and the start of the subsequent duty period. If the 10-hour block cannot be guaranteed at the time the 8-hour block is scheduled, the reduction is not available and the 9-hour figure stands.
5. **Prohibit anything during the rest block** (b)(11): no duty, no call-out, no training, no positioning, no administrative assignment inside the 9 (or 8) hours.
6. **Check the 24-in-7 separately** (b)(13) before publishing the pairing.
7. **Compare with company minimums.** The Operations Manual or a collective bargaining agreement may be more restrictive; the rule figures above are the regulatory floor, not a ceiling.

## 4. Worked example (arithmetic check)

Scheduled duty period 06:00-20:00 local = 14.0 h (inside the (b)(2) row).

- **Base case:** rest must be at least 9 consecutive hours. Earliest legal next report if rest starts at 20:30 = **05:30** the following day (20:30 + 9:00).
- **Reduced case:** rest scheduled 21:00-05:00 = 8 consecutive hours. The 10-hour compensatory rest must *begin* no later than 21:00 the next day (24 hours after 21:00 on day 1). It must be at least 10 consecutive hours and must sit between the end of the scheduled duty period and the start of the subsequent duty period. So the duty period following the 8-hour rest must be built to end early enough that a 10-hour block can start by 21:00 the next day; if it cannot, the 8-hour option is unavailable.
- **Interaction check:** 8 < 9 (reduction is downward only) and 10 > 8 (the payback exceeds the reduction) — both consistent with the rule's structure.

## 5. Boundary table — do not cross the rows

| Scheduled duty period | Required rest | May be reduced to | Compensatory rest and deadline |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **14 hours or less** | **9 consecutive hours** — 135.273(b)(2) | **8 consecutive hours** — 135.273(b)(3) | **at least 10 consecutive hours**, starting no later than **24 hours** after the start of the reduced rest |
| More than 14 hours (extended duty period authorized under (b)(4)-(b)(6)) | **12 consecutive hours** — 135.273(b)(7) | **10 consecutive hours** — 135.273(b)(8) | **at least 14 consecutive hours**, starting no later than **24 hours** after the start of the reduced rest; plus (b)(9): no duty period of more than 14 hours during the 24-hour period beginning at the start of the reduced rest |

The second row is shown only so the first row is not misapplied. The 9/8 pair answers only scheduled duty periods of 14 hours or less. The extended-duty authorizations in (b)(4)-(b)(6) require additional flight attendants to be assigned and are outside the scope of this question; the operator must read (b)(4)-(b)(6) in full before using any duty period above 14 hours.

## 6. The one condition that changes the answer

135.273(c) allows a certificate holder to apply the **flight-crewmember** flight-time, duty and rest requirements of Part 135 to flight attendants for all operations under Part 135, provided it establishes written procedures that apply to all flight attendants used in its operation (and meets the remaining (c) conditions). If — and only if — that election is in place, the rest is keyed to **scheduled flight time**, not to duty period length (135.267(b)/(c) as fetched):

- 9 consecutive hours for less than 8 hours of scheduled flight time;
- 10 consecutive hours for 8 or more but less than 9 hours;
- 11 consecutive hours for 9 or more hours;

reducible respectively to 8, 8 and 9 hours, each with its own compensatory rest of 10, 11 and 12 hours beginning no later than 24 hours after the commencement of the reduced rest.

Unless the operator's manual contains that written (c) election, the answers in section 1 govern. If the operator has made the election, the answer to Ask 1 becomes a flight-time-keyed 9/10/11 hours and the answer to Ask 2 becomes 8/8/9 hours — the operator should confirm its election status before publishing either figure in a manual.

## 7. Common errors this answer guards against

- **Applying the pilot 10-hour figure (135.267) to a flight attendant** without a (c) election. Wrong rule, wrong number.
- **Treating 14 hours as the first extended-duty row.** The text says "14 hours or less," so 14.0 h gets 9 hours, not 12.
- **Reading the 24 hours as a rest length.** It is the deadline for *starting* the 10-hour compensatory rest, measured from the *beginning of the reduced rest period*, not from the end of duty.
- **Taking the 8-hour reduction without scheduling the 10-hour payback.** (b)(3) is conditional; without the subsequent 10-hour block, the minimum is 9.
- **Assuming the 24-in-7 relief (b)(13) substitutes for the daily rest.** It is cumulative.
- **Assuming an OpSpecs can lower the figure.** Part 135 operations specifications do not waive 135.273 rest minimums; relief would require a separately granted exemption or deviation authority, which the operator must be able to produce.

## 8. Compliance record to keep

For each pairing, record: scheduled duty period start/end; the rest block start/end and its length (9 or 8); where the 8-hour reduction is used, the scheduled start and end of the 10-hour compensatory rest and proof it begins within 24 hours of the reduced rest's start; and the rolling 24-consecutive-hours-in-7-calendar-days relief. These entries are what demonstrates compliance with 135.273(b)(2), (b)(3), (b)(10) and (b)(11) on inspection.

question: M7
answer:
# Current HTTP/2 specification and its obsoleted RFCs

## Answer

1. **Current specification of HTTP/2: RFC 9113**, "HTTP/2", Proposed Standard, published June 2022, editors M. Thomson (Mozilla) and C. Benfield (Apple Inc.), stream = IETF, WG = HTTP (httpbis), derived from draft-ietf-httpbis-http2bis-07, DOI 10.17487/RFC9113, 78 pages.
2. **RFC 9113 obsoletes: RFC 7540 and RFC 8740** — exactly two documents, no others.

## Evidence for ask 1 (which RFC is current)

The decisive point is that RFC 7540 is no longer current: it has itself been superseded. Three independent primary sources agree.

| Source | Quoted evidence |
|---|---|
| RFC 9113 title block (datatracker HTML) | `RFC: 9113` / `Obsoletes: 7540, 8740` / `Category: Standards Track` / `Published: June 2022` |
| RFC Editor metadata (rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.json) | `doc_id: RFC9113`, `title: HTTP/2`, `pub_status: PROPOSED STANDARD`, `pub_date: June 2022`, `obsoletes: RFC7540`, `obsoletes: RFC8740`, `doi: 10.17487/RFC9113` |
| RFC Editor HTTP/2 subject page | RFC 7540 entry carries `Obsoleted by RFC 9113`; RFC 8740 entry carries `Obsoleted by RFC 9113` |

RFC 9113's abstract states its scope directly: *"This specification describes an optimized expression of the semantics of the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP), referred to as HTTP version 2 (HTTP/2)."* Its status-of-memo block confirms *"This is an Internet Standards Track document."*

No RFC published after RFC 9113 (June 2022) appears in the retrieved material as obsoleting it, so RFC 9113 is the current specification as of the retrieval date, 2026-11-16.

## Evidence for ask 2 (what it obsoletes)

RFC 9113's own "Obsoletes" header names two documents, and the body text repeats it verbatim:

> "This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740."

- **RFC 7540** — "Hypertext Transfer Protocol Version 2 (HTTP/2)", Belshe, Peon, Thomson, May 2015, Proposed Standard. The original HTTP/2 specification. Its own abstract notes it is "an alternative to, but does not obsolete, the HTTP/1.1 message syntax"; it is now marked "Obsoleted by RFC 9113".
- **RFC 8740** — "Using TLS 1.3 with HTTP/2", D. Benjamin, February 2020, Proposed Standard. This was an *Updates: 7540* document that forbade TLS 1.3 post-handshake authentication. Because it amended RFC 7540 rather than replacing it, RFC 9113 has to obsolete it as well as 7540 in order to fold that restriction into a single consolidated specification. It too is now marked "Obsoleted by RFC 9113".

## Scope decisions (stated so the answer is unambiguous)

- **"Current" = the latest IETF Standards Track RFC that specifies HTTP/2, as of the retrieval date.** Drafts (e.g., draft-ietf-httpbis-http2bis-07, the precursor of RFC 9113) and non-standards documents are excluded.
- **"Obsoletes" = the documents named in RFC 9113's `Obsoletes:` header only.** Documents that RFC 9113 *updates* or that merely reference/extend HTTP/2 are deliberately excluded from the list above. For completeness, these are **not** obsoleted by RFC 9113 and remain in force alongside it:
  - RFC 7541 (HPACK), RFC 8441 (Bootstrapping WebSockets with HTTP/2), RFC 8336 (ORIGIN frame), RFC 8164 (Opportunistic Security for HTTP/2), and the HTTP semantics/caching documents RFC 9110 / RFC 9111 published in the same cycle.
  - If a requester wants the *updates* relation instead, RFC 9113's header does not declare one; the `Obsoletes` and `Updates` headers are distinct and must not be conflated.
- **Errata are not part of the RFC number answer.** RFC 9113 has an errata page (`https://www.rfc-editor.org/errata/rfc9113`); errata correct text within RFC 9113 and do not change which RFC is current or what it obsoletes. Anyone relying on the text operationally should check that page for verified errata before implementation.

## How to re-verify (authoritative check)

1. Fetch `https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.json` and read the `obsoletes` fields — expect `RFC7540` and `RFC8740`, and nothing else.
2. Fetch `https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc7540` and `https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8740`; each should display "Obsoleted by RFC 9113". If either shows no successor, or if RFC 9113 itself later shows "Obsoleted by", the answer has changed and must be revised.
3. Confirm RFC 9113's status is still "Proposed Standard" and that no later Standards Track RFC (an Internet Standard elevation, or a further revision) has superseded it.

## One-line answer

**RFC 9113 is the current HTTP/2 specification; it obsoletes RFC 7540 and RFC 8740.**

question: M9
answer:
# UK statutory minimum wage rates effective 1 April 2026

## Direct answers

| # | Ask | Rate from 1 April 2026 | Previous rate (to 31 Mar 2026) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **National Living Wage (NLW), workers aged 21 and over** | **£12.71 per hour** (gross) | £12.21 | +£0.50 (+4.1%) |
| 2 | **National Minimum Wage (NMW), 18–20 Year Old Rate** | **£10.85 per hour** (gross) | £10.00 | +£0.85 (+8.5%) |

Both figures are **statutory** rates set by HM Government under the National Minimum Wage Act 1998, are **gross** (before tax and National Insurance), and apply UK-wide to England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland. They took effect on **1 April 2026**, the standard annual uprating date, and remain in force until 31 March 2027.

## Full April 2026 rate table (for context and to prevent band confusion)

| Band | Rate from 1 Apr 2026 | Annual increase |
|---|---|---|
| National Living Wage (21 and over) | £12.71 | +£0.50 (4.1%) |
| 18–20 Year Old Rate | £10.85 | +£0.85 (8.5%) |
| 16–17 Year Old Rate | £8.00 | +£0.45 (6.0%) |
| Apprentice Rate | £8.00 | +£0.45 (6.0%) |
| Accommodation Offset (per day) | £11.10 | +£0.44 (4.1%) |

## Statutory basis

**The National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026, SI 2026/357.** Made 19 March 2026; coming into force 1 April 2026; extends to England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland. Signed by Kate Dearden, Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State, Department for Business and Trade.

The instrument amends the National Minimum Wage Regulations 2015 (SI 2015/621) as follows:

- **Regulation 2(2)** — in regulation 4 (the national living wage), for "£12.21" substitute **"£12.71"**. *Explanatory note: "increases the rate of the national living wage for workers who are aged 21 or over from £12.21 to £12.71 per hour".*
- **Regulation 2(3)(a)** — in regulation 4A(1)(b), for "£10.00" substitute **"£10.85"**. *Explanatory note: "increases the rate of the national minimum wage for workers who are aged 18 or over (but not yet aged 21) from £10.00 to £10.85 per hour".*
- Regulation 2(3)(b) — reg 4A(1)(c) (under 18): £7.55 → £8.00.
- Regulation 2(3)(c) — reg 4A(1)(d) (apprentice rate): £7.55 → £8.00.
- Regulation 2(4) — reg 16(1) (accommodation offset): £10.66 → £11.10 per day.

The age-band structure itself is **not** changed by this instrument: the NLW continues to attach to regulation 4 (age 21 and over) and the 18–20 rate to regulation 4A(1)(b).

## Timeline and status

- **October 2025** — Low Pay Commission recommends the 2026 rates.
- **26 November 2025** — Government announces the increases; LPC publishes *Minimum wage rates for 2026*, stating the Government accepted the LPC's recommendations in full. (Announcement stage.)
- **19 March 2026** — SI 2026/357 made. (Legal certainty stage.)
- **1 April 2026** — SI 2026/357 in force; rates legally binding. (In-force stage.)
- **1 April 2026** — LPC publishes *The National Minimum Wage in 2026*, confirming the operative table.

These are therefore **confirmed, in-force** rates as at the retrieval date (16 November 2026), not forecasts or projections.

## Disambiguation — this is NOT the "Real Living Wage"

The figures above are the **statutory National Living Wage** (a legal minimum enforced by HMRC and payable by all employers covered by the NMW). They are **not** the **Living Wage Foundation's "Real Living Wage"**, which is a separate, voluntary benchmark calculated by the Resolution Foundation and accredited by the Living Wage Foundation, with different (higher) rates and a separate, non-April announcement cycle. Requests for "the UK living wage" routinely conflate the two; the sourcing here (legislation.gov.uk and GOV.UK) settles it on the statutory side.

## Scope notes

1. **No devolved variation.** Minimum wage is a reserved matter. The SI expressly extends to England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, and there are no separate Scottish, Welsh or Northern Irish statutory minimum wage rates. (The voluntary Real Living Wage does publish a separate London rate, which is a further reason not to conflate the two.)
2. **Apprentices are an exception to the age bands.** An apprentice aged 21+ is entitled to £12.71 only if they are 19 or over **and** have completed the first year of their apprenticeship. Otherwise (under 19, or 19+ in the first year) the Apprentice Rate of £8.00 applies — including for a 21-year-old in year one.
3. **Accommodation offset** is £11.10 per day (£77.70 per week on a seven-day basis) — the maximum an employer may charge for living accommodation before the deduction breaches NMW.
4. **Gross, hourly, cash pay.** Rates are gross hourly cash pay; the NMW/NLW calculation rules on what counts as pay, deductions, salary sacrifice, uniforms, tips and unpaid working time are outside the scope of this rate answer but govern compliance.
5. **Forward look.** GOV.UK already lists the April 2027 row (21+ £13.21; 18–20 £11.27; under 18 and apprentice £8.31). Those are **not** the rates asked for and do not apply before 1 April 2027. The LPC report also notes government policy to eventually remove the 18–20 Year Old Rate; that policy is **not** in force for April 2026 and does not alter £10.85.

## Worked check

A 21-year-old working 37.5 hours per week at exactly the NLW earns 37.5 × £12.71 = **£476.63** gross per week. An 18-year-old on the same hours at the 18–20 rate earns 37.5 × £10.85 = **£406.88** gross per week. The differential (37.5 × £1.86 = £69.75) is the remaining gap between the adult and young-worker rates, which the 8.5% uplift to the 18–20 rate is deliberately narrowing.

## Sources

1. *The National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026*, SI 2026/357 — https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2026/357/made/data.html (made 19 Mar 2026; in force 1 Apr 2026). Primary legislation source.
2. GOV.UK, *National Minimum Wage rates* — https://www.gov.uk/national-minimum-wage-rates (April 2026 row: 21 and over £12.71; 18 to 20 £10.85).
3. Low Pay Commission, *The National Minimum Wage in 2026* — https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-national-minimum-wage-in-2026 (published 1 April 2026).
4. Low Pay Commission, *Minimum wage rates for 2026* — https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/minimum-wage-rates-for-2026 (published 26 November 2025; announcement of the accepted recommendations).

All sources retrieved 2026-11-16 and mutually consistent to the penny on both figures requested.

answer:
FMCSA short-haul exception (RODS exemption) — current 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)

Direct answers:
1. Radius: 150 air miles (172.6 statute miles) from the normal work reporting location. Citation: 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)(i).
2. Release: within 14 consecutive hours. Citation: 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)(ii). The driver must return to the work reporting location and be released from work within that 14-consecutive-hour period.

How to apply the two figures:
- Measure the radius in air miles, not road miles. The regulation itself equates the 150 air-mile radius to 172.6 statute miles.
- The 14-hour clock runs from the time the driver comes on duty. The driver must both return to the work reporting location and be released from work by the end of the 14th consecutive hour.
- The 14-hour figure is a duty-period/release limit, not a 14-hour driving limit.
- The regulatory text excepts a driver-salesperson from the return-and-release condition in (e)(1)(ii); the other conditions of the exception still need to be checked.

Companion conditions — the two figures alone do not complete the exemption:
- Property-carrying driver: at least 10 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty. Passenger-carrying driver: at least 8 consecutive hours off-duty. 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)(iii).
- The motor carrier must maintain and retain for 6 months accurate and true time records showing the time the driver reports for duty, total on-duty hours, time released from duty, and, for new or intermittent drivers, total time for the preceding 7 days. 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)(iv).
- The exception exempts the driver from the record-of-duty-status requirement in 395.8 and the supporting-documents requirement in 395.11. If the driver exceeds the 150 air-mile radius or is not returned to the work reporting location and released within 14 consecutive hours, the exception is unavailable for that day and the driver must record duty status (paper RODS or ELD) for the day.

Scope and distinction notes:
- Both figures are the same for property-carrying and passenger-carrying drivers under (e)(1); only the required off-duty hours differ.
- Do not confuse this with 395.1(e)(2), the non-CDL property-carrying exception. It also uses a 150 air-mile radius, but it limits driving after the 14th hour on 5 days and after the 16th hour on 2 days of any period of 7 consecutive days; it is a separate exception.
- Do not confuse this with 395.1(p), the motion picture production exception, which uses a 100 air-mile radius.
- The current 150-air-mile/14-hour figures reflect the 2020 hours-of-service final rule. For a historical date before that rule's effective date, verify the version then in effect; older short-haul rules used 100 air miles and 12 hours. The answer above is for current operations under the cited eCFR text.

question: M1
answer:
BASICMED AIRCRAFT LIMITS (US, 14 CFR 61.113(i)(1), as amended by Section 828 of the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024, Pub. L. 118-63, effective for operations on or after November 12, 2024)

ANSWERS
1. Maximum takeoff weight: 12,500 lb. The aircraft must have a maximum takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds. This is the aircraft's certificated/design-approval maximum takeoff weight for type-certificated aircraft (or the operator-established maximum for experimental aircraft), not the actual ramp or takeoff weight of the flight. An aircraft whose approved maximum takeoff weight exceeds 12,500 lb does not qualify, even if flown light.
2. Occupants the aircraft may be authorized to carry: 7. The aircraft must be authorized to carry not more than 7 occupants, counting required flightcrew members. This is a characteristic of the aircraft (its type certificate, supplemental type certificate, amended TC, or equivalent authorization for experimental aircraft), not the number of seats installed. An aircraft certificated for 8 or more occupants does not qualify even if only 7 seats are fitted; conversely, an aircraft originally certificated above the limit that is altered under a new design approval (STC/ATC) to 7 or fewer occupants does qualify.
3. Passengers on board: 6. The flight must be operated with no more than 6 passengers on board. Passengers are the occupants other than the pilot in command and any other required flightcrew members; hence 6 passengers + 1 pilot = the 7-occupant ceiling. If the aircraft is type certificated for two required pilots, the operating ceiling is 4 passengers plus the 2 required flightcrew members, but the regulatory maximum number of passengers remains 6.

GOVERNING TEXT
14 CFR 61.113(i)(1) as revised by the November 18, 2024 final rule (FR 2024-26935): 'The aircraft is authorized to carry not more than 7 occupants, has a maximum takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds, is operated with no more than 6 passengers on board, and is not a [transport category rotorcraft certificated under part 29].' The final rule also amended 49 U.S.C. 44703 note (FESSA sec. 2307(j)) to raise the covered-aircraft occupant limit from 6 to 7 and the weight limit from 6,000 lb to 12,500 lb, and added the exclusion for transport category rotorcraft certificated under part 29. Section 91.319(j) imposes the same 7-occupant ceiling on experimental aircraft operated under BasicMed. FAA Notice N 8000.386 (11/14/24) states the new aircraft limitations apply on or after November 12, 2024: 'authorized to carry no more than seven occupants,' 'MTOW of no more than 12,500 pounds,' 'operated with no more than six passengers on board.' The current FAA BasicMed page states the same: 'Any aircraft authorized under federal law to carry not more than 7 occupants; Has a maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds; Carries not more than six passengers.'

SUPERSEDED FIGURES (do not use for current flights)
Before November 12, 2024 the limits were 6,000 lb maximum takeoff weight, 6 occupants authorized, 5 passengers on board. These are the figures in AC 68-1A (dated 5/3/17) and the July/August 2017 FAA Safety Briefing, and they remain correct only for flights conducted before that date. AC 68-1A has not been read as current authority here; where it conflicts with the 2024 rule text and the current FAA BasicMed page, the rule text and current page control.

INTERPRETATION NOTES (matters that are easy to conflate with the three figures)
- 'Authorized to carry' = the occupant capacity in the aircraft's design approval, not seats installed and not persons actually on board. Confirm via the Type Certificate Data Sheet (or STC/ATC, or the experimental operating limitations).
- The weight test is the aircraft's maximum takeoff weight, not the planned or actual takeoff weight.
- The 7-occupant and 12,500-lb limits and the 6-passenger limit apply to the entire flight, takeoff to touchdown; if the flight exceeds any of them, a BasicMed pilot may not act as PIC at any point on it, even while another pilot with a medical certificate is acting as PIC.
- Adjacent BasicMed aircraft/operation limits not asked but commonly bundled: no flight for compensation or hire; within the United States (or a country where BasicMed is authorized); at or below 18,000 ft MSL; indicated airspeed not more than 250 knots; transport category rotorcraft certificated under part 29 are excluded.

CAVEAT ON EDITION
If the question is being asked about a flight that occurred before November 12, 2024, the applicable figures are 6,000 lb / 6 occupants / 5 passengers; for any flight on or after that date the figures are 12,500 lb / 7 occupants / 6 passengers as stated in the answers above.
