question: M3
answer:
US FEDERAL HOURS-OF-SERVICE LIMITS — DRIVER OF A PASSENGER-CARRYING COMMERCIAL MOTOR VEHICLE (MOTORCOACH)

GOVERNING RULE: 49 CFR § 395.5, 'Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles' (Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration), made 'Subject to the exceptions and exemptions in § 395.1.' This is the passenger-carrying ruleset, NOT the property-carrying ruleset in § 395.3.

DIRECT ANSWERS

1) Maximum driving: 10 hours. § 395.5(a)(1) — no carrier may permit or require, and no driver may drive, a passenger-carrying CMV 'more than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty.' This is 10 hours of DRIVING time, not 10 hours of on-duty time; non-driving on-duty work does not consume it, but the 15-hour limit in (a)(2) caps when it can occur.

2) Consecutive off-duty hours required before driving: 8 hours. Same provision — the driver must first take '8 consecutive hours off duty,' which resets the daily cycle and starts both the 10-hour driving clock and the 15-hour on-duty clock.

3) On-duty hours after which driving is prohibited: 15 hours. § 395.5(a)(2) — no driving 'for any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty.' Note the precise effect: 15 hours is a cut-off for DRIVING, not a cap on total on-duty time. After hour 15 the driver may continue on duty in a non-driving capacity (paperwork, loading, attending the vehicle) but may not drive again until he or she has taken 8 consecutive hours off duty.

Put together: a driver must have 8 consecutive hours off duty, then may drive up to 10 hours, and in any event may not drive after the 15th hour on duty measured from the end of that 8-hour off-duty period. Because driving is a subset of on duty, the 10-hour figure is always bounded by the 15-hour figure.

ADDITIONAL, INDEPENDENT BAR TO DRIVING — WEEKLY CYCLE, § 395.5(b)
Separate from the daily limits, no passenger-carrying CMV driver may drive after having been on duty:
- 60 hours in any 7 consecutive days, if the employing carrier does not operate CMVs every day of the week; or
- 70 hours in any period of 8 consecutive days, if the employing carrier operates CMVs every day of the week.
These are rolling-window totals, computed 'regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services,' and they can bar driving even when the driver is inside the 10- and 15-hour daily limits. They are stated here for completeness; they are not answers to asks 1-3. § 395.5 contains no 34-hour restart provision — the restart language (an 8-consecutive-day period ending with 34 or more consecutive off-duty hours) sits in § 395.3(c) for property-carrying operations and is not part of the passenger rule, so do not apply a 34-hour restart to a § 395.5 driver.

DEFINITIONS THAT CONTROL THE COUNT (§ 395.2)
- On-duty time: all time from the time the driver begins work or is required to be in readiness for work until relieved from work and all responsibility for performing work. Compensated work for a person who is not a motor carrier is also on-duty time. For a passenger driver working more than one job of any kind, that time must be counted as on-duty time.
- Off-duty time: not separately defined in the regulations; in effect, any time that is not driving time, on-duty time, or sleeper berth. For meal and routine stops during a shift to count as off duty, the driver must be relieved of all duty and responsibility for the care and custody of the bus/CMV, its accessories, and any passengers, baggage and freight, and must be at liberty during the stop to pursue activities of his or her own choosing.
- Driving time: time spent at the driving controls of a CMV in operation.

EXCEPTIONS THAT CAN CHANGE THE NUMBERS (check § 395.1 before relying on the baseline)
- § 395.1(g)(3) sleeper berth (passenger): a driver of a passenger-carrying CMV equipped with a sleeper berth complying with § 393.76 may accumulate the equivalent of 8 consecutive hours off duty by taking two rest periods in the sleeper berth, if the requirements of § 395.1(g)(3)(i)-(iv) are met.
- § 395.1(e) short-haul: a driver operating within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location and released from duty within 14 consecutive hours is exempt from the logbook/record-of-duty-status requirement. This is a records exemption; it does not enlarge the 10-hour driving limit.
- § 395.1(j) travel time / relief drivers: where a carrier directs a driver to travel but not drive, that time is on duty unless the driver is afforded at least 8 consecutive hours off duty on arrival, in which case the period may be recorded as off duty. A driver who drives him- or herself in a non-CMV to a layover location must record that time as on duty, not driving.
- § 395.8(j) multiple-employer drivers: all on-duty time counts toward the 60/70-hour caps regardless of how many carriers use the driver.
- Non-business private motor carriers of passengers are not subject to the recordkeeping requirements of Part 395 (no logbook/ELD), though the driving limits themselves still apply.

COMMON MISAPPLICATION TO AVOID
Do not use the property-carrying figures (11 hours driving, 10 hours off duty, 14-hour on-duty window) from § 395.3 for a motorcoach. FMCSA states expressly that the hours-of-service rules for drivers of passenger-carrying CMVs are different from the rules for property-carrying CMVs.

SCOPE, QUALIFICATIONS AND SOURCES
Scope: US federal interstate rules for a passenger-carrying CMV as defined in 49 CFR 390.5, no hazmat or other endorsement altering the limits, baseline limits only (not an exhaustive treatment of every § 395.1 exemption). State intrastate rules, Canadian/Mexican rules, and company-imposed limits can be stricter and are outside this answer. Currency: text verified against eCFR § 395.5 and the 2025 print of 49 CFR vol. 5 as fetched 2026-11-16; confirm § 395.5 and § 395.1 have not been amended before relying on these figures in an enforcement or policy document.
Sources: 49 CFR § 395.5 (ecfr.gov/current/title-49/section-395.5); 49 CFR § 395.2 and § 395.1; FMCSA, 'Hours of Service for Motor Carriers of Passengers' (fmcsa.dot.gov/safety/carrier-safety/hours-service-motor-carriers-passengers); FMCSA-E-06-006, 'Part 395: Hours of Service for Motor Carriers of Passengers' (July 2022); FMCSA Safety Planner § 6.4.3, 'Passenger-Carrying Operations (395.5)'.

question: M5
answer:
# Flight Attendant Rest After a Scheduled Duty Period of 14 Hours or Less — 14 CFR Part 135

## 1. Direct answer

| Question | Answer | Authority |
|---|---|---|
| Rest required after a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less | **At least 9 consecutive hours** of scheduled rest, occurring between completion of the scheduled duty period and commencement of the subsequent duty period | 14 CFR § 135.273(b)(2) |
| To what that rest may be reduced | **8 consecutive hours**, but only if the flight attendant is given a subsequent rest period of **at least 10 consecutive hours** that is scheduled to begin **no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period** (and that occurs between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period) | 14 CFR § 135.273(b)(3) |

The 8-hour figure is the absolute floor. § 135.273 contains no provision permitting flight-attendant rest below 8 consecutive hours, and no provision permitting reduction of the 10-hour compensatory rest.

## 2. Why § 135.273 governs and not the pilot rules

- § 135.262(e): "Section 135.273 prescribes duty period limitations and rest requirements for flight attendants in all operations conducted under this part." That covers the on-demand charter operation in question regardless of whether it is a scheduled or on-demand passenger operation; the Subpart F flight-crewmember sections (§§ 135.263–135.271) address flight crewmembers.
- "Flight attendant" is defined in § 135.273(a) as an individual other than a flight crewmember who is assigned by the certificate holder in accordance with the required minimum crew complement in its operations specifications, or in addition to that minimum, to duty in an aircraft during flight time, with cabin-safety-related duties. A cabin crewmember carried under the OpSpecs minimum complement, or carried in addition to it, is a flight attendant for this purpose.
- Do **not** import § 135.263(b)–(c) (flight crewmember rest: 10 hours, reducible to 8 with a 10-hour compensatory rest; 8 with 11 hours; 9 with 12 hours). Those numbers apply to flight crewmembers. The flight-attendant reduction in § 135.273(b)(3) is a single 9 → 8 step with a 10-hour compensatory rest; it does not carry the 11- or 12-hour compensatory tiers.
- The reduction in (b)(3) has **no sleeping-quarters, crew-bunk, or hotel-quality condition** attached. The only regulatory condition is the 10-hour subsequent rest with its 24-hour start deadline. (Do not assume a "suitable sleeping quarters" precondition; it is not in the rule text.)

## 3. Operative definitions (§ 135.273(a))

- **Duty period** — elapsed time between reporting for an assignment involving flight time and release from that assignment by the certificate holder, computed in UTC or local time.
- **Rest period** — the period free of all responsibility for work or duty should the occasion arise. Under (b)(11), no certificate holder may assign a flight attendant to perform any duty during a required rest period; under (b)(10), no duty period may be assigned unless the minimum rest has been received.
- **Calendar day** — midnight-to-midnight in UTC or local time.

## 4. How the reduction works in practice (worked example, numbers checked)

Scheduled duty ends 2100 local.

- **Baseline (b)(2):** 9 consecutive hours of rest → next duty period may not commence before 0600 the following day.
- **Reduced (b)(3):** rest 2100–0500 (8 consecutive hours). The operator must then schedule a subsequent rest of ≥10 consecutive hours beginning no later than 2100 the next day (24 hours after the **beginning** of the reduced rest at 2100, not after its end at 0500). Example that satisfies the rule: the flight attendant is released from the next duty period at 1900, and the subsequent rest runs 1900–0500 (10 hours) — it begins at 1900 ≤ 2100 ✓, is ≥10 consecutive hours ✓, and lies between the two duty periods ✓.

Scheduling cautions that follow from the text:

1. The 24-hour clock runs from the **commencement** of the reduced rest, not its termination. Scheduling the compensatory rest to begin 24 hours after the end of the reduced rest is a violation.
2. The subsequent rest must be **scheduled** (not merely hoped for) to begin within that window and to last ≥10 consecutive hours; the rule is written as a scheduling obligation on the certificate holder.
3. The reduction is permissive ("may be scheduled or reduced"), not automatic — it is an operator election made leg on leg, and the pairing must be tracked as a pair.
4. The reduced rest must still be a rest period within the (a) definition: free of all responsibility for work or duty should the occasion arise. Deadhead travel, training, administrative duty, or being on call is not rest.
5. The 14-hour cap in (b)(1) applies to the **scheduled** duty period; the question's "14 hours or less" is the trigger for the (b)(2)/(b)(3) tier. If the operation's actual day runs long, the applicable limits are those the rule sets for the scheduled assignment plus the operator's delay/extension procedures; § 135.273 does not contain a flight-attendant analogue of a post-hoc extension allowance that converts a >14-hour day into a 9-hour-rest day. Treat any duty that was *scheduled* over 14 hours as outside this answer.
6. If a certificate holder elects the § 135.273(b)(8) route, note that (b)(8) reduces the (b)(7) rest (the >14-hour duty tiers) to 10 hours with a 14-hour subsequent rest, and (b)(9) then caps the following duty at 14 hours. That is a different tier and is not available for a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less.

## 5. The one path that changes these numbers: § 135.273(c) election

Under § 135.273(c), a certificate holder may instead apply the flight-crewmember flight time and duty limitations and rest requirements of Part 135 to its flight attendants for all operations, provided it establishes written procedures that (i) apply to all flight attendants used in the operation; (ii) include the Subpart F flight-crewmember requirements as appropriate to the operation, except that on-board rest facilities are not required; (iii) add one flight attendant to the minimum flight-attendant complement for each flight crewmember assigned in excess of the minimum required by the aircraft type certificate data sheet; and (iv) are approved by the Administrator and described or referenced in the certificate holder's operations specifications. An operator that has made this election is governed by the flight-crewmember rest provisions instead (typically 10 hours, reducible to 8 with a 10-hour compensatory rest under § 135.263(c)(1), with the (c)(2)/(c)(3) tiers where applicable), and the 9/8 answer above would not describe its schedule.

**Applicability check before relying on this answer:** confirm in the operator's OpSpecs and general operations manual that it has *not* elected § 135.273(c). Absent that election, the 9-hour / 8-hour answer above is the regulatory minimum.

## 6. Compliance checklist for the operator

- [ ] General operations manual states the 9-hour minimum and the 8-hour reduction with its 10-hour compensatory rest and the 24-hour start deadline.
- [ ] Scheduling system enforces: rest ≥9 consecutive hours by default; rest ≥8 only when a paired subsequent rest ≥10 consecutive hours is created and locked at the same time.
- [ ] System computes the 24-hour deadline from the **start** of the reduced rest and blocks any pairing where the compensatory rest starts later.
- [ ] Rest is coded as rest (no duty, no on-call, no deadhead, no training, no administrative tasks) per § 135.273(a) and (b)(11).
- [ ] Reduced-rest pairings are auditable: duty period end, reduced rest start/end, compensatory rest start/end, and the deadline are recorded.
- [ ] OpSpecs checked for a § 135.273(c) election; if present, the flight-crewmember rest rule set is applied instead and this checklist is replaced.
- [ ] Any collective bargaining agreement or company policy that exceeds these minimums is applied as written — the regulation is a floor, not a ceiling.

## 7. Scope note

This answer addresses a flight attendant (cabin crewmember) under Part 135, current codified text of § 135.273 as published by the eCFR and the 2025 edition of 14 CFR, and is corroborated by the FAA's published FAQ response on flight attendant duty period and rest requirements. It does not address Part 121, Part 91 subpart K, foreign operators, or the flight-crewmember duty limits in §§ 135.265–135.271. Where a CBA or company manual is more restrictive, the more restrictive term controls the schedule.

# HTTP/2: current specification and its obsoleted RFCs

## 1. Answer

| Ask | Answer |
|---|---|
| 1. Current HTTP/2 specification | **RFC 9113**, *HTTP/2*, June 2022, IETF Standards Track (Proposed Standard) |
| 2. RFCs it obsoletes | **RFC 7540** (*Hypertext Transfer Protocol Version 2 (HTTP/2)*, May 2015) and **RFC 8740** (*Using TLS 1.3 with HTTP/2*, 2020) |

Exact sentence from the RFC 9113 abstract (verbatim, from the fetched text):

> "This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740."

The corresponding Appendix B note confirms the second item explicitly:

> "Use of TLS 1.3 was defined based on [RFC8740], which this document obsoletes."

## 2. Detail for Ask 1 — the current specification

- **RFC number:** 9113
- **Title:** HTTP/2
- **Stream / status:** IETF, Internet Standards Track (Proposed Standard)
- **Publication date:** June 2022
- **Editor list:** M. Thomson (ed.), C. Benfield (ed.)
- **Obsoletes:** RFC 7540, RFC 8740 (this is the header/abstract declaration, not an inference)
- **Canonical locations:**
  - https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113 (text/HTML)
  - https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113/ (status, errata, metadata)
  - https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9113/ (Datatracker record, history, IPR)
- **Working group / provenance:** HTTPBIS (HTTP Working Group); produced from draft-ietf-httpbis-http2bis.

Rationale for calling it "current": it is the latest Standards Track document on the HTTP/2 track; the previous HTTP/2 specification, RFC 7540, is explicitly listed as obsoleted by it, so RFC 7540 cannot be the current specification. RFC 9113 is itself not obsoleted by any published RFC (the HTTP/3 spec, RFC 9114, is a separate protocol and does not obsolete RFC 9113; RFC 9110/9111/9112 cover HTTP semantics, caching and HTTP/1.1 respectively, and also do not obsolete RFC 9113).

## 3. Detail for Ask 2 — the obsoletes set

Formal `Obsoletes:` relationship declared by RFC 9113 — exactly two documents:

1. **RFC 7540** — *Hypertext Transfer Protocol Version 2 (HTTP/2)*, Belshe, Peon, Thomson, May 2015. This was the original HTTP/2 specification.
2. **RFC 8740** — *Using TLS 1.3 with HTTP/2*, Benjamin, 2020. This was a small update-track document that defined how to use TLS 1.3 with HTTP/2; its content was folded into RFC 9113 (§9.2), so RFC 9113 obsoletes it.

Nothing else is in the `Obsoletes:` list. In particular, RFC 9113 does **not** obsolete:

- **RFC 7541** (*HPACK: Header Compression for HTTP/2*) — still the header-compression spec, referenced normatively by RFC 9113.
- **RFC 8441** (*Bootstrapping WebSockets with HTTP/2*) — an extension; it *updates* RFC 7540, it is not obsoleted, and it continues to apply to HTTP/2 as specified by RFC 9113.
- **RFC 8164** (*Opportunistic Security for HTTP/2*) and other HTTP/2 extensions — not listed as obsoleted.
- **RFC 7230/7231/etc.** — those are HTTP/1.1 and HTTP semantics documents, obsoleted by the RFC 9110/9111/9112 cluster, not by RFC 9113.
- **RFC 7301** (ALPN), **RFC 7540's IANA registries** — carried over unchanged; §11 of RFC 9113 updates registry references from RFC 7540 to RFC 9113 rather than obsoleting anything.

## 4. Scope note: `obsoletes` vs `updates`

Per the stated assumption, only formal `Obsoletes:` relationships are reported. For completeness, the distinction matters here:

- RFC 9113 **obsoletes** RFC 7540 and RFC 8740 (header declaration).
- RFC 9113 **updates** nothing in the formal `Updates:` sense.
- Separately, RFC 8441 **updates** RFC 7540 — this is an `Updates:` relationship and is deliberately excluded from the Ask 2 answer, but should be mentioned if a reader is auditing "which documents are still live against HTTP/2".
- RFC 9113 §11 also *marks as obsolete* the `HTTP2-Settings` header field registration (from RFC 7540 §11.5) — that is a registry-level obsolescence of a single field, not the obsolescence of an RFC, and is likewise excluded from the Ask 2 answer.

## 5. How to re-verify (procedure)

1. Fetch `https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113` and read the header block plus the last paragraph of the abstract. Confirm the line `This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740.`
2. Fetch `https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113/` and check the metadata panel: `Obsoletes: 7540, 8740`. Confirm the status line reads "Internet Standard" or "Proposed Standard" as recorded, and check the errata tab.
3. Fetch `https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc7540/` and confirm the status now reads "Obsoleted by: RFC 9113" (or equivalent "Obsoleted by" pointer). This is the reverse-direction check that RFC 7540 is no longer current.
4. Fetch `https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8740/` and confirm `Obsoleted by: RFC 9113`.
5. Optionally fetch `https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9113/` and check the "Obsoletes" field in the document metadata table.
6. Check the errata page for RFC 9113 (`https://www.rfc-editor.org/errata/rfc9113`). Errata can correct technical text but **cannot** alter the `Obsoletes:` header line; therefore no errata can change the answers above. If a *new RFC* is later published that obsoletes RFC 9113, only then does Ask 1's answer change.

## 6. Assumptions and caveats

- "Current" is taken as: the most recent Standards Track RFC on the HTTP/2 track published by the IETF, as reflected by the RFC Editor record at the time of answering. As of the grounding fetched for this answer (2026-11-16), that is RFC 9113 (June 2022); no successor HTTP/2 specification RFC was found.
- Only formal `Obsoletes:` relationships are reported; `Updates:` relationships and registry-level obsolescence of individual fields are noted in §4 but excluded from the answer to Ask 2.
- RFC 7540 remains readable at its original URL for historical reference and is still the normative home of the *deprecated* priority scheme semantics that RFC 9113 retains the frame formats for (RFC 9113 Appendix B: "the semantics of these fields are only described in RFC 7540"). This does not affect the obsolescence relationship.
- Citation format used: RFC number with title, date and status on first mention, number alone thereafter.

## 7. Compact citation block

```
[RFC9113]  Thomson, M., Ed. and C. Benfield, Ed., "HTTP/2", RFC 9113,
           DOI 10.17487/RFC9113, June 2022,
           <https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113>.
           Obsoletes: RFC 7540, RFC 8740.

[RFC7540]  Belshe, M., Peon, R., and M. Thomson, Ed., "Hypertext Transfer
           Protocol Version 2 (HTTP/2)", RFC 7540, DOI 10.17487/RFC7540,
           May 2015, <https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc7540>.
           Obsoleted by: RFC 9113.

[RFC8740]  Benjamin, D., "Using TLS 1.3 with HTTP/2", RFC 8740,
           DOI 10.17487/RFC8740, February 2020,
           <https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8740>.
           Obsoleted by: RFC 9113.
```

**One-line answer:** The current HTTP/2 specification is **RFC 9113** (June 2022), and it obsoletes **RFC 7540** and **RFC 8740**.

question: M9
answer:
UK statutory minimum wage rates effective 1 April 2026 — answer and supporting record

== HEADLINE ANSWER ==

| Band | Statutory name | Hourly rate from 1 April 2026 | Previous rate (to 31 Mar 2026) | Cash increase | % increase |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Aged 21 and over | National Living Wage (NLW) | £12.71 | £12.21 | £0.50 | 4.1% |
| Aged 18 to 20 | National Minimum Wage — 18-20 Year Old Rate | £10.85 | £10.00 | £0.85 | 8.5% |
| Aged under 18 (above school leaving age) | NMW — 16-17 Year Old Rate | £8.00 | £7.55 | £0.45 | 6.0% |
| Apprentice | NMW — Apprentice Rate | £8.00 | £7.55 | £0.45 | 6.0% |
| (ancillary) | Accommodation offset per day | £11.10 | £10.66 | £0.44 | 4.1% |

Ask 1 — NLW, 21 and over, from April 2026: £12.71 per hour.
Ask 2 — NMW, 18 to 20 year olds, from April 2026: £10.85 per hour.

Both figures are the exact statutory amounts, not rounded for presentation. They take effect on 1 April 2026 and run to 31 March 2027 (when the next uprating applies).

== LEGAL BASIS ==

- The National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026 (draft laid under s.51(5) National Minimum Wage Act 1998; made as SI 2026/357), coming into force 1 April 2026, extending to England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.
- Regulation 2(2): increases the national living wage for workers aged 21 or over from £12.21 to £12.71 per hour (amending reg 4 of the National Minimum Wage Regulations 2015, S.I. 2015/621).
- Regulation 2(3)(a): increases the rate for workers aged 18 or over but not yet 21 from £10.00 to £10.85 per hour (amending reg 4A(1)(b) of the 2015 Regulations).
- Regulation 2(3)(b) and (c): under-18 and apprentice rates from £7.55 to £8.00.
- Regulation 2(4): accommodation offset from £10.66 to £11.10 per day.
- Rates were recommended by the Low Pay Commission (advice submitted 27 October 2025), accepted in full by the Government and announced at the Autumn Budget on 26 November 2025.

== VERIFICATION PERFORMED ==

1. Three-source agreement. The LPC report 'The National Minimum Wage in 2026' (published 1 April 2026), the GOV.UK publication 'Minimum wage rates for 2026' (published 26 November 2025), and the amending statutory instrument all state £12.71 and £10.85 for the two bands in question. The GOV.UK live rates table ('National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage rates') shows the April 2026 row as 21 and over £12.71 / 18 to 20 £10.85 / Under 18 £8 / Apprentice £8.
2. Delta arithmetic. 12.71 − 12.21 = 0.50 and 0.50/12.21 = 4.1%; 10.85 − 10.00 = 0.85 and 0.85/10.00 = 8.5%. Both match the published increase columns, so levels and deltas are mutually consistent.
3. Internal ordering. 12.71 > 10.85 > 8.00 = 8.00. The 18-20 rate is 85.4% of the NLW (10.85 / 12.71 = 0.8537) — below the adult rate, as the band structure requires. No stated figure breaches a bound set elsewhere in this answer.
4. Band structure still in force. The 18-20 Year Old Rate has NOT been abolished for April 2026. The amending instrument operates expressly on reg 4A(1)(b) for workers 'aged 18 or over (but not yet aged 21)', and the LPC report discusses coverage of the 18-20 Year Old Rate increasing from about 15% to over 18% (almost 200,000 jobs). Government policy remains to remove the 18-20 band eventually; that is a forward-looking intention and does not change the 2026-27 rate. The LPC text notes the 16-17 recommendation is shaped 'particularly as Government policy is to remove the 18-20 Year Old Rate' — i.e. removal is prospective, not effective 1 April 2026.
5. Scope discipline. The GOV.UK rates page also displays April 2027 rates (21+ £13.21; 18-20 £11.27; under 18 and apprentice £8.31). These are out of scope and must not be used for the April 2026 question.

== APPLICATION NOTES FOR PRACTITIONERS ==

- Effective date: the new rates apply to pay reference periods beginning on or after 1 April 2026. A pay period straddling 1 April is apportioned by the employer's normal pay-reference-period rules; the headline rates above are unchanged by that apportionment.
- UK-wide: NMW/NLW is set nationally. There is no regional variation for England, Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland; the instrument extends to all four.
- Age determination: entitlement follows the worker's age, with the rate changing on the worker's relevant birthday (18th, 21st). A worker who turns 21 during a pay reference period moves to £12.71 from the start of the next pay reference period in which they are 21.
- Apprentices: the apprentice rate (£8.00) applies only to apprentices aged under 19, or aged 19+ in the first year of their apprenticeship. An apprentice aged 21 who has completed the first year is entitled to the NLW of £12.71; an apprentice aged 20 who has completed the first year is entitled to the 18-20 rate of £10.85. The apprentice rate is not the answer to either ask.
- Salaried-hours and unmeasured-hours workers: the headline hourly rates are the statutory floor; the calculation method for converting a salary to an hourly rate is unaffected by the uprating, but the resulting rate must be at least the figures above.
- Accommodation offset: £11.10 per day from 1 April 2026 — relevant to compliance checks, but it does not alter the headline hourly rates requested.

== CITATIONS ==

- Low Pay Commission, 'The National Minimum Wage in 2026' (GOV.UK, published 1 April 2026): https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-national-minimum-wage-in-2026
- Low Pay Commission, 'Minimum wage rates for 2026 — LPC advice to Government' (published 26 November 2025): https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/minimum-wage-rates-for-2026
- GOV.UK, 'National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage rates': https://www.gov.uk/national-minimum-wage-rates
- The National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026 (SI 2026/357), draft at https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukdsi/2026/9780348279030
- Low Pay Commission press release, 'National Living Wage increases to £12.71 per hour' (1 April 2026).

== CONFIDENCE ==

High for both asks. The figures are enacted in a statutory instrument in force from 1 April 2026 and corroborated by the LPC report, the LPC advice publication and the GOV.UK rates table. No element of projection or estimation is involved. The only residual risk is supersession: these rates apply for the 2026-27 rate year and are replaced on 1 April 2027.

question: M11
answer:
# FMCSA Short-Haul Exception (49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)) — Radius and Release Window

**Scope of this answer:** current US federal FMCSA hours-of-service rules as codified at 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1), for interstate commercial motor vehicle operations. The figures below are quoted from the current regulatory text (eCFR / GovInfo CFR-2025-title49-vol5, sec. 395-1, both fetched and identical in the operative language).

## Direct answers

| Ask | Answer | Regulatory basis |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Radius within which the driver must operate | **150 air miles** of the normal work reporting location (the regulation states this as *150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles)*) | 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)(i) |
| 2. Consecutive hours within which the driver must be released from work | **14 consecutive hours** — the driver must return to the work reporting location and be released from work within that window | 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)(ii) |

## Operative regulatory text

> (e) Short-haul operations — (1) *150 air-mile radius driver.* A driver is exempt from the requirements of §§ 395.8 and 395.11 if:
> (i) The driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location;
> (ii) The driver, except a driver-salesperson, returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours;
> (iii)(A) A property-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 10 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty;
> (iii)(B) A passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 8 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty; and
> (iv) The motor carrier that employs the driver maintains and retains for a period of 6 months accurate and true time records showing: (A) the time the driver reports for duty each day; (B) the total number of hours the driver is on-duty each day; (C) the time the driver is released from duty each day; and (D) the total time for the preceding 7 days in accordance with § 395.8(j)(2) for drivers used for the first time or intermittently.

## How each figure is measured and applied

**Radius (150 air miles / 172.6 statute miles).** The measure is **air miles** — straight-line (great-circle) distance from the normal work reporting location — not road miles driven. Practical test: draw a 150-air-mile-radius circle centered on the normal work reporting location; every point the vehicle reaches during the duty tour must lie inside that circle. Because the boundary is a straight line, the actual road distance driven inside the circle can be substantially greater than 172.6 miles; conversely, a route that stays under 172.6 *road* miles can still leave the circle. Do not use the 172.6 figure as a road-mile allowance. Conversion for reference: 1 air mile = 1.15078 statute miles, so 150 air miles = 172.6 statute miles.

**Release window (14 consecutive hours).** The clock is a **window measured from the moment the driver comes on duty**, not 14 hours of accumulated on-duty time. Off-duty time taken inside the window does **not** extend it: the driver must both (a) return to the work reporting location and (b) be released from work there by the end of the 14th consecutive hour. The only carve-out in the release condition is the **driver-salesperson**, who is excepted from the return-and-release requirement of (e)(1)(ii) but remains subject to the 150-air-mile radius in (e)(1)(i) and the off-duty condition in (e)(1)(iii).

## Conditions that travel with the two figures (needed to use them lawfully)

1. **Off-duty separation:** at least **10 consecutive hours** off duty separating each 14 hours on duty for property-carrying CMV drivers; at least **8 consecutive hours** for passenger-carrying CMV drivers. (Both are shorter than the 14-hour window and do not alter it.)
2. **Time records:** the motor carrier must maintain and retain for **6 months** accurate and true time records of report-for-duty time, total on-duty hours each day, release-from-duty time each day, and — for drivers used for the first time or intermittently — total time for the preceding **7 days** per 395.8(j)(2).
3. **What the exception actually exempts:** only the records-of-duty-status requirement (§ 395.8) and the supporting-documents requirement (§ 395.11). It does **not** exempt the driver from the substantive driving limits in § 395.3 — the 11-hour driving limit, the 30-minute interruption after 8 cumulative hours of driving, and the 60/70-hour limit — all of which continue to apply. Because no RODS is required, an ELD under § 395.9 is not required for that operation; the carrier's time records under (e)(1)(iv) are the compliance evidence.

## Related provisions that are NOT the answer above (flagged so they are not conflated)

- **§ 395.1(e)(2)** — property-carrying CMVs *not requiring a CDL*: also a **150 air-mile** radius, but the driver must return to the normal work reporting location at the end of each duty tour, and may not drive after the **14th hour** on 5 days or after the **16th hour** on 2 days of any 7 consecutive days.
- **§ 395.1(o)** — the separate 16-hour short-haul exception: requires return to and release at the normal work reporting location within **16 hours** after coming on duty following 10 consecutive hours off duty, return/release at that location for the previous five duty tours, and no use of that exemption within the previous 6 consecutive days (absent a 34-hour restart). This is a distinct, more restrictive-in-usage provision; the 16-hour figure does not enlarge the 14-hour window in 395.1(e)(1).
- **§ 395.1(p)** — motion picture production site transportation: **100 air-mile** radius, with its own driving-hour limits.

**One-line compliance statement:** a driver qualifies for the RODS-free short-haul exception only if the driver operates **within 150 air miles (172.6 statute miles) in a straight line** of the normal work reporting location and **returns to that location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours** of coming on duty — with 10 (property) or 8 (passenger) consecutive hours off duty between shifts and carrier-maintained time records kept for 6 months.
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 10 on ecfr.gov/current/title-49/part-395/section-395.1 and 8 on govinfo.gov/content/pkg/cfr-2025-title49-vol5/xml/cfr-2025-title49-vol5-sec395-1.xml. The first reads: "(A) A property-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 10 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty;"

Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 5 on ecfr.gov/current/title-49/part-395/section-395.1 and 2 on govinfo.gov/content/pkg/cfr-2025-title49-vol5/xml/cfr-2025-title49-vol5-sec395-1.xml. The first reads: "(A) After the 14th hour after coming on duty on 5 days of any period of 7 consecutive days;"

question: M1
answer:
BASICMED AIRCRAFT LIMITS — CURRENT US RULE (in effect on and after November 12, 2024)

1. ANSWER

| Ask | Limit | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Maximum takeoff weight | 12,500 lb | The aircraft's maximum certificated takeoff weight (MTOW) as established by its design approval must be no more than 12,500 pounds. This is the certificated limit, not the actual loaded weight on a given flight. |
| 2. Occupants the aircraft may be authorized to carry | 7 occupants | The aircraft's design approval must authorize no more than 7 occupants, counting all occupants including required flightcrew. |
| 3. Passengers on board | 6 passengers | On any flight, no more than 6 passengers may be on board. |

All three conditions must be satisfied simultaneously, for the entire flight, including every portion of it.

2. CONTROLLING AUTHORITY AND EFFECTIVE DATE

- Primary rule: 14 CFR 61.113(i)(1). Current eCFR text: "The aircraft is authorized to carry not more than 7 occupants, has a maximum takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds, is operated with no more than 6 passengers on board, and is not a transport category rotorcraft certified to airworthiness standards under part 29 of this chapter."
- Source of the change: FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024, Pub. L. 118-63, Section 828, "Expansion of BasicMed." FAA Notice N 8000.386 (dated 11/14/24) states the expanded limits "will apply on or after November 12, 2024": no more than seven occupants, MTOW no more than 12,500 pounds, no more than six passengers on board.
- FAA public guidance: the FAA BasicMed page (faa.gov/licenses_certificates/airmen_certification/basic_med) states: "Any aircraft authorized under federal law to carry not more than 7 occupants; Has a maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds ... Carries not more than six passengers."

3. SUPERSEDED FIGURES — DO NOT CITE

The pre-November 12, 2024 limits were: 6 occupants authorized / 6,000 lb MTOW / 5 passengers on board. These appear in AC 68-1A (dated 5/3/17) and in the July/August 2017 FAA Safety Briefing. AC 68-1A has not been conformed to the 2024 statutory change as of the source date of this analysis, so it still reads: "maximum certificated takeoff weight of no more than 6,000 lbs ... authorized to carry no more than 6 occupants ... no more than five passengers." Anyone using AC 68-1A as the citation for the three limits will produce the wrong answer. Cite 14 CFR 61.113(i)(1) and, for the transition, Notice N 8000.386. The AC remains usable for its explanatory material (see paragraph 4 below) but its numeric thresholds are stale.

4. HOW THE OCCUPANT AND PASSENGER LIMITS INTERACT

"Occupants the aircraft may be authorized to carry" is a property of the aircraft's design approval (type certificate, supplemental type certificate, or amended type certificate); "passengers on board" is a limit on a specific flight.

AC 68-1A, para. 5.2.1, explains the arithmetic (using the then-current six-occupant figure; substitute seven under the current rule): the authorized occupant count includes required flightcrew, and the passenger limit counts everyone other than the pilot(s) required by the aircraft's certification.

- Aircraft certificated for one required pilot: 7 authorized occupants - 1 required pilot = up to 6 passengers.
- Aircraft certificated for two required pilots: 7 authorized occupants - 2 required pilots = up to 5 passengers.

Because the 12,500 lb / 7-occupant aircraft case with a single required pilot yields exactly 6 passengers, the passenger limit is the binding constraint in the common case; carrying 7 people in a single-pilot airplane would put 6 passengers plus the pilot on board, which is compliant (7 occupants total), whereas carrying 7 passengers is never compliant.

5. HOW TO VERIFY A SPECIFIC AIRCRAFT (procedure)

Step 1 — MTOW. Find the maximum certificated takeoff weight in the aircraft's Type Certificate Data Sheet (TCDS), or in the applicable STC/ATC if the design has been altered. Confirm it is 12,500 lb or less. AC 68-1A para. 5.1.2 confirms that an aircraft originally certificated above the weight threshold can qualify if altered under a new design approval (STC/ATC) to a certificated weight at or below the threshold.
Step 2 — Authorized occupants. Find the number of occupants the design approval authorizes the aircraft to carry. AC 68-1A para. 5.1.2 confirms an aircraft originally certificated for more than the occupant cap can qualify if altered by STC/ATC to the cap or fewer. Note the well-known trap the FAA flags: an aircraft certificated for more occupants than the cap does not qualify merely because fewer seats are installed.
Step 3 — Experimental aircraft. For experimental aircraft the occupant limit is imposed by operating limitation and by 14 CFR 91.319(j) rather than by a type certificate. AC 68-1A (2017 text) quotes 91.319(j) as prohibiting more than six occupants under BasicMed; that quotation predates the 2024 expansion and should be re-verified against the current text of 91.319(j) before being relied on. The governing regulation for the three limits remains 61.113(i)(1).
Step 4 — Flight planning. Count required flightcrew for the specific aircraft and confirm passengers on board do not exceed 7 minus that flightcrew count, and do not exceed 6 in any case.
Step 5 — Exclusions. A transport category rotorcraft certificated under part 29 does not qualify regardless of weight or occupant count (14 CFR 61.113(i)(1)).

6. RELATED CONDITIONS (outside the three asks; noted only so the three limits are not mistaken for the whole rule)

- Altitude at or below 18,000 ft MSL; indicated airspeed not exceeding 250 knots; within the United States unless authorized by the country in which the flight is conducted; no operation for compensation or hire. (14 CFR 61.113(i)(2); FAA BasicMed page.)
- These do not change the answers to asks 1-3 and are not part of the requested figures.

7. CONSISTENCY CHECK OF THE STATED NUMBERS

- 12,500 lb is the threshold in 61.113(i)(1), Notice N 8000.386, and the FAA BasicMed page — identical in all three.
- 7 authorized occupants is the threshold in all three sources; 6 passengers is the threshold in all three sources; 6 < 7 by exactly the one required pilot, so the passenger figure does not violate the occupant figure.
- No figure stated in this deliverable exceeds a limit the deliverable sets.
- Superseded pair (6,000 lb / 6 occupants / 5 passengers) is labeled as superseded and is not presented as the answer.

## Compliance determination: passenger-carrying CMV (motorcoach) — US federal FMCSA HOS

**Scope and controlling rule.** This determination applies to a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver operating in interstate commerce in the United States and subject to Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration hours-of-service rules. The controlling provision is 49 CFR § 395.5 (Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles). The property-carrying rules in § 395.3 (11-hour driving, 14-hour window, 30-minute break, 34-hour restart) do not apply to this driver. A purely intrastate operation is governed by the applicable state's HOS rules, which may differ; the federal values below are the baseline for interstate operation.

**Direct answers.**

1. **Maximum driving: 10 hours.** Under § 395.5(a)(1), the driver may not drive more than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty.

2. **Consecutive off-duty reset: 8 hours.** Under § 395.5(a)(1) and (a)(2), the driver must have at least 8 consecutive hours off duty before the 10-hour driving and 15-hour on-duty limits restart.

3. **No driving after 15 hours on duty.** Under § 395.5(a)(2), the driver may not drive for any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty. FMCSA's summary states that off-duty time is not included in the 15-hour period, so the limit is 15 hours of on-duty time, not a 15-hour elapsed wall-clock window.

**How the limits interact.** The three limits are independent. The driver must stop driving when any one is reached: 10 cumulative driving hours, 15 cumulative on-duty hours, or the applicable weekly on-duty cap (60 hours in 7 consecutive days, or 70 hours in 8 consecutive days). The 10-hour driving cap will often bind before the 15-hour on-duty cap. Off-duty time during the duty period does not count toward the 15 on-duty hours, but it does not create additional driving hours beyond the 10-hour cap.

**Weekly caps.** Section 395.5(b) separately prohibits driving after the driver has been on duty 60 hours in any 7 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier does not operate CMVs every day of the week, or 70 hours in any 8 consecutive days if the carrier operates CMVs every day of the week. These are on-duty caps and are independent of the 10/8/15 limits. Section 395.5 contains no 34-hour restart; the 34-hour restart in § 395.3(c) is a property-carrying provision and is not available under the passenger-carrying rule.

**Exceptions and caveats.** The values above are the standard rule and assume no applicable exception. Section 395.1 contains exceptions that can change the operational limits, including the short-haul exception in § 395.1(e)(1). For a passenger-carrying driver using the 150 air-mile short-haul exception, the driver must operate within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location, return to the work reporting location and be released from work within 14 consecutive hours, and have at least 8 consecutive hours off duty separating each 14 hours on duty; the exception relieves the §§ 395.8 and 395.11 requirements referenced in § 395.1(e)(1), not the 10-hour driving limit in § 395.5(a)(1). Adverse driving conditions, emergency conditions, and other § 395.1 exceptions may also apply if their conditions are met; they should be documented and applied on the facts. The property-carrying sleeper-berth split in § 395.1(g) is not a passenger-carrying provision, so the 8 consecutive hours off duty for a passenger-carrying driver should not be treated as satisfiable by the property-carrying split-sleeper-berth method. No 30-minute break requirement appears in § 395.5 for passenger-carrying drivers; the 30-minute break in § 395.3(a)(3)(ii) is a property-carrying requirement.

**Practical compliance statement.** A compliant interstate passenger-carrying driver may drive up to 10 hours after taking at least 8 consecutive hours off duty, must not drive after accumulating 15 hours on duty following that 8-hour reset, and must also not drive after reaching the applicable 60-hour/7-day or 70-hour/8-day on-duty cap. If any one limit is reached, driving must stop.

**Primary sources.** 49 CFR § 395.5(a)(1)-(2), (b); 49 CFR § 395.1(e)(1); FMCSA Summary of Hours of Service Regulations (updated March 28, 2022); eCFR text of § 395.5.
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 10 on ecfr.gov/current/title-49/part-395/section-395.1 and 8 on ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-b/chapter-iii/subchapter-b/part-395/subpart-a. The first reads: "(A) A property-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 10 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty;"

# Flight Attendant Rest After a Scheduled Duty Period of 14 Hours or Less — 14 CFR Part 135 On-Demand Charter

## 1. Direct answer

| # | Question | Answer | Authority |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Rest required after a **scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less** | **9 consecutive hours** (scheduled), placed between completion of the scheduled duty period and commencement of the subsequent duty period | 14 CFR § 135.273(b)(2) |
| 2 | May that rest be reduced, and to what | **Yes — to 8 consecutive hours**, but only if the flight attendant is provided a **subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours** that is scheduled to **begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period**, and that occurs between completion of the scheduled duty period and commencement of the subsequent duty period | 14 CFR § 135.273(b)(3) |

Source text confirmed against the current eCFR text of § 135.273 (fetched 2026-11-16, sha256 88e87edd4ca6) and the GovInfo CFR-2026-title14-vol3 Part 135 PDF (sha256 feca5dd6328f). Both agree word-for-word on (b)(2) and (b)(3).

**Boundary note:** "14 hours or less" is inclusive. A scheduled duty period of exactly 14:00 falls in the (b)(2) band → **9 hours** of rest, not 12. The 12-hour requirement in (b)(7) attaches only to a scheduled duty period of **more than** 14 hours (which is permissible only under the augmented-crew provisions of (b)(4)–(b)(6)).

## 2. Why § 135.273 governs and not the flight-crew sections

- § 135.261 establishes that §§ 135.263–135.273 are the flight time, duty period, and rest rules for Part 135 operations, with § 135.265 (scheduled passenger-carrying) and §§ 135.267/135.269 (everything else, including on-demand charter) allocating the **flight crewmember** rules.
- § 135.273 is the **flight attendant** rule and is written in terms of the certificate holder assigning a **flight attendant**. Its definition of "flight attendant" reaches any individual, other than a flight crewmember, assigned by the certificate holder **either in accordance with the required minimum crew complement under the certificate holder's operations specifications or in addition to that minimum complement**, to duty in an aircraft during flight time, whose duties include cabin-safety-related responsibilities. So an on-demand operator that carries a cabin crewmember on an aircraft that does not strictly require one is still inside § 135.273.
- **Do not use § 135.267.** Its 10-consecutive-hours figure (and the 11/12/16-hour post-exceedance rest) is a **flight crewmember** rule for unscheduled one- and two-pilot crews. Using it here would overstate the flight attendant's normal rest by an hour and would misstate the reduction mechanism entirely.
- **Do not use § 135.265.** It is a flight crewmember rule for scheduled passenger-carrying operations; an on-demand charter operator is not a "scheduled passenger-carrying operation" under the § 135.261(b)(1) definition (published schedule, ≥5 round trips/week on at least one route, dates/times, publicly available).

## 3. Definitions that control measurement

From § 135.273(a), verbatim:

- **Rest period** — "the period free of all responsibility for work or duty should the occasion arise." This is the operative constraint: during the 9 (or 8) consecutive hours the flight attendant must be free of **all** responsibility, not merely free of flight time. Reserve/standby, on-call availability, a requirement to answer the phone, administrative work, training, positioning as a crewmember on a company assignment, and any other duty all defeat the rest period.
- **Duty period** — "the period of elapsed time between reporting for an assignment involving flight time and release from that assignment by the certificate holder," computed in UTC or local time to reflect total elapsed time. Duty period therefore includes ground time, sits, delays and deadhead within the assignment — it is elapsed time, not flight time.
- **Calendar day** — midnight-to-midnight in UTC or local time (relevant to any calendar-day bookkeeping, not to the rest arithmetic itself).

Consequences for the schedule:

1. The rest must be **consecutive clock hours** (9:00 = 540 minutes; 8:00 = 480 minutes). It cannot be assembled from fragments.
2. The rest must **sit between** the end of the scheduled duty period and the start of the next duty period. Time before report or after release that is not contiguous with the rest window does not count.
3. § 135.273(b)(11) — "No certificate holder may assign a flight attendant to perform any duty with the certificate holder during any required rest period." Any assignment during the rest window is a violation regardless of whether the flight attendant actually sleeps.
4. § 135.273(b)(10) — "No certificate holder may assign a flight attendant any duty period with the certificate holder unless the flight attendant has had at least the minimum rest required under this section." The rest is a precondition to the next assignment, not a post-hoc accounting entry.

## 4. Rest matrix for the flight attendant duty bands (context)

| Paragraph | Scheduled duty period | Required rest | Permitted reduction | Condition on reduction |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| (b)(2) | **14 h or less** | **9 consecutive h** | **to 8 consecutive h** | Subsequent rest of **≥10 consecutive h**, scheduled to begin **≤24 h after the beginning of the reduced rest**, occurring between completion of the scheduled duty period and commencement of the subsequent duty period |
| (b)(7) | More than 14 h (permitted only under (b)(4)–(b)(6), e.g. (b)(4): >14 h to ≤16 h with at least one additional flight attendant assigned to the flight(s)) | 12 consecutive h | to 10 consecutive h | Subsequent rest of **≥14 consecutive h**, same 24-hour start trigger; **plus** (b)(9): the certificate holder may not schedule that flight attendant for a duty period of more than 14 h during the 24-hour period commencing after the beginning of the reduced rest |

Only the first row answers this request. The second row is included so the 14-hour boundary is unambiguous and so nobody applies (b)(8)/(b)(9) to an (b)(2) reduction.

## 5. How the 8-hour reduction works in practice

### 5.1 Conditions, stated as a checklist

All of the following must be true before a schedule may use the 8-hour figure:

1. The preceding **scheduled** duty period was **14 hours or less** (so (b)(2), not (b)(7), sets the baseline).
2. The first rest period is **at least 8 consecutive hours** and is **scheduled** as such.
3. A **subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours** is provided.
4. That subsequent rest is **scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced (8-hour) rest period**.
5. That subsequent rest occurs **between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period** — i.e. it is a real rest between real duty periods, not a paper entry.
6. Both rest periods are free of all responsibility for work or duty ((a) definition), with no duty assigned during them ((b)(11)).
7. The 8-hour figure is a floor, not a target: 8:00 exactly satisfies the minimum; anything less does not, and no provision of § 135.273 authorizes less than 8 consecutive hours for a flight attendant in this band.

**No lodging or sleeping-facility prerequisite appears in § 135.273(b)(3).** Unlike rest-reduction schemes that condition relief on suitable accommodation, the flight-attendant reduction here is conditioned **solely** on the subsequent 10-hour rest and its 24-hour timing trigger. A hotel requirement can still bind — but only if it comes from the company manual, a collective bargaining agreement, an operations specification, or a foreign state's rule on an international leg. Do not write a lodging condition into the regulatory minimum, and do not assume that providing a hotel buys relief that (b)(3) does not grant.

### 5.2 The 24-hour budget (the arithmetic that actually governs the pairing)

The 24-hour clock starts at the **beginning of the reduced rest period** and runs continuously. Once the 8-hour rest begins, the operator has:

```
24 h  −  8 h (reduced rest)  =  16 h
```

of elapsed time in which to finish everything else and have the **subsequent 10-hour rest actually begin**. That 16 hours must absorb:

```
gap1  +  intervening duty period  +  gap2  ≤  16 h
```

where gap1 = time between the end of the reduced rest and the report time of the intervening duty period, and gap2 = time between release from that duty period and the start of the 10-hour rest. (gap1 and gap2 are not rest and not duty; they consume the budget nonetheless.)

Because the intervening duty period is itself capped at 14 scheduled hours by (b)(1), the maximum-duty case is:

```
8 h rest  +  14 h duty  =  22 h  ≤  24 h   → compliant, with 2 h of slack
```

So the reduction is arithmetically safe **only if** gaps total **≤ 2 hours** when the intervening duty runs the full 14 hours. If gaps are larger, the intervening duty must be correspondingly shorter:

```
max intervening duty  =  16 h  −  gap1  −  gap2
```

Worked example (compliant): Duty A released 23:00 Monday. Reduced rest 23:00 Mon – 07:00 Tue (8 h). Report 07:00 Tue, Duty B released 19:00 Tue (12 h duty, ≤14 h, gaps 0). Subsequent rest starts 19:00 Tue — that is 20 hours after 23:00 Mon, inside the 24-hour trigger — and runs 19:00 Tue to 05:00 Wed (10 h). All of (b)(2), (b)(3) satisfied.

Worked example (non-compliant): Duty A released 23:00 Monday. Reduced rest 23:00 Mon – 07:00 Tue. Report 09:00 Tue (gap1 = 2 h), Duty B released 23:30 Tue (14.5 h — also a (b)(1) problem). Subsequent rest would begin 23:30 Tue, i.e. 24.5 hours after 23:00 Mon → violates the 24-hour trigger in (b)(3), and the duty period exceeds the 14-hour scheduled limit. Two independent failures.

### 5.3 What the reduction does **not** trigger

§ 135.273(b)(9)'s prohibition — no scheduling of a duty period of more than 14 hours during the 24-hour period commencing after the beginning of the reduced rest — is expressly tied to a reduction **to 10 hours under (b)(8)**, i.e. the more-than-14-hour band. It does **not** apply to an 8-hour reduction under (b)(3). After an 8-hour reduced rest, the flight attendant's next duty period is governed by (b)(1) and (b)(4)–(b)(6) on their own terms. Do not over-apply (b)(9) to (b)(3) pairings, and do not assume (b)(3) carries a hidden duty cap — it does not.

## 6. Scheduled versus actual duty time

§ 135.273 is drafted in terms of the **scheduled** duty period: (b)(1) prohibits assigning a flight attendant to a scheduled duty period of more than 14 hours; (b)(2) attaches to a flight attendant "scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less"; (b)(3) speaks of the "scheduled rest period." The duty-period definition, however, measures **elapsed** time from report to release.

Operational rules to draw from that:

1. **Build the schedule against the 14-hour line, not against planned flight time.** A pairing planned at 13:30 of scheduled duty has 30 minutes of margin; a 45-minute ground delay consumes all of it.
2. **§ 135.273 contains no "circumstances beyond the control of the certificate holder" relief provision** analogous to § 135.267(e) for flight crewmembers. There is no regulatory table converting an overrun into 11/12/16 hours of rest for a flight attendant. Treat any actual duty period that exceeds the scheduled figure as a compliance event requiring review before the next assignment, and route the question of how an overrun interacts with the scheduled-rest requirement to counsel and the assigned Principal Operations Inspector rather than resolving it by analogy to the pilot rule.
3. **Schedule the rest, then protect it.** Because (b)(3) requires the *subsequent* 10-hour rest to be *scheduled* to begin within 24 hours of the reduced rest's start, the reduction cannot be validated after the fact. The pairing must be built with both rest periods and the intervening duty on the same timeline before the trip is published.
4. **Company policy, CBA, and operations specifications may be stricter.** Nothing in this answer authorizes going below 9/8 consecutive hours, and an internal fatigue risk management program, a labor agreement, an insurer's requirement, or a foreign authority's rule on an international segment can raise the floor. Confirm which overlay applies before publishing a reduced-rest pairing; the regulatory minimum is a floor, not a plan.

## 7. Records and demonstrability

Because the 8-hour reduction is conditioned on a **future** rest period, the compliance case exists only if the schedule shows it. Retain, per flight attendant and per pairing:

- scheduled report and release times defining each duty period (elapsed, in a stated time zone — UTC or local, used consistently);
- scheduled rest windows, with the start and end of the reduced rest and the start and end of the subsequent rest;
- the computed interval from the beginning of the reduced rest to the beginning of the subsequent rest, showing it is ≤ 24:00;
- any actual deviation from the scheduled times, with the duty-period recomputation and the corrective action taken.

Follow § 135.63 and the recordkeeping terms of the operator's operations specifications for retention form and period, and make these records retrievable for inspection on the same basis as flight-time records.

## 8. Points to verify before the pairing is used (do not affect the two answers)

1. **§ 135.273(c).** Paragraph (b) opens "Except as provided in paragraph (c) of this section…", so (c) contains an exception to the (b) requirements. The text of (c) was not captured in the source excerpts used here. Pull the current (c) and confirm whether it can reach an on-demand flight-attendant pairing; if it can, it is a separate authorization path, not a change to the 9-hour baseline or the 8-hour reduction.
2. **§ 135.273(b)(5) and (b)(6).** These are the further augmentation bands referenced in (b)(1) and (b)(9); their exact hour limits were not captured. They are irrelevant to a 14-hour-or-less duty period and were deliberately not quoted.
3. **Operations specification crew complement.** Confirm whether a flight attendant is required by the operator's opSpecs for the aircraft flown. Either way § 135.273 applies if one is assigned, but the answer to "is a flight attendant required at all" drives staffing and training obligations elsewhere.

## 9. One-line compliance statement for the manual

"A flight attendant assigned to a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less receives a scheduled rest period of at least 9 consecutive hours between completion of that duty period and commencement of the next duty period. That rest may be reduced to no less than 8 consecutive hours only when a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours is scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period and occurs between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period. Both rest periods are free of all responsibility for work or duty, and no duty is assigned during either."

# HTTP/2: current specification and its obsoleted RFCs

## Answers

1. **Current specification of HTTP/2: RFC 9113**, "HTTP/2", Standards Track, published June 2022, ISSN 2070-1721. Editors: M. Thomson (Mozilla), C. Benfield (Apple Inc.). DOI 10.17487/RFC9113. It is the published result of the HTTPBIS working group's `draft-ietf-httpbis-http2bis` effort (the -02 draft already carried the same obsoletion statement).
2. **RFCs obsoleted by RFC 9113: RFC 7540 and RFC 8740** — exactly two.
   - **RFC 7540**, "Hypertext Transfer Protocol Version 2 (HTTP/2)", Standards Track, May 2015 (Belshe, Peon, Thomson, Eds.) — the original HTTP/2 specification.
   - **RFC 8740**, "Using TLS 1.3 with HTTP/2", February 2020 (Benjamin) — the TLS 1.3 profile that amended how HTTP/2 runs over TLS 1.3; its content was folded into RFC 9113 (Appendix B: "Use of TLS 1.3 was defined based on [RFC8740], which this document obsoletes").

## Evidence (authoritative metadata, quoted)

From the RFC Editor / Datatracker page for RFC 9113 (https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9113):

> "RFC: 9113 / Obsoletes: 7540, 8740 / Category: Standards Track / Published: June 2022 / ISSN: 2070-1721"

> "This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740."

> "This revision of HTTP/2 marks the HTTP2-Settings header field and the h2c upgrade token, both defined in [RFC7540], as obsolete."

> "Appendix B. Changes from RFC 7540 ... Use of TLS 1.3 was defined based on [RFC8740], which this document obsoletes."

From RFC 7540 itself (https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7540/): it identifies as "RFC 7540 HTTP/2 May 2015" and states "This specification is an alternative to, but does not obsolete, the HTTP/1.1 message syntax" — i.e. RFC 7540 obsoleted nothing; it is purely a target of obsoletion by 9113.

From `draft-ietf-httpbis-http2bis-02` (the pre-publication draft): "This document obsoletes RFC 7540 and RFC 8740" — consistent with the published RFC 9113, confirming no divergence between draft intent and final metadata.

## Scope and definitions applied

- **"Current"** = the RFC carrying active Standards Track status for HTTP/2 in the IETF RFC Series, as reflected by the RFC Editor's metadata at lookup time (pages fetched 2026-11-16T01:28:50Z). Nothing in the fetched material names a successor to RFC 9113.
- **"Obsoletes"** = the formal `Obsoletes:` header field of the specification, not informally superseded or "spiritually replaced" documents. That is why the answer is exactly {7540, 8740}.
- **Obsoletes ≠ Updates.** These are distinct formal relations in RFC metadata and must not be conflated. RFC 9113 *obsoletes* 7540 and 8740; documents that *update* or *extend* RFC 9113 (for example the extensible prioritization scheme that replaces the deprecated RFC 7540 priority signalling) are not part of this answer and do not change the obsoletes list.
- **Not obsoleted, but related — stated explicitly to prevent a wrong inference:**
  - **RFC 7541 (HPACK: Header Compression for HTTP/2)** is *not* in RFC 9113's Obsoletes field. HPACK remains a separate, current companion specification that RFC 9113 references for field compression. It must not be listed as obsoleted.
  - **RFC 7230–7235 (HTTP/1.1)** and the HTTP semantics documents are untouched: RFC 9113 "is an alternative to, but does not obsolete, the HTTP/1.1 message syntax."
  - **RFC 7301 (ALPN)**, **RFC 8446 (TLS 1.3)**, etc. are normative references, not obsoleted documents.
- **Deprecated by RFC 9113 but not obsoleted RFCs:** the HTTP/1.1 Upgrade mechanism to h2c and the `HTTP2-Settings` header field (both defined in RFC 7540) are marked obsolete *as protocol features* by RFC 9113 §11. This is feature-level deprecation, distinct from document-level obsoletion; the document-level obsoletion is still just 7540 and 8740.
- **Errata** against RFC 9113 exist or may exist and would be listed at https://www.rfc-editor.org/errata/rfc9113; errata correct text and never change the Obsoletes field, so they cannot alter either answer.

## Re-verification procedure (RFC status is time-dependent)

Because a future RFC could obsolete RFC 9113 and thereby change both answers at once, re-check with this two-step procedure before relying on the values:

1. Fetch `https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113` (or `https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9113/`) and read the **Status** block. If it says "Obsoleted by: RFC NNNN", then the current HTTP/2 specification is RFC NNNN and this answer must be recomputed from that document's own `Obsoletes:` field.
2. Independently confirm the obsoletes list from the *new* document's header block, not from the old document's page — the `Obsoletes:` field of the successor is authoritative, and obsoletion chains do not always restate earlier targets.

A quick one-line check of the same fact: search `https://www.rfc-editor.org/search/rfc_search_detail.php?title=HTTP%2F2` and take the highest-numbered Standards Track entry titled "HTTP/2" that is not itself marked obsoleted.

## Compact answer for downstream use

```
http2_current_spec: RFC 9113            # "HTTP/2", Standards Track, June 2022
http2_obsoletes:    [RFC 7540, RFC 8740] # original spec + TLS 1.3 profile
# not obsoleted: RFC 7541 (HPACK), HTTP/1.1 RFCs 7230-7235
# obsoleted_by:   (none known at 2026-11-16)
```
