# UK statutory minimum wage rates from April 2026

## 1. Headline answer

| Age band | Statutory rate from 1 April 2026 | Rate it replaces (to 31 March 2026) | Cash increase | % increase |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **National Living Wage — 21 and over** | **£12.71 per hour** | £12.21 | +£0.50 | 4.1% |
| **National Minimum Wage — 18 to 20** | **£10.85 per hour** | £10.00 | +£0.85 | 8.5% |

- Ask 1 answer: **£12.71/hour** (National Living Wage, workers aged 21 and over).
- Ask 2 answer: **£10.85/hour** (18–20 Year Old Rate of the National Minimum Wage).
- Currency: pounds sterling (GBP), published to the penny. Rates are per hour worked.
- These are **confirmed statutory rates**, not projections: the Government announced them on **26 November 2025**, accepting in full the Low Pay Commission's recommendations, and they took effect on **1 April 2026**.

## 2. Effective date and wage year

- The rates apply **from 1 April 2026** and remain in force until **31 March 2027** (the 2026/27 minimum wage year). The statutory rates change on 1 April each year.
- "From April 2026" is therefore read as the wage year beginning 1 April 2026. Any figure quoted for a date before 1 April 2026 should use the previous rates (£12.21 for 21+; £10.00 for 18–20); any figure for on/after 1 April 2026 uses £12.71 / £10.85.
- Statutory basis: National Minimum Wage Act 1998 as amended, with the annual uprating given effect by regulations made under it. The NLW age threshold has been 21 since April 2024 (it was 25+ before April 2021 and 23+ from April 2021), and the age structure is unchanged for 2026/27.

## 3. Full 2026/27 rate table (for completeness and to prevent band mix-ups)

| Rate | From 1 April 2026 | Increase (£) | Increase (%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| National Living Wage (21 and over) | £12.71 | £0.50 | 4.1 |
| 18–20 Year Old Rate | £10.85 | £0.85 | 8.5 |
| 16–17 Year Old Rate | £8.00 | £0.45 | 6.0 |
| Apprentice Rate | £8.00 | £0.45 | 6.0 |
| Accommodation Offset (daily, maximum deduction) | £11.10 | £0.44 | 4.1 |

Apprentice-rate eligibility (unchanged): apprentices aged under 19, or aged 19+ in the first year of their apprenticeship, are entitled to the apprentice rate (£8.00). An apprentice aged 19+ who has completed the first year moves onto the rate for their age — e.g. an apprentice aged 21+ in year two or later is entitled to £12.71.

## 4. Sources (primary, GOV.UK)

1. **Low Pay Commission press release, "LPC recommendations take the National Living Wage to £12.71", published 26 November 2025** — https://www.gov.uk/government/news/lpc-recommendations-take-the-national-living-wage-to-1271. States: "The National Living Wage, the minimum wage rate for all workers aged 21 and over, will rise by 4.1 per cent to £12.71. The minimum wage for 18-20 year olds will increase to £10.85..." and gives the full rate table. (Fetched 2026-11-16; sha256 8c9e3af8cfea.)
2. **"Minimum wage rates for 2026" (LPC advice to Government), published 26 November 2025** — https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/minimum-wage-rates-for-2026. "These will be effective from April 2026. The Government accepted in full the recommendations of the independent Low Pay Commission." Table repeats £12.71 / £10.85 / £8.00 / £8.00 / £11.10. (sha256 6dffcb981ddd.)
3. **"The National Minimum Wage in 2026" (LPC impact report), published 1 April 2026** — https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-national-minimum-wage-in-2026. "From 1 April 2026, all rates of the National Minimum Wage, including the National Living Wage, increase." Same table. (sha256 40f99264be4b.)
4. **Low Pay Commission Report 2025, published 2 February 2026, last updated 18 March 2026** — https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/low-pay-commission-report-2025. "The rates which will come into force from 1 April 2026 are as follows... National Living Wage (21 and over) £12.71... 18-20 Year Old Rate £10.85..." (sha256 71375eacc474.)
5. **GOV.UK standing guidance, "National Minimum Wage rates"** — https://www.gov.uk/national-minimum-wage-rates. Row "April 2026": 21 and over £12.71; 18 to 20 £10.85; Under 18 £8; Apprentice £8. (sha256 ef041e4e0285.)

Five independent GOV.UK pages agree on both figures, and the April 2026 impact report post-dates commencement, so the values are confirmed both prospectively (announcement) and retrospectively (in-force).

**Source caveat to record:** the LPC Report 2025 page carries an update log noting "4 February 2026 — Corrected rates for youth, apprentices and accommodation offset" and "18 March 2026 — correction slip added to the report PDF". The operative youth figures after correction (£10.85, £8.00, £8.00, £11.10) match the 26 November 2025 announcement and the April 2026 report, so the headline answer is unaffected; anyone citing an early-February PDF draft of the youth rates should re-check against the corrected version.

## 5. Arithmetic verification (all published figures reconcile)

| Rate | Prior year | New | Difference | Computed % | Published % |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| NLW 21+ | £12.21 | £12.71 | £0.50 | 0.50/12.21 = 4.095% -> 4.1% | 4.1 |
| 18–20 | £10.00 | £10.85 | £0.85 | 0.85/10.00 = 8.500% | 8.5 |
| 16–17 | £7.55 | £8.00 | £0.45 | 0.45/7.55 = 5.960% -> 6.0% | 6.0 |
| Apprentice | £7.55 | £8.00 | £0.45 | 5.960% -> 6.0% | 6.0 |
| Accommodation offset | £10.66 | £11.10 | £0.44 | 0.44/10.66 = 4.128% -> 4.1% | 4.1 |

All percentage increases stated in the deliverable match the ratios implied by the cash figures to one decimal place; no internal contradiction.

## 6. Derived equivalents (clearly labelled as computed, not published)

For a 37.5-hour week, the 2026/27 rates imply:

- NLW 21+: £12.71 x 37.5 = **£476.63/week** gross; annualised at 52 weeks = £24,784.50.
- 18–20 rate: £10.85 x 37.5 = **£406.88/week** gross; annualised at 52 weeks = £21,157.50.

These are arithmetic illustrations only; the statutory figure is the hourly rate. (Note: no statutory salaried-hours threshold is asserted here — the salary-basis rules use a different calculation and should be checked separately if needed.)

## 7. Scope, jurisdiction and common-confusion guards

- **UK-wide including Northern Ireland.** The National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage are reserved, UK-wide rates set under the NMW Act 1998; they apply in England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland alike. There is no separate NI minimum wage rate, so £12.71 and £10.85 are the correct figures for all four nations.
- **Not the Real Living Wage.** These are statutory rates. The Living Wage Foundation's voluntary "Real Living Wage" is a separate, higher, voluntarily-paid benchmark calculated by the Resolution Foundation and announced in the autumn; it is not the National Living Wage and should not be substituted here.
- **Not the April 2027 figures.** The GOV.UK guidance page also shows a forward-looking "April 2027" row (£13.21 for 21+, £11.27 for 18–20, £8.31 for under-18/apprentice). Those are the following year's rates and must not be used for April 2026.
- **Band boundaries.** "21 and over" gets the NLW; workers aged 20 and under get the NMW age rates. Someone who turns 21 during the pay period is entitled to the NLW from their 21st birthday (not from the start of the pay period). The Government has stated an ambition, with an LPC-designed path, to extend the NLW to 20-year-olds in 2027 and to 18–19-year-olds in 2028 or 2029, subject to economic conditions — this does not change the 2026/27 rates.

## 8. Context notes on the 2026/27 uprating (optional supporting detail)

- The NLW rise of 4.1% is intended to keep the rate at or above two-thirds of median hourly earnings for the NLW population, and the LPC's remit required it to take account of the cost of living including inflation forecasts between April 2026 and April 2027.
- The 8.5% rise in the 18–20 rate is explicitly framed by the LPC as progress towards extending the NLW to younger workers; it is smaller than recent double-digit youth increases and well below the ~25% that immediate alignment would have required.
- The LPC judged that recent NLW increases had not had a significant negative impact on jobs, while noting pressure on employers (including the April 2025 National Insurance changes) and concerns about the strength of the youth labour market.
- Rates are enforced by HMRC; workers who believe they are underpaid can use the GOV.UK minimum wage calculator or contact Acas.

## 9. One-line answer for reuse

"From 1 April 2026 the UK National Living Wage for workers aged 21 and over is **£12.71 per hour**, and the National Minimum Wage for 18–20 year olds is **£10.85 per hour** (GOV.UK / Low Pay Commission, announced 26 November 2025, in force 1 April 2026)."

question: M11
answer:
FMCSA SHORT-HAUL EXCEPTION — THE TWO REQUESTED FIGURES

Governing provision: 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1), "150 air-mile radius driver" (current text, post-2020 revision; mandatory compliance since September 29, 2020).

ANSWER 1 — RADIUS: 150 air miles (the regulation states the equivalent as 172.6 statute miles) measured from the driver's normal work reporting location.

ANSWER 2 — RELEASE TIME: 14 consecutive hours. The driver must return to the work reporting location and be released from work within 14 consecutive hours.

VERBATIM REGULATORY TEXT (49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)):
"(e) Short-haul operations —
(1) 150 air-mile radius driver. A driver is exempt from the requirements of §§ 395.8 and 395.11 if:
(i) The driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location;
(ii) The driver, except a driver-salesperson, returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours;
(iii)(A) A property-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 10 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty;
(B) A passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 8 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty; and
(iv) The motor carrier that employs the driver maintains and retains for a period of 6 months accurate and true time records showing: (A) The time the driver reports for duty each day; (B) The total number of hours the driver is on-duty each day; (C) The time the driver is released from duty each day; and (D) The total time for the preceding 7 days in accordance with § 395.8(j)(2) for drivers used for the first time or intermittently."

TWO THINGS THE FIGURES DO NOT DEPEND ON
1. Property-carrying vs. passenger-carrying. Both are 150 air miles and 14 consecutive hours. The only property/passenger difference inside (e)(1) is the off-duty block that must separate each 14-hour on-duty period: 10 consecutive hours for property-carrying, 8 consecutive hours for passenger-carrying. FMCSA's own side-by-side summary table prints the identical short-haul sentence in both the property and passenger columns.
2. Whether the driver holds a CDL, for purposes of (e)(1).

UNIT AND MEASUREMENT NOTES (operationally important, and the most common error)
- The radius is AIR MILES (straight-line), not road miles. A driver whose road route exceeds 150 miles may still qualify if every point stays inside the 150 air-mile circle; conversely a driver on a short road route can leave the circle. 150 air miles = 172.6 statute miles.
- The radius is measured from the normal work reporting location, and the driver must both start and end the duty period at that location. FMCSA guidance permits the reporting location to change from shift to shift so long as each individual shift starts and ends at the same place.
- The 14 hours run from the time the driver comes on duty; release must occur at the reporting location within that window. If the driver cannot return and be released within 14 consecutive hours, the exception is unavailable for that day and the driver must record duty status (paper log or ELD) for that day.

SCOPE CAVEATS
- Superseded figures: before the 2020 revision the exception was a 100 air-mile radius with a 12-hour duty period. Those numbers are historical only and are NOT the answer under the current rule.
- Separate provision, same radius, different release rule: 49 CFR 395.1(e)(2) covers drivers of property-carrying CMVs for which no CDL is required. It also uses a 150 air-mile radius, but it does not impose a single release deadline — instead the driver must return to the normal work reporting location at the end of each duty tour and may not drive after the 14th hour on 5 days of any 7 consecutive days or after the 16th hour on 2 days of any 7 consecutive days. If the operation in question is a non-CDL property operation, the radius answer is unchanged at 150 air miles, but the release-time answer should be read against (e)(2), not (e)(1).
- The exception relieves the driver of the record-of-duty-status requirement (§ 395.8) and the ELD-related requirement of § 395.11; it does not relieve the carrier of the 6-month time-record obligation quoted above, and it does not by itself resolve state-level rules that may apply in addition to the federal rule.
- Other short-haul-type provisions carry different radii (e.g., the motion-picture exception in § 395.1(p) uses 100 air miles) and must not be conflated with the RODS exception asked about here.

SOURCES CONSULTED
- eCFR, 49 CFR 395.1 (current), paragraphs (e)(1), (e)(2), (p).
- FMCSA, Summary of Hours of Service Regulations (property and passenger columns).
- FMCSA, Hours of Service for Motor Carriers of Passengers.
- FMCSA HOS Visor Card and June 2020 HOS presentation (2020 final rule changes: radius 100 -> 150 air miles; duty period 12 -> 14 hours).

question: M1
answer:
BASICMED (US) — AIRCRAFT LIMITS ON THE PILOT ACTING AS PIC
Authority: 14 CFR § 61.113(i)(1), as amended by Pub. L. 118-63 (FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024), § 828, 'Expansion of BasicMed.' Current limits took effect November 12, 2024.

1. MAXIMUM TAKEOFF WEIGHT — 12,500 lb (maximum certificated takeoff weight, MTOW)
   The aircraft must have a maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds. This is the certificated MTOW in the aircraft's design approval (TC, STC, or amended TC) or, for experimental/other aircraft, the weight established by the operator — not the actual weight on a given flight.
   Exception: transport category helicopters are excluded from the weight increase and remain limited to 6,000 lb MTOW under BasicMed. If the aircraft in question is a transport category helicopter, the applicable figure is 6,000 lb, not 12,500 lb.

2. NUMBER OF OCCUPANTS THE AIRCRAFT MAY BE AUTHORIZED TO CARRY — 7 occupants
   The aircraft must be authorized to carry no more than seven occupants, counting every person the design approval permits on board, including required flightcrew. 'Authorized' means the number specified in the aircraft's design approval (type certificate, supplemental type certificate, or amended type certificate) or, for experimental aircraft, the number established by the operator — it is a property of the aircraft, not of who is actually seated. An aircraft certificated for more than seven occupants does not qualify for BasicMed even if fewer seats are installed. (For experimental aircraft, § 91.319(j) independently bars carrying more than seven occupants under BasicMed.)

3. NUMBER OF PASSENGERS ON BOARD — 6 passengers
   The flight may be operated with no more than six passengers on board. Occupants and passengers are not the same count: the pilot in command operating under BasicMed is an occupant but not a passenger. Six passengers plus the BasicMed PIC equals seven occupants, which is exactly at — and does not exceed — the seven-occupant authorization in item 2. If the aircraft is type certificated for two required pilot crewmembers, the second pilot is an occupant and a required flightcrew member rather than a passenger, so the passenger count reduces accordingly; the seven-occupant total still governs.

ARITHMETIC CONSISTENCY
   passengers (6) + PIC (1) = occupants (7) ≤ authorized occupants (7). No figure stated above exceeds any limit stated above.

COMPANION OPERATING LIMITS (same rule; stated because they are routinely applied together and a pilot checking the aircraft limits will need them)
   - Within the United States (or another country in which BasicMed is authorized).
   - At or below 18,000 ft MSL.
   - At an indicated airspeed not exceeding 250 knots.
   - Not for compensation or hire.
   - No flight during a medical deficiency (§ 61.53).
   - BasicMed relief applies only to the pilot acting as PIC; a safety pilot or instructor who is not PIC needs a medical certificate.
   These do not change the three answers above; they are listed for completeness of the aircraft/operation check.

CURRENCY WARNING — SUPERSEDED FIGURES
The following pre-November 12, 2024 figures still appear in widely circulated FAA material and must NOT be used:
   - AC 68-1A (dated 5/3/17), § 3.2: 6,000 lb MTOW / 6 occupants / 5 passengers.
   - FAA Safety Briefing, July/August 2017: 6,000 lb / 6 occupants / 5 passengers.
   - FAA Notice N 8000.386 (11/14/24) itself recites both sets, labeling the 6,000 / 6 / 5 set as the pre-expansion values and the 12,500 / 7 / 6 set as applying 'on or after November 12, 2024.'
The current FAA BasicMed webpage and the FAA newsroom release of November 15, 2024 ('FAA Updates BasicMed Program') both state the expanded limits: not more than 7 occupants, not more than 12,500 lb MTOW, not more than 6 passengers. Any answer citing 6,000 lb / 6 occupants / 5 passengers is out of date.

VERIFICATION NOTE
   Before relying on these numbers for a specific flight, confirm against the current text of § 61.113(i)(1) in 14 CFR (eCFR) and the aircraft's own design approval (TCDS or operating limitations) for the certificated MTOW and authorized occupant count, since those are aircraft-specific values that the rule only caps.
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 6 on faa.gov/documentlibrary/media/advisory_circular/ac_68-1a.pdf and 7 on faa.gov/documentlibrary/media/notice/n_8000.386.pdf. The first reads: "Fly an aircraft that is authorized to carry no more than 6 occupants."

question: M3
answer:
HOURS-OF-SERVICE LIMITS — DRIVER OF A PASSENGER-CARRYING CMV (MOTORCOACH), INTERSTATE, US FEDERAL RULES

Governing provision: 49 CFR 395.5, 'Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles' (current eCFR; identical text in the 2025 printed CFR, 49 CFR vol. 5, sec. 395.5; originally added at 70 FR 50073, Aug. 25, 2005). This is the passenger-carrying rule, not the property-carrying rule in 395.3, so the property-carrier figures (11-hour driving / 14-hour on-duty / 10-hour off-duty) do NOT apply here. Section 395.5 is expressly '[s]ubject to the exceptions and exemptions in 395.1' — see the exceptions note at the end.

1. THE THREE LIMITS (direct answers)

| # | Question | Answer | Regulatory basis |
|---|----------|--------|------------------|
| 1 | How many hours may they drive? | 10 hours of driving time following 8 consecutive hours off duty | 395.5(a)(1) |
| 2 | After how many consecutive hours off duty? | 8 consecutive hours off duty (may be off duty, sleeper berth, or any combination; no on-duty or driving time within them) | 395.5(a)(1) and (a)(2) |
| 3 | After how many hours on duty may they no longer drive? | 15 hours on duty following 8 consecutive hours off duty — no driving at any time after the 15th on-duty hour | 395.5(a)(2) |

Text of the rule as published (eCFR, current):

'395.5 Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles.
Subject to the exceptions and exemptions in 395.1:
(a) No motor carrier shall permit or require any driver used by it to drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle, nor shall any such driver drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle:
(1) More than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty; or
(2) For any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty.'

2. HOW THE THREE LIMITS INTERACT (operational reading)

- The 8-hour reset starts both clocks. A driver may not begin a new 10-hour driving period or a new 15-hour on-duty window until he or she has had 8 consecutive hours off duty (off duty, sleeper berth, or a combination, with no on-duty or driving time inside the 8 hours).
- The 10-hour limit is a cap on cumulative driving time within the work window, not a cap on any single continuous stint. The driver may drive in as many separate segments as desired; once cumulative driving in the window reaches 10 hours, no further driving is permitted until another 8 consecutive hours off duty.
- The 15-hour limit is a cap on the elapsed on-duty window, not a cap on driving. After the 15th on-duty hour, the driver may continue non-driving work but may not drive. Off-duty time taken during the day (a lunch break, a nap) does not extend the 15-hour clock.
- Whichever limit is reached first governs. Because 10 < 15, a driver who drives continuously will hit the driving limit first and stop at 10 hours of driving; a driver who spends substantial time on duty but not driving (loading, passenger handling, inspections, waiting) will hit the 15-hour on-duty limit first. The 10-hour figure can never be reached after the 15-hour clock has expired, because no driving is permitted past hour 15.

3. WORKED EXAMPLE (internally consistent)

Driver reports for duty at 06:00 after 8 consecutive hours off duty (22:00 previous night to 06:00). The 15-hour on-duty clock therefore expires at 21:00.
- Drives 06:00-10:00 (4.0 driving hours).
- On duty not driving 10:00-11:00 (passenger boarding, pre-trip).
- Drives 11:00-15:00 (4.0 more; cumulative 8.0 driving hours).
- Off duty 15:00-15:30 (lunch — does not extend the 15-hour clock; the clock still expires at 21:00).
- Drives 15:30-17:30 (2.0 more; cumulative 10.0 driving hours — driving limit reached).
Result: the driver may not drive again until 8 consecutive hours off duty, even though the 15-hour on-duty window does not expire until 21:00. If instead the driver had accumulated only 7 driving hours by 21:00, the 15-hour limit would stop all further driving at 21:00 with 3 driving hours unused.

4. CONTEXT NOT INCLUDED IN THE THREE ANSWERS — WEEKLY LIMITS, 395.5(b)

The same section also bars driving after 60 hours on duty in any 7 consecutive days (carrier does not operate CMVs every day of the week) or 70 hours on duty in any 8 consecutive days (carrier operates CMVs every day of the week). These are outside the three questions asked, which concern the daily cycle, but they operate cumulatively with the 10- and 15-hour limits: a driver may be within the 10-hour and 15-hour daily limits and still be barred from driving by the 60/70-hour cap. All on-duty time for any employer counts toward the weekly total. Returning below the cap requires dropping under 60 (or 70) hours over the rolling 7- (or 8-) day period, not a fixed 34-hour restart (the 34-hour restart is a property-carrying provision, 395.3(c), and is not part of 395.5).

5. EXCEPTIONS THAT CAN ALTER THE EFFECTIVE FIGURES

Because 395.5 is '[s]ubject to the exceptions and exemptions in 395.1,' the 10/8/15 figures above are the baseline limits and can be modified in specific circumstances, including but not limited to: the adverse driving conditions exception (395.1(b)(1)), the sleeper-berth provisions (395.1(g)), the short-haul exception (395.1(e)), and the various exemptions in 395.1 (e.g., certain intrastate, government, and emergency-relief operations). Any of these must be checked against the specific operation before relying on the baseline numbers; none of them changes the answer to the three questions as posed for a standard interstate passenger-carrying operation.

6. SCOPE AND ASSUMPTIONS

- Assumed: interstate operation by a passenger-carrying CMV (motorcoach) under federal FMCSA jurisdiction, so 49 CFR Part 395 governs; current rules, not historical editions. If the operation is intrastate, the state's own HOS rules apply and must be checked separately — the figures above are the federal figures.
- Recordkeeping: such a driver is subject to the record-of-duty-status requirements of 395.8 and, absent a 395.1 exception (e.g., short-haul), must use an ELD.
- Citations: 49 CFR 395.5(a)(1), 395.5(a)(2), 395.5(b); FMCSA, 'Interstate Passenger Carrying Driver's Guide to Hours of Service' (15-hour on-duty limit, 10-hour driving limit, 60/70-hour duty limit).

question: M5
answer:
REGULATORY DETERMINATION — 14 CFR Part 135, flight attendant rest after a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less

== 1. ANSWER ==

(1) Minimum rest: at least 9 consecutive hours of scheduled rest, occurring between completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period. Citation: 14 CFR 135.273(b)(2).

(2) Reducible to: 8 consecutive hours, but only if the certificate holder provides a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours, which must be scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced (8-hour) rest period and must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period. Citation: 14 CFR 135.273(b)(3).

The 8-hour figure is a floor, not a target: it is available only when the 10-hour compensatory rest is actually delivered inside the 24-hour window.

== 2. GOVERNING TEXT ==

14 CFR 135.273(b) provides, in relevant part:

- (b)(1): "Except as provided in paragraphs (b)(4), (b)(5), and (b)(6) of this section, no certificate holder may assign a flight attendant to a scheduled duty period of more than 14 hours."
- (b)(2): "Except as provided in paragraph (b)(3) of this section, a flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less as provided under paragraph (b)(1) of this section must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 9 consecutive hours. This rest period must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period."
- (b)(3): "The rest period required under paragraph (b)(2) of this section may be scheduled or reduced to 8 consecutive hours if the flight attendant is provided a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours; this subsequent rest period must be scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period and must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period."

Applicability: 14 CFR 135.273(e) — "Section 135.273 prescribes duty period limitations and rest requirements for flight attendants in all operations conducted under this part." The rule is not limited to scheduled passenger operations; it reaches on-demand charter operations under Part 135 that use flight attendants. The 135.265 / 135.267 / 135.269 flight-time schemes govern flight crewmembers, not flight attendants, unless the operator affirmatively elects the 135.273(c) alternative described in section 5 below.

== 3. THE REDUCTION — CONDITIONS THAT MUST ALL BE TRUE ==

A dispatch/scheduling desk may use the 8-hour rest only if every one of the following holds:

1. The preceding scheduled duty period was 14 hours or less (135.273(b)(1)-(b)(2)). If the duty period exceeded 14 hours under (b)(4)-(b)(6), the (b)(2)/(b)(3) scheme does not apply — a longer baseline rest applies under (b)(7), itself reducible to 10 consecutive hours under (b)(8) only with a subsequent rest of at least 14 consecutive hours beginning no later than 24 hours after the beginning of that reduced rest.
2. The rest given is at least 8 consecutive hours — consecutive meaning uninterrupted, not 8 hours aggregate across a split.
3. The 8-hour rest falls between completion of the scheduled duty period and commencement of the subsequent duty period.
4. A subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours is affirmatively scheduled (not merely hoped for).
5. That 10-hour rest is scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the 8-hour reduced rest period. The clock runs from the START of the reduced rest, not from its end and not from the start of the next duty period.
6. That 10-hour rest also falls between the completion of the intervening scheduled duty period and the commencement of the next duty period.

Related prohibitions that make the above enforceable rather than advisory:
- 135.273(b)(10): "No certificate holder may assign a flight attendant any duty period with the certificate holder unless the flight attendant has had at least the minimum rest required under this section."
- 135.273(b)(11): "No certificate holder may assign a flight attendant to perform any duty with the certificate holder during any required rest period." This bars deadhead legs, training, positioning, administrative work, or any other duty inside the 9-hour (or 8-hour) rest window.

Note on the word "scheduled": (b)(3) permits the shorter period to be "scheduled or reduced." An operator may build 8 hours into a published pairing in advance; it need not wait for an irregular-operation event. The compensatory 10-hour rest obligation attaches identically either way.

Note on frequency: the rule text states no numeric cap on how many times per week or month the 8-hour reduction may be used. What it does impose, per use, is the independent 10-hour compensatory rest with its 24-hour deadline, plus (b)(10)-(b)(11). An operator that reduces rest repeatedly must be able to show, trip by trip, that each reduction was paired with a compliant 10-hour rest inside the window. Many collective bargaining agreements and company manuals impose tighter limits or prohibit the reduction outright; those are contractual/policy constraints layered on top of the regulatory minimum, not regulatory ones.

== 4. WORKED EXAMPLE (arithmetic check) ==

Scheduled duty period: 0600-2000 local, 14.0 hours (at the (b)(1) ceiling, so (b)(2) governs).

Baseline case: rest begins at 2000. Nine consecutive hours of rest runs 2000-0500. Earliest permissible report for the next duty period is 0500.

Reduced case: rest scheduled 2000-0400 (8 consecutive hours). The 24-hour clock starts at 2000. The subsequent 10-hour rest must therefore BEGIN no later than 2000 the following day, and must be at least 10 consecutive hours (e.g., 2000 Day 2 to 0600 Day 3), sitting between the end of the intervening duty period and the start of the next one. If the intervening duty period ends at 2300 on Day 2, the 10-hour rest cannot begin at 2000 — it can only begin at 2300, which is 3 hours past the deadline, and the reduction is therefore not available for that pairing. The schedule must be rebuilt with a 9-hour rest or the intervening duty must end early enough that a 10-hour rest can start by 2000 Day 2.

This example is the practical failure mode: the 24-hour trigger is measured from the start of the reduced rest, and an intervening long duty can push the compensatory rest past the deadline even when the 10 hours themselves exist later in the week.

== 5. SCOPE CONDITIONS — WHERE THIS ANSWER WOULD NOT GOVERN ==

- Part 121 is different. The FAA final rule at ARM-220928-001 (Oct 4, 2022), implementing section 335(a) of the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2018, amended 14 CFR 121.467 to require at least 10 consecutive hours of rest for a flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less, and eliminated the reduced-rest option for Part 121. That rulemaking addressed 121.467, not 135.273. Part 135 flight attendants remain at 9 hours reducible to 8 under 135.273(b)(2)-(b)(3). Do not import the 10-hour/non-reducible Part 121 standard into a Part 135 analysis; the FAA's own FAQ for flight attendant duty and rest states the 9-hour/8-hour scheme with the 10-hour/24-hour compensatory condition.
- The 135.273(c) election. A certificate holder may, by written procedures approved by the Administrator and described or referenced in its operations specifications, apply the flight crewmember flight time and duty limitations and rest requirements of Part 135 subpart F to its flight attendants instead of the (b) scheme. If an operator has made that election, the applicable rest numbers are those of the elected flight crewmember section (e.g., the 135.265/135.267/135.269 rest tables), and this answer does not apply. Confirm against the operator's ops specs before relying on 9/8.
- Stricter instruments. A collective bargaining agreement, company manual, or ops spec may require more rest than 9 hours or forbid the reduction. The regulatory minimum is a floor; the binding number for a given crewmember is the highest applicable requirement.
- Definitional predicate. The analysis assumes the crewmember is a "flight attendant" within the meaning of 135.273(a) and is assigned as such on the trip in question. A cabin crewmember carried under some other authority is outside this answer.

== 6. COMPLIANCE PRACTICE NOTES ==

- Track scheduled versus actual duty. The rule is written in terms of the scheduled duty period; a schedule built to 14:00 that runs long does not retroactively convert the pairing into a (b)(4)-(b)(6) extension, but it does create a rest-start shift that must be re-checked against the 24-hour deadline on any reduced-rest pairing.
- Rest starts at the completion of duty, not at hotel arrival. Post-flight debrief, transport, and any assigned duty erode rest and are the usual source of non-compliance.
- Do not assign any duty inside the rest window, including positioning/deadhead, ground instruction, or paperwork (135.273(b)(11)).
- Records: retain flight time, duty time, and rest period records supporting each pairing, including the start and end timestamps of any reduced rest and the corresponding 10-hour compensatory rest, so the 24-hour deadline can be demonstrated on inspection. Records are the only defense to a (b)(10) allegation.

== 7. SOURCES ==

- 14 CFR 135.273(b)(1)-(b)(3), (b)(8)-(b)(11), (c), (e) — eCFR, current as fetched 2026-11-16 (sha256 88e87edd4ca6).
- 14 CFR Part 135 subpart F, § 135.273(e) applicability sentence — eCFR (sha256 f2b546df3c9b / 5af3a666334b).
- FAA, "What are the flight attendant duty period and rest requirements?" — states 9 consecutive hours, reducible to 8 with a subsequent 10 consecutive hours beginning no later than 24 hours after the start of the 8-hour rest (sha256 ae59e0f94f4d).
- FAA final rule, Flight Attendant Duty Period Limitations and Rest Requirements, ARM-220928-001 (Oct 4, 2022) — Part 121 / § 121.467 amendment to 10 hours and elimination of reduced rest; cited here to distinguish, not to apply (sha256 ef79f96400a9).

The first reads: "(1) A rest required under paragraph (b)(1) of this section may be scheduled for or reduced to a minimum of 8 hours if the flight crewmember is given a rest period of at least 10 hours that must begin no later than 24 hours after the commenc"

question: M7
answer:
# HTTP/2: current specification and what it obsoletes

## Answers

| Ask | Answer |
|---|---|
| 1. Current specification of HTTP/2 | **RFC 9113**, *HTTP/2*, Standards Track, June 2022, ISSN 2070-1721, editors M. Thomson (Mozilla) and C. Benfield (Apple Inc.) |
| 2. RFCs it obsoletes | **RFC 7540** and **RFC 8740** |

## Evidence (quoted from the fetched pages)

From the RFC 9113 header block (identical on `rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.html`, `rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113/`, and `datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9113`):

```
RFC:            9113
Obsoletes:      7540, 8740
Category:       Standards Track
Published:      June 2022
ISSN:           2070-1721
Authors:        M. Thomson, Ed. (Mozilla)
                C. Benfield, Ed. (Apple Inc.)
```

From the RFC 9113 abstract:

> "This specification describes an optimized expression of the semantics of the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP), referred to as HTTP version 2 (HTTP/2). … **This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740.**"

From the RFC 9113 Status of This Memo:

> "This is an Internet Standards Track document. … It represents the consensus of the IETF community and has received public review and been approved for publication by the IESG."

Cross-check from `rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7540.json` (metadata for the previous HTTP/2 specification):

```
title:        Hypertext Transfer Protocol Version 2 (HTTP/2)
pub_status:   PROPOSED STANDARD
pub_date:     May 2015
obsoleted_by: RFC9113
updated_by:   RFC8740
```

That metadata is consistent with the 9113 header: 7540 was first updated by 8740, then both were obsoleted together by 9113.

## What each obsoleted document is

- **RFC 7540** — *Hypertext Transfer Protocol Version 2 (HTTP/2)*, May 2015, Proposed Standard; the original HTTP/2 specification (Belshe, Peon, Thomson, Ed.). Confirmed by the fetched `rfc7540.html` text and `rfc7540.json`.
- **RFC 8740** — the other document named in RFC 9113's Obsoletes header. The fetched evidence establishes its *relationship* (it is recorded as an update to RFC 7540 in the RFC Editor metadata, and it is obsoleted by RFC 9113) but the fetched passages do not include its title. **Do not guess the title; confirm at <https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8740/> if a title is needed in downstream copy.**

## Important distinctions (per the task's assumptions)

1. **Obsoletes ≠ Updates.** "Obsoletes" is a formal RFC-stream designation declared in the document header. RFC 9113 *obsoletes* 7540 and 8740. Separately, RFC 9113 is *updated by* other documents (e.g., extensions), and those updates do **not** change the answer to ask 2. Only the `Obsoletes:` header does.
2. **HTTP/2 core vs. HTTP/2 extensions.** Documents such as the extensible prioritization scheme (RFC 9218), HTTP/2 Server Push discussions, or HTTP/3 (RFC 9114) are not "the HTTP/2 specification" and do not appear in RFC 9113's Obsoletes header. RFC 9113 sits in the June 2022 HTTP revision set (RFC 9110–9114); RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics) and RFC 9111 (HTTP/1.1) are siblings, not replacements for 9113.
3. **"Current" is time-indexed.** The evidence was fetched 2026-11-16. As of that date no successor document obsoleting RFC 9113 appears in any fetched source, so RFC 9113 is current. RFC 9113 itself records errata; errata correct text but do not change which document is current and do not add obsoleted RFCs.
4. **HTTP/1.1 is not obsoleted.** As RFC 7540's abstract already said, HTTP/2 "is an alternative to, but does not obsolete, the HTTP/1.1 message syntax." RFC 9113 inherits that position; 9111 (HTTP/1.1) remains current alongside 9113.

## Reproduction procedure (any engineer can run this)

```bash
# 1. Read the authoritative header of the current HTTP/2 spec
curl -s https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.txt | sed -n '1,25p'
#   expect:  "Obsoletes:  7540, 8740"
#            "Category:   Standards Track"
#            "Published:  June 2022"

# 2. Confirm the reverse pointer from the old spec
curl -s https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7540.json \
  | grep -E 'obsoleted_by|updated_by'
#   expect:  "obsoleted_by: RFC9113"
#            "updated_by: RFC8740"

# 3. Confirm no later obsoletion of 9113
curl -s https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113/ | grep -i 'obsoleted\|updated by'
#   expect: no "Obsoleted-by" entry
```

**Acceptance criterion:** step 1 prints `Obsoletes: 7540, 8740`. If a future revision prints a different list, the answer to ask 2 changes to that list and the answer to ask 1 changes to the new document number; nothing else in this deliverable needs rewriting.

## Caveats

- RFC numbers here are the RFC Editor's own (9113, 7540, 8740); no draft names (`draft-ietf-httpbis-http2-*`) are substituted, because drafts are not specifications once published.
- The only unverified detail is the *title* of RFC 8740, which the fetched sources did not supply; its number and its obsoletion status are directly verified.
cautions: The recompute vote disagrees with this answer on ask 2.

question: M9
answer:
UK MINIMUM WAGE RATES FROM 1 APRIL 2026 — HR BRIEFING

1. ANSWER
- National Living Wage (workers aged 21 and over): £12.71 per hour, effective 1 April 2026. Up 50p (4.1%) from £12.21.
- National Minimum Wage, 18–20 Year Old Rate: £10.85 per hour, effective 1 April 2026. Up 85p (8.5%) from £10.00.
Both are gross hourly rates in pounds sterling, stated to the penny, applying across the UK (England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland). They apply for the rate year 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027.

2. LEGAL BASIS AND STATUS — why these are the operative figures, not a forecast
- Operative instrument: The National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026 (draft SI laid under s.51(5) of the National Minimum Wage Act 1998). Regulation 2(2) substitutes '£12.71' for '£12.21' in regulation 4 of the National Minimum Wage Regulations 2015 (the national living wage). Regulation 2(3)(a) substitutes '£10.85' for '£10.00' in regulation 4A(1)(b) of the 2015 Regulations (workers aged 18 or over but not yet 21). Coming into force 1 April 2026; extends to England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.
- Policy chain: LPC recommendations submitted to Government 27 October 2025; Government accepted them in full at the Autumn Budget on 26 November 2025; rates brought into force 1 April 2026.
- Corroboration: the same two figures appear identically in (i) GOV.UK 'National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage rates', (ii) GOV.UK news story 'National Living Wage increases to £12.71 per hour' (1 April 2026), (iii) the Low Pay Commission report 'The National Minimum Wage in 2026' (1 April 2026), and (iv) the amending statutory instrument itself. Four independent official sources, no divergence. There is no unconfirmed-announcement risk on these two numbers.

3. FULL RATE TABLE FOR THE 2026–27 RATE YEAR (context — only rows 1 and 2 are in scope)
| Band | From 1 Apr 2026 | From 1 Apr 2025 | Increase |
| National Living Wage, 21 and over | £12.71 | £12.21 | +£0.50 (4.1%) |
| 18–20 Year Old Rate | £10.85 | £10.00 | +£0.85 (8.5%) |
| 16–17 Year Old Rate | £8.00 | £7.55 | +£0.45 (6.0%) |
| Apprentice Rate | £8.00 | £7.55 | +£0.45 (6.0%) |
| Accommodation offset (per day) | £11.10 | £10.66 | +£0.44 (4.1%) |
Rows 3–5 are included because the same instrument changes them on the same date and they will hit the same payroll run, not because they were asked for.

4. WHO GETS WHICH RATE — operating rules for HR
- 21 and over on the relevant date → £12.71. The NLW age threshold is 21; it came down from 25 to 23 in April 2021 and from 23 to 21 in April 2024, so any legacy 23+ or 25+ banding still sitting in an HRIS or job-evaluation grid must be retired.
- 18 or over but not yet 21 → £10.85.
- Under 18 but above school leaving age → £8.00. Below school leaving age → no entitlement (except apprentices within the apprentice rate conditions).
- Apprentices: entitled to the apprentice rate (£8.00) if aged under 19, or aged 19 or over and in the first year of their apprenticeship. An apprentice aged 19+ who has completed the first year moves to the age-based rate — so a 21-year-old apprentice past year one is entitled to £12.71, and an 18–20-year-old apprentice past year one to £10.85. This is the single most common mispayment in apprentice-heavy workforces.
- Birthdays: age is tested against the pay reference period. Safe system rule — promote the worker to the higher band from the start of the pay reference period in which the relevant birthday falls. That can never underpay; pro-rating from the exact birthday is also permissible if the time records are clean, but the start-of-period rule is the one to configure.
- Transitional pay reference period: where a pay reference period straddles 1 April 2026, apply the new rate from the start of that period. Confirm this against the payroll provider's NMW treatment, but over-applying on the boundary is the low-risk direction.
- No local variation. Minimum wage is reserved/UK-wide; there are no Scottish, Welsh or Northern Irish variants. Distinguish this from (a) devolved social care commissioning rates and (b) the voluntary Real Living Wage set by the Living Wage Foundation, which is a separate, higher, voluntary accreditation standard — if the organisation is an accredited Living Wage Employer, that commitment runs on its own timetable and is not satisfied by paying £12.71.

5. COSTING — derived figures (gross, before employer NICs and pension)
37.5-hour week:
- 21+: £12.71 × 37.5 = £476.63 per week (exact £476.625); × 52 = £24,784.50 per year; monthly equivalent £2,065.38.
- 18–20: £10.85 × 37.5 = £406.88 per week (exact £406.875); × 52 = £21,157.50 per year; monthly equivalent £1,763.13.
40-hour week:
- 21+: £508.40 per week; £26,436.80 per year; £2,203.07 per month.
- 18–20: £434.00 per week; £22,568.00 per year; £1,880.67 per month.
Marginal cost of the uprating per full-time equivalent, full year:
- 21+ at 37.5 h: £0.50 × 37.5 × 52 = £975.00; at 40 h: £1,040.00.
- 18–20 at 37.5 h: £0.85 × 37.5 × 52 = £1,657.50; at 40 h: £1,768.00.
- Multiply by headcount in each band and add employer NICs and auto-enrolment pension to get the true budget effect; the 18–20 uplift is proportionately nearly double the adult uplift, so a young workforce carries a materially larger percentage cost increase than the headline 4.1%.
Accommodation offset: £11.10 per day (from £10.66). Maximum weekly offset 7 × £11.10 = £77.70 (was £74.62); for a 5-day week, 5 × £11.10 = £55.50 (was £53.30). Any employer-provided living accommodation deduction above these daily limits takes pay below the minimum wage.

6. COMPLIANCE RISK REGISTER — actions before the first April 2026 payroll
(a) Update all rate tables in HRIS and payroll with an effective date of 1 April 2026, and run a parallel test payroll for the first period.
(b) Automate age-band promotion; audit every worker with a birthday falling in the rate year and every worker currently sitting in a legacy 23+ or 25+ band.
(c) Audit apprentice records for the first-year anniversary — those crossing it move to the age-based rate.
(d) Differential compression: the 18–20 rate is now 85.4% of the NLW (10.85 ÷ 12.71), up from 81.9% last year (10.00 ÷ 12.21). Expect knock-on pressure on team-leader and junior-supervisor differentials above the 18–20 band, and note the Government's stated policy direction of removing the 18–20 rate over time — model the convergence now rather than reacting to it.
(e) Check every deduction and payment-in-kind that can pull effective hourly pay below the floor: salary sacrifice, uniform and tool charges, training cost recovery, accommodation, and unpaid working time (handovers, opening/closing, mandatory training, trial shifts, travel between assignments, sleep-ins). The statutory rate is a floor on pay for time worked, not on the contractual salary line alone.
(f) Retain minimum wage records for six years; the burden of proof sits with the employer.
(g) Update offer letters, job adverts and agency/umbrella contracts from 1 April 2026 — agency workers are entitled to at least the NMW, and 'pay between assignments' models need re-testing at the new rates.
(h) Brief line managers, because the failure mode is almost always local rota and overtime practice, not the rate table.

7. SOURCES
- GOV.UK, 'National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage rates' — https://www.gov.uk/national-minimum-wage-rates
- GOV.UK / Low Pay Commission news, 'National Living Wage increases to £12.71 per hour', 1 April 2026 — https://www.gov.uk/government/news/national-living-wage-increases-to-1271-per-hour
- Low Pay Commission, 'The National Minimum Wage in 2026', 1 April 2026 — https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-national-minimum-wage-in-2026
- Low Pay Commission, 'Minimum wage rates for 2026' (advice to Government), 26 November 2025 — https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/minimum-wage-rates-for-2026
- The National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026 (draft SI), coming into force 1 April 2026 — https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukdsi/2026/9780348279030

8. SCOPE AND CAVEATS
- These are statutory minimum gross hourly rates for the 2026–27 rate year, not a pay recommendation or a benchmark above the floor.
- The 16–17 and apprentice rates and the accommodation offset are quoted for payroll completeness only and are outside the two asks.
- Out of scope and flagged only so it is not mistaken for the answer: the same GOV.UK rates page also lists April 2027 figures (National Living Wage £13.21, 18–20 rate £11.27). The LPC describes 2027 figures as indicative estimates at this stage, so treat them as planning-only and re-verify before relying on them.
- No devolved or regional variation exists for these rates.

question: M11
answer:
FMCSA SHORT-HAUL EXCEPTION — THE TWO LIMITS

Authority: 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1), "Short-haul operations — (1) 150 air-mile radius driver." Current text as published on eCFR (fetched for this analysis).

ANSWERS

1. RADIUS — 150 air miles.
   Regulatory text: "The driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location." 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)(i).
   The limit is a 150 air-mile radius, not a 150-statute-mile radius; the regulation supplies the conversion (172.6 statute miles) in parentheses so the two units are not confused. "Air miles" are measured in straight-line (great-circle) distance from the normal work reporting location, not along the route driven.

2. CONSECUTIVE HOURS — 14 consecutive hours.
   Regulatory text: "The driver, except a driver-salesperson, returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours." 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)(ii).
   The 14 hours run from the moment the driver comes on duty; the driver must both (a) return to the work reporting location and (b) be released from work, within that 14-consecutive-hour span. A driver-salesperson is excluded from the release requirement of (e)(1)(ii).

COMPLETE TEXT OF THE PROVISION (for reference and for the dependent conditions below)

   "(e) Short-haul operations —
   (1) 150 air-mile radius driver. A driver is exempt from the requirements of §§ 395.8 and 395.11 if:
   (i) The driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location;
   (ii) The driver, except a driver-salesperson, returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours;
   (iii)(A) A property-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 10 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty;
        (B) A passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 8 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty; and
   (iv) The motor carrier that employs the driver maintains and retains for a period of 6 months accurate and true time records showing: (A) the time the driver reports for duty each day; (B) the total number of hours the driver is on-duty each day; (C) the time the driver is released from duty each day; and (D) the total time for the preceding 7 days in accordance with § 395.8(j)(2) for drivers used for the first time or intermittently."

WHAT THE EXCEPTION ACTUALLY EXCUSES

A driver meeting all of (e)(1) is exempt from 49 CFR 395.8 (records of duty status) and 395.11 (supporting documents). FMCSA's own guidance (ELD FAQ 17) confirms that drivers using the short-haul/timecard exception are not required to keep RODS or use an ELD, and FMCSA's HOS guidance confirms such drivers also need not take the 30-minute break under 395.1(e)(1). The carrier must still keep the 6-month time records described in (e)(1)(iv); the exception replaces the graph grid/ELD, not the underlying time record.

SCOPE AND APPLICABILITY NOTES (read these before applying the two numbers)

- The (e)(1) exception is available to both property-carrying and passenger-carrying CMV drivers. The property/passenger split shows up in (e)(1)(iii): 10 consecutive hours off-duty for property-carrying, 8 for passenger-carrying. It does not change either of the two answers above.
- The exemption is conditioned, not automatic. If on a given day the driver exceeds the 150 air-mile radius or is not released within 14 consecutive hours, the exception does not apply to that day and the driver must complete RODS (paper log or ELD, per the 8-days-in-30 threshold in 395.8 and the ELD rule). FMCSA's 2020 short-haul webinar states this explicitly: "When a driver no longer meets the exception (drives too far/works too many hours), the driver must complete a regular log or use an ELD for the day."
- Do not confuse (e)(1) with the adjacent provisions in the same section:
  * 395.1(e)(2) — the non-CDL property-carrying short-haul provision — also uses a 150 air-mile radius but imposes a different time structure: no driving after the 14th hour on 5 days of any 7 consecutive days, and no driving after the 16th hour on 2 days of any 7 consecutive days. Its 16-hour figure is NOT the answer to ask 2; the answer to ask 2 is the 14-consecutive-hour release rule in (e)(1)(ii).
  * 395.1(p) — motion picture production sites — uses a 100 air-mile radius. That is a separate exception and does not apply here.
  * 395.1(b)(1)-(3) — the 16-hour "unforeseen driving conditions" extension — is a separate provision with its own 5-prior-duty-tour and 6-consecutive-day conditions.
- Version control: these are the limits as currently in effect following the 2020 HOS final rule, which "extends the maximum duty period allowed under the short-haul exception from 12 hours to 14 hours" and "extends the maximum radius of the short-haul exception from a 100 air-mile radius to a 150 air-mile radius." If any record, logbook form, or internal policy in your materials still says 100 air miles and/or 12 hours, it predates the 2020 rule and is out of date.

ONE-LINE ANSWER FOR A POLICY OR TRAINING DOCUMENT

"A driver qualifies for the federal short-haul exception to the records-of-duty-status requirement only if the driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location and returns to that location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours (49 CFR 395.1(e)(1))."

BOUNDARY OF THIS ANSWER

This is the federal FMCSA hours-of-service rule for interstate CMVs. It does not address state intrastate hours-of-service rules, which several states set independently, nor does it address enforcement discretion, penalty exposure, or how a specific carrier should document compliance — those fall outside the scope of the two questions asked.

question: M1
answer:
REGULATORY DETERMINATION — FAA BasicMed aircraft limits (current law, effective November 12, 2024)

Controlling authority: 14 CFR § 61.113(i)(1), as amended to implement § 828 of the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 (Pub. L. 118-63). Corroborating FAA materials: FAA Notice N 8000.386 (11/14/24) and FAA news release dated November 15, 2024. The current eCFR text of § 61.113(i)(1) states that the aircraft must be “authorized to carry not more than 7 occupants,” have “a maximum takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds,” be “operated with no more than 6 passengers on board,” and not be “a transport category rotorcraft certified to airworthiness standards under part 29.”

ANSWERS

1. Maximum takeoff weight: 12,500 pounds.
   This is the aircraft’s maximum certificated/design takeoff weight (MTOW), not the actual loaded weight on a given flight. The aircraft must have an MTOW of not more than 12,500 lb.

2. Number of occupants the aircraft may be authorized to carry: 7 occupants.
   “Occupants” includes required flightcrew members. The aircraft’s design approval — type certificate, supplemental type certificate, amended type certificate, or, for experimental aircraft, its operating limitations — must authorize no more than 7 occupants.

3. Number of passengers on board: 6 passengers.
   This is a separate, additional limit. Because occupants include required flightcrew, the practical passenger maximum is 7 minus the number of required flightcrew. With one required pilot, the maximum is 6 passengers; with two required flightcrew, the maximum is 5 passengers. In no case may more than 6 passengers be on board.

ADDITIONAL AIRCRAFT-ELIGIBILITY LIMIT

The aircraft must not be a transport category rotorcraft certified to airworthiness standards under 14 CFR part 29. This is an additional eligibility restriction and does not change the three numeric limits above.

OPERATING LIMITS THAT ACCOMPANY THE AIRCRAFT LIMITS

BasicMed also requires the flight to be conducted at or below 18,000 feet MSL, at an indicated airspeed not exceeding 250 knots, within the United States or a country in which BasicMed is authorized, and not for compensation or hire. These are operational limits, not aircraft-dimension limits, but they apply conjunctively with the three aircraft limits.

HISTORICAL NOTE

Before November 12, 2024, the BasicMed aircraft limits were 6,000 pounds MTOW, 6 occupants, and 5 passengers. AC 68-1A (dated 5/3/17) and the July/August 2017 FAA Safety Briefing still show those older figures; they are superseded for current-law purposes by the amended § 61.113(i)(1), Notice N 8000.386, and the November 2024 FAA announcement.

SCOPE

This is a US federal regulatory answer. More restrictive state law, insurance requirements, rental agreements, or the pilot’s underlying certificate privileges may apply.
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 6 on faa.gov/documentlibrary/media/advisory_circular/ac_68-1a.pdf and 7 on faa.gov/documentlibrary/media/notice/n_8000.386.pdf. The first reads: "Fly an aircraft that is authorized to carry no more than 6 occupants."

question: M3
answer:
## Hours of service — driver of a passenger-carrying CMV (motorcoach), US federal rules

**Governing provision: 49 CFR 395.5, 'Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles'** (interstate, no exception applied).

### Answers

| # | Question | Answer | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | How many hours may they drive? | **10 hours** | §395.5(a)(1) |
| 2 | After how many consecutive hours off duty? | **8 consecutive hours** off duty | §395.5(a) |
| 3 | After how many hours on duty may they no longer drive? | **15 hours** on duty | §395.5(a)(2) |

All three are one rule read as a sentence: *no driver may drive a passenger-carrying CMV more than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty, or for any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty.*

### Regulatory text (verbatim, §395.5(a))

> "Subject to the exceptions and exemptions in § 395.1:
> (a) No motor carrier shall permit or require any driver used by it to drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle, nor shall any such driver drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle:
> (1) More than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty; or
> (2) For any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty."

Corroborated by the FMCSA passenger-carrier brochure (FMCSA-E-06-006, July 2022): "More than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty, or ... For any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty."

### Correction to a common assumption (important)

These are **not** the property-carrying numbers. The property-carrying rule (§395.3) is 11 hours driving after 10 consecutive hours off duty, with a 14-hour on-duty window. For **passenger-carrying** CMVs the figures are **10 driving hours / 8 consecutive off-duty hours / 15-hour on-duty window**. Do not substitute 10 or 14 into this operation. (FMCSA states it directly: "The hours-of-service rules for drivers of passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicles (CMVs) are different from the rules for property-carrying CMVs.")

### How the three numbers interlock

- The **8 consecutive off-duty hours** is the single reset. It restarts both the 10-hour driving clock and the 15-hour on-duty window. It is not a per-day figure and is not 10 hours.
- The **15-hour window** runs from the end of the qualifying 8-hour off-duty period. Within it, at most **10 hours** may be driving. Non-driving on-duty work (loading, paperwork, compensated work for a non-carrier employer, and — under §395.1(j) — most travel/cushioning time absent 8 consecutive hours off at destination) consumes the window without consuming the 10 driving hours.
- Driving is barred at the earlier of: 10 driving hours elapsed, or 15 on-duty hours elapsed, or a weekly cap being reached.
- **The 15-hour limit bars driving, not all work.** A driver may remain on duty after hour 15; the prohibition is on driving. This matters for dispatching a relief driver or a hotel move.

### Additional limit the driver is also subject to (§395.5(b)) — stated so 15 is not mistaken for the only cap

No driving after being on duty:
- **60 hours in any 7 consecutive days**, if the carrier does **not** operate CMVs every day of the week; or
- **70 hours in any 8 consecutive days**, if the carrier **does** operate CMVs every day of the week.

This applies "regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services" — multi-employer on-duty time counts (§395.8(j) requires a signed statement of the prior 7 days' on-duty time when a driver is used intermittently).

### Off-duty time — what counts

Off-duty time is not separately defined in Part 395; it is any time that is not driving, on-duty, or sleeper-berth time under §395.2. For a meal or routine stop to count as off duty, the driver must be relieved of all duty and responsibility for the care and custody of the vehicle and its passengers. On-duty time runs from when the driver begins work or must be ready for work until relieved of work and all responsibility for it, and includes compensated work for a non-motor-carrier employer.

Sleeper berth: a passenger-carrying CMV equipped with a sleeper berth as defined in §393.76 may accumulate the equivalent of the 8 consecutive off-duty hours through two rest periods in the berth, provided the four requirements of §395.1(g)(3)(i)–(iv) are met. The specific conditions of those four subparagraphs are not reproduced here and should be read at the source before relying on the split-rest option.

### When these numbers do not apply (check before quoting them)

§395.5 is expressly "[s]ubject to the exceptions and exemptions in §395.1." Before applying 10/8/15, confirm none of the following fits:
- **Adverse driving conditions** — §395.1(b) relief may permit driving beyond the limits to complete the run; it does not raise the base limits. Read §395.1(b) at the source for its conditions.
- **Local emergencies** — §395.1(c) suspends §§395.3 and 395.5 during direct assistance in a government-declared emergency, for the period of assistance or 5 days from the initial declaration, whichever is less.
- **State-specific rules** (the §395.1 Alaska/Hawaii provisions, which as written in the fetched text address property-carrying CMVs) and any **intrastate** state regime.
- **Short-haul / non-CMV / private-carrier** situations — e.g., non-business private motor carriers of passengers are not subject to the Part 395 record-of-duty-status requirements.

If any of these applies, the answer is jurisdiction- or operation-specific and 10/8/15 should not be quoted as the limit.

### Implementation (duty-status check)

```
Given: dutyStatus events for the current cycle, plus prior 7/8-day on-duty totals.
Constants (passenger-carrying, §395.5):
  OFF_RESET_HOURS   = 8     # consecutive off-duty (or §395.1(g)(3) sleeper equivalent)
  MAX_DRIVE_HOURS   = 10    # after the reset
  MAX_WINDOW_HOURS  = 15    # on-duty hours after the reset
  WEEKLY = {7: 60, 8: 70}   # keyed by carrier operates-every-day ? 8 : 7

1. Find lastReset = end of the most recent block of >= OFF_RESET_HOURS consecutive off-duty time.
2. driveSinceReset  = sum of driving time after lastReset.
3. onDutySinceReset = elapsed on-duty time after lastReset (driving + on-duty-not-driving).
4. weeklyOnDuty = on-duty hours in the trailing 7 or 8 consecutive days per carrier schedule.
5. mayDrive = driveSinceReset  < MAX_DRIVE_HOURS
          and onDutySinceReset < MAX_WINDOW_HOURS
          and weeklyOnDuty    < WEEKLY[window]
          and no applicable §395.1 exception is in force.
6. Remaining drive time = min(MAX_DRIVE_HOURS - driveSinceReset,
                              MAX_WINDOW_HOURS - onDutySinceReset).
```

Note step 6: the binding constraint is whichever of the 10-hour and 15-hour clocks runs out first, so a driver who has burned window time on non-driving duty has less than 10 driving hours available. The weekly check is a hard stop independent of both.

### Sources

- 49 CFR §395.5 (eCFR, current) — quoted above.
- 49 CFR Part 395, CFR 2025 ed., GovInfo PDF — identical text of §395.5.
- FMCSA, *Hours of Service for Motor Carriers of Passengers* (FMCSA-E-06-006, July 2022) and the FMCSA passenger-carrier HOS web page — identical limits; plus off-duty, on-duty, travel-time, sleeper-berth, multiple-employer and ELD notes.
- 49 CFR §395.1(c) — emergency relief; §395.2 — on-duty definition; §395.8(j) — multiple-employer driver statement.

# Flight Attendant Rest After a Scheduled Duty Period of 14 Hours or Less — 14 CFR Part 135 On-Demand Charter

## Bottom line

| Question | Answer | Authority |
|---|---|---|
| Rest required after a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less | **9 consecutive hours** of rest, scheduled to occur between completion of the duty period and commencement of the next duty period | 14 CFR 135.273(b)(2) |
| To what may that rest be reduced | **8 consecutive hours**, and only if the flight attendant is given a subsequent rest period of at least **10 consecutive hours** that is scheduled to begin no later than **24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period** and that occurs between completion of the scheduled duty period and commencement of the subsequent duty period | 14 CFR 135.273(b)(3) |

The 8-hour figure is not free-standing. It is available only as a pair: 8 hours now **plus** a scheduled 10-hour compensatory rest inside the following 24-hour window. If the operator cannot schedule and protect the 10-hour payback, the floor is 9 consecutive hours.

## 1. Applicability — does the rule reach this person at all?

Part 135's flight/duty/rest subpart is written around flightcrew, but 135.273 is the flight-attendant-specific provision and it reaches cabin crew on a Part 135 on-demand certificate:

- **135.263(e)** (retrieved): "Section 135.273 prescribes duty period limitations and rest requirements for flight attendants in all operations conducted under this part." There is no scheduled/on-demand carve-out — on-demand charter is covered.
- **135.273(a) definition** (retrieved): a "flight attendant" is an individual, other than a flight crewmember, assigned by the certificate holder in accordance with the required minimum crew complement under its operations specifications **or in addition to that minimum complement**, to duty in an aircraft during flight time, whose duties include but are not necessarily limited to cabin-safety-related responsibilities.
- **FAA legal interpretations** (retrieved): the Kalt memorandum (June 10, 2014, AGC-200/AFS-240) and the Doan memorandum both hold that an individual voluntarily assigned in addition to the minimum crew, who is given cabin-safety responsibilities during flight time, is a "flight attendant" for purposes of 135.273 and is subject to its flight, duty and rest rules. Flight attendants are not *required* below 19 passenger seats (135.107), but if carried and assigned safety duties they are *covered*.

**Gate to apply before using the 9/8 figures:** the person must be assigned cabin-safety-related duties during flight time. A person carried solely for service/catering with no assigned cabin-safety responsibility during flight time does not meet the 135.273(a) definition, and then no FAA rest minimum attaches — only company policy or a CBA would.

## 2. The baseline: 9 consecutive hours (135.273(b)(2))

For a flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less (the limit in 135.273(b)(1) is a scheduled duty period of not more than 14 hours), the certificate holder must give a scheduled rest period of at least **9 consecutive hours**, occurring between completion of the scheduled duty period and commencement of the subsequent duty period.

Definitions that control the arithmetic (135.273(a), retrieved):

- **Duty period** — elapsed time between reporting for an assignment involving flight time and release from that assignment by the certificate holder, computed in UTC or local time to reflect total elapsed time. The clock starts at report, not at first engine start, and stops at release.
- **Rest period** — "the period free of all responsibility for work or duty should the occasion arise." Reserve/standby, required check-ins, training, positioning as a crewmember, or any assignable duty destroys the rest period. Nine hours must be nine *consecutive* hours of actual freedom from responsibility.
- **135.273(b)(10)-(11)** (retrieved): no assignment of any duty period without at least the minimum rest required by the section, and no assignment to any duty during a required rest period.

## 3. The reduction: 8 consecutive hours (135.273(b)(3))

The 9-hour rest may be scheduled for or reduced to **8 consecutive hours** only if all three conditions hold:

1. The flight attendant is provided a **subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours**;
2. That subsequent rest period is **scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period**; and
3. That subsequent rest period **occurs between completion of the scheduled duty period and commencement of the subsequent duty period**.

Operational consequence: use of reduced rest compresses the following duty day. The duty period that follows the 8-hour rest must be built so the flight attendant is released in time for the 10-hour payback to *begin* by the 24-hour deadline measured from the start of the reduced rest. Practically, an 8-hour rest followed by a full 14-hour duty period will almost never satisfy the 24-hour deadline; the scheduler must compute it per pairing.

## 4. Do not confuse this with the extended-duty reduction

135.273(b)(7)-(b)(9) (partially retrieved) provide a separate scheme for duty periods that exceed 14 hours: a longer scheduled rest that may be "scheduled or reduced to 10 consecutive hours" with a subsequent rest of at least 14 consecutive hours, and, under (b)(9), a prohibition on scheduling more than 14 hours of duty during the 24-hour period commencing after the beginning of that reduced rest. Those paragraphs are keyed to extended duty periods and to the additional-flight-attendant extensions; they are **not** the answer for a duty period of 14 hours or less. The correct pair for the question as asked is (b)(2) / (b)(3): 9 hours, reducible to 8.

## 5. The alternative scheme the operator may have elected — check the ops specs

135.273(c) (retrieved) lets a certificate holder apply the **flightcrew** flight-time/duty/rest rules of Part 135 Subpart F to its flight attendants instead, provided it establishes written procedures that:

- apply to all flight attendants used in the operation;
- include the Subpart F flightcrew requirements as appropriate to the operation (except that on-board rest facilities are not required);
- add one flight attendant to the minimum complement for each flight crewmember in excess of the minimum required by the aircraft type certificate data sheet who is assigned under Subpart F; and
- are **approved by the Administrator and described or referenced in the certificate holder's operations specifications**.

If — and only if — this operator holds that approval, the 9/8 answer is displaced and the flightcrew rest rules govern instead (for example, under 135.267 for unscheduled operations, a required rest of at least 10 consecutive hours in the 24 hours preceding, reducible to 8 with a compensatory rest; under 135.265(c) for scheduled operations, 9/10/11 hours depending on scheduled flight time, reducible to 8/8/9 with compensatory rests). Absent an approved 135.273(c) procedure referenced in the ops specs, the flight-attendant rule of (b)(2)/(b)(3) governs and the answer remains 9, reducible to 8.

Also check: any exemption, deviation, or opspec authorization that alters the baseline (the request states none is assumed); and any CBA or company manual term. The regulation is a floor — a collective bargaining agreement or company policy may impose more rest, and the more restrictive term controls as a matter of contract even though the FAA minimum is 9/8.

## 6. Scheduler's compliance procedure

For each flight-attendant pairing, before publication:

1. **Identify status.** Confirm the individual is assigned cabin-safety duties during flight time (135.273(a)). If not, 135.273 does not apply; document the basis and apply company/CBA rest.
2. **Confirm the governing scheme.** Check the ops specs for a 135.273(c) election. If present, apply Subpart F flightcrew rest rules per the approved written procedures. If absent, apply step 3.
3. **Compute the duty period.** Report time to release time, in local or UTC, consistently. Verify scheduled duty is 14:00 or less.
4. **Apply baseline rest.** Schedule at least 9:00 consecutive hours free of all responsibility between release and the next report time. Record the rest start and end.
5. **If reduced rest is intended,** verify all of: rest is at least 8:00 consecutive hours; a subsequent rest of at least 10:00 consecutive hours is scheduled; its start time is no later than (reduced-rest start + 24:00); it falls between completion of the scheduled duty period and the start of the following duty period. If any leg fails, revert to 9:00.
6. **Protect the rest.** No assignment, call-out, standby, positioning, or training inside the rest window (135.273(b)(11)); no duty period assignment without the minimum rest (b)(10)).
7. **Compare with contract/company minimums** and apply the more restrictive value.
8. **Record the basis** (paragraph relied on, rest start/end, and, for reduced rest, the 24-hour deadline and the scheduled payback rest) in the crew-tracking record.

## 7. Worked example

Scheduled duty period 07:00-21:00 local (14:00), release 21:00.

- **Baseline:** rest 21:00-06:00 = 9:00 consecutive hours; next report no earlier than 06:00.
- **Reduced:** rest 21:00-05:00 = 8:00 consecutive hours. The 10-hour compensatory rest must begin no later than 05:00 the following day (reduced-rest start 21:00 + 24:00 = 21:00 next day is the outer bound on the *beginning* of the reduced rest plus 24; applying the rule from the reduced-rest start of 21:00 gives a deadline of 21:00 the next day for the start of the 10-hour rest, so the duty period following the 8-hour rest must release the flight attendant by 21:00 the next day at the latest, and in practice earlier to allow the 10 hours to run). The scheduler must compute this per pairing; if release cannot be assured inside the window, the 8-hour option is unavailable and 9:00 applies.

## 8. Verification note

The retrieved excerpt set quoted 135.273(a), (b)(1), (b)(8)-(b)(11) and (c), plus 135.263(e), 135.265 and 135.267. The operative paragraphs for this answer — (b)(2) and (b)(3) — were not returned verbatim by the fetch. The 9-hour baseline and the 8-hour reduction with a 10-hour compensatory rest are stated here from the regulation's text and are corroborated by the parallel structure of the extended-duty reduction in (b)(8) (reduction paired with a longer subsequent rest and a 24-hour deadline). Before publishing this into a manual or ops-spec document, read (b)(2) and (b)(3) directly at 14 CFR 135.273 on eCFR and confirm the numbers 9, 8 and 10 and the 24-hour deadline are unchanged in the current amendment.

The first reads: "(1) A rest required under paragraph (b)(1) of this section may be scheduled for or reduced to a minimum of 8 hours if the flight crewmember is given a rest period of at least 10 hours that must begin no later than 24 hours after the commenc"
