# HTTP/2: current specification and what it obsoletes

## Answers

| Ask | Answer |
|---|---|
| Current specification of HTTP/2 | **RFC 9113** |
| RFCs obsoleted by RFC 9113 | **RFC 7540** and **RFC 8740** |

## 1. Current specification — RFC 9113

- **Number:** RFC 9113
- **Title:** HTTP/2
- **Authors/Editors:** M. Thomson, Ed. (Mozilla); C. Benfield, Ed. (Apple Inc.)
- **Publication date:** June 2022
- **Stream / category:** IETF, Standards Track (Proposed Standard)
- **ISSN:** 2070-1721
- **Canonical citation:** M. Thomson, Ed. and C. Benfield, Ed., "HTTP/2", RFC 9113, DOI 10.17487/RFC9113, June 2022, <https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113>.

The document's own header block reads, verbatim:

```
Stream:   Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF)
RFC:      9113
Obsoletes: 7540, 8740
Category:  Standards Track
Published: June 2022
ISSN:      2070-1721
```

and its abstract states: "This specification describes an optimized expression of the semantics of the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP), referred to as HTTP version 2 (HTTP/2). ... This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740."

## 2. RFCs obsoleted by RFC 9113

Exactly two, as listed in RFC 9113's `Obsoletes:` header and repeated in its abstract:

| Obsoleted RFC | Title | Original status | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **RFC 7540** | Hypertext Transfer Protocol Version 2 (HTTP/2) | Proposed Standard, May 2015 (Belshe, Peon, Thomson, Eds.) | The original HTTP/2 specification. Its errata page now carries "⚠ This RFC has been obsoleted! Obsoleted by: RFC9113; Updated by: RFC8740". |
| **RFC 8740** | Using TLS 1.3 with HTTP/2 | Proposed Standard, February 2020 (D. Benjamin) | It had *updated* RFC 7540 (forbidding TLS 1.3 post-handshake authentication); RFC 9113 folded that requirement in and obsoletes RFC 8740 as a separate document. RFC 9113 Appendix B: "Use of TLS 1.3 was defined based on [RFC8740], which this document obsoletes." |

Corroboration from independent directions (all three agree):
- RFC Editor info page for RFC 9113 — `Obsoletes: 7540, 8740`.
- RFC Editor HTTP/2 subject page — RFC 7540 marked "Obsoleted by RFC 9113"; RFC 8740 marked "Obsoleted by RFC 9113".
- RFC 7540 errata search page — "Obsoleted by: RFC9113 / Updated by: RFC8740".

## 3. Scope boundaries (what is *not* obsoleted)

Stated explicitly so the answer is not over-read:

- **RFC 7541 (HPACK: Header Compression for HTTP/2)** is **not** obsoleted by RFC 9113; it remains the compression specification referenced by HTTP/2.
- **HTTP/2 extension documents are not obsoleted:** RFC 8441 (Bootstrapping WebSockets with HTTP/2), RFC 8336 (The ORIGIN HTTP/2 Frame), RFC 8164 (Opportunistic Security for HTTP/2, Historic) all remain as-is.
- **Obsoletes ≠ Updates.** RFC 9113 also *updates* other documents and IANA registries (e.g., it moves the ALPN, HTTP/2 Frame Type, HTTP/2 Settings, HTTP/2 Error Code and HTTP Method registry references from RFC 7540 to itself; it marks the `HTTP2-Settings` header field registration and the `h2c` upgrade token as obsolete). Those are update/registry actions, not additions to the Obsoletes list.

## 4. Qualification on "current"

"Current" here means: the latest published IETF Standards Track RFC that specifies HTTP/2 itself, as of the sources consulted (fetched 2026-11-16). RFC 9113 is that document; no successor RFC obsoleting RFC 9113 appears in any consulted source. HTTP/2 has exactly one prior specification (RFC 7540) plus one amending document (RFC 8740), so the revision lineage is short and fully accounted for above.

**Re-verification procedure** (cheap, and the only thing that could change this answer): open <https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113/> and read the header block. If the page shows "Obsoleted by: RFC NNNN" or the `Obsoletes:` line differs from `7540, 8740`, the answer above is superseded and must be updated to RFC NNNN and that document's own `Obsoletes:` list. Equivalently, check <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9113/> or the RFC Editor's HTTP/2 subject page at <https://www.rfc-editor.org/subjects/http2/>.

question: M9
answer:
# UK statutory minimum wage rates effective 1 April 2026 — HR briefing note

## 1. Headline answers

| # | Ask | Rate from 1 April 2026 | Previous rate (to 31 Mar 2026) | Cash increase | % increase |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **National Living Wage (NLW), workers aged 21 and over** | **£12.71 per hour** | £12.21 | £0.50 | 4.1% |
| 2 | **National Minimum Wage (NMW), 18–20 Year Old Rate** | **£10.85 per hour** | £10.00 | £0.85 | 8.5% |

Both figures are **confirmed statutory rates**, not forecasts or projections. They apply in England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland (SI 2026/357 extends to all four) and take effect **1 April 2026**. They remain in force until the next annual uprating on 1 April 2027.

## 2. Authority and verification trail

Use in this order of precedence:

1. **Primary legislation (operative law):** The National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026, SI 2026/357, made 19 March 2026, coming into force 1 April 2026. Regulation 2(2) substitutes "£12.21" with "**£12.71**" in regulation 4 of the National Minimum Wage Regulations 2015 (the NLW rate). Regulation 2(3)(a) substitutes "£10.00" with "**£10.85**" in regulation 4A(1)(b) (workers aged 18 or over but not yet 21). Signed by Kate Dearden, Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State, Department for Business and Trade.
2. **Government announcement:** GOV.UK, "Minimum wage rates for 2026" (Low Pay Commission advice to Government), published 26 November 2025 — states the Government announced the 2026 increases and **accepted the LPC's recommendations in full**.
3. **Operational guidance:** GOV.UK, "National Minimum Wage rates" — live rates table, April 2026 row: 21 and over £12.71; 18 to 20 £10.85; under 18 £8.00; apprentice £8.00.
4. **LPC impact report:** "The National Minimum Wage in 2026", published 1 April 2026 — restates the same table and confirms increases follow the LPC's October 2025 recommendations.

All four agree on both requested figures; there is no conflicting value in the record.

## 3. Full April 2026 rate card (for payroll configuration)

| Band | Rate from 1 Apr 2026 | Increase | % |
|---|---|---|---|
| National Living Wage (21 and over) | £12.71 / hour | £0.50 | 4.1% |
| 18–20 Year Old Rate | £10.85 / hour | £0.85 | 8.5% |
| 16–17 Year Old Rate | £8.00 / hour | £0.45 | 6.0% |
| Apprentice Rate | £8.00 / hour | £0.45 | 6.0% |
| Accommodation Offset | £11.10 **per day** | £0.44 | 4.1% |

Note the unit change on the accommodation offset: it is a **daily** cap on the amount an employer may deduct from pay for accommodation, not an hourly rate. Do not load it into an hourly-rate field in the payroll system.

## 4. Rules HR must apply alongside the headline figures

**Age band, not job role, drives the rate.**
- NLW applies to workers aged **21 and over** (the age of entitlement moved from 23 to 21 with effect from 1 April 2024 and remains at 21 through April 2026).
- The 18–20 Year Old Rate applies to workers aged **18 or over but not yet 21**.
- A worker moves to the higher band on their **21st birthday**, not at the following 1 April. Payroll must be driven by date of birth, not by a manual band flag set once a year.
- Workers under 18 (above school leaving age) are on the 16–17 Year Old Rate; apprentices have their own rules (below).

**Apprentices.** The apprentice rate (£8.00) applies only if the apprentice is **aged under 19**, or is **aged 19 or over and in the first year** of their apprenticeship. An apprentice aged 19+ who has completed the first year moves to the full rate for their age — e.g. an apprentice aged 21 who has finished year one is entitled to £12.71.

**What counts toward the minimum.** Pay for NMW/NLW purposes includes most pay elements but excludes tips, service charge, overtime premium, unsocial-hours premium, and expenses. Deductions for uniforms, tools, equipment, training or breakages, and any required payment to the employer, reduce *disposable* pay and can push an apparently compliant rate below the statutory floor. **Salary sacrifice must not take pay below the applicable minimum** — check pension and cycle-to-work arrangements against £12.71/£10.85, not against the pre-April figures.

**Salaried and annualised-hours staff.** For monthly-salaried employees, verify compliance by dividing actual pay by actual hours worked in each pay period. Term-time-only and annualised-hours contracts are the highest-risk groups at an 8.5% youth-rate increase.

**Accommodation.** Where accommodation is provided, the employer may deduct no more than £11.10 per day; anything above that counts as a deduction from pay and risks breaching the minimum.

**Records.** Keep NMW/NLW records for **at least six years** — sufficient to show pay, hours, deductions and the age band applied for every worker.

## 5. HR action checklist for the 1 April 2026 uplift

1. **Payroll configuration** — load all five figures above, effective 1 April 2026; run a parallel test payroll before the live run; confirm the pro-rata treatment for anyone whose pay period straddles 31 March / 1 April.
2. **Full-population sweep** — extract every worker paid at or near the floor and re-test against the new rate, including commission-only, piece-rate, zero-hours and agency-supplied staff. The 8.5% uplift on the 18–20 band is the larger shock; 18–20s who were comfortably above £10.00 may now be below £10.85.
3. **Age-band audit** — reconcile date of birth to rate code for every worker aged 17–22; correct any worker who turned 21 but was left on the youth rate.
4. **Differential compression** — where team members or supervisors were paid a premium above the old floor, check whether the uplift has flattened differentials; decide and document whether to preserve them (retention risk sits with newly hired supervisors earning close to their reports).
5. **Contracts and offer letters** — update template rates, salary bands and any clause referencing the NLW/NMW by figure rather than by reference to statute.
6. **Communications** — brief line managers before the change lands in payslips; issue a short employee note explaining the increase and the effective date.
7. **Budgeting** — model the cost at 4.1% on the 21+ population and 8.5% on the 18–20 population, plus the knock-on effect on employer National Insurance, pension contributions and any pay scales contractually linked to the minimum wage.
8. **Risk** — underpayment exposes the employer to arrears plus a penalty of up to 200% of arrears (capped per worker), public naming, and director disqualification consideration. Treat any identified underpayment as remediable immediately, with arrears backdated to 1 April 2026.

## 6. Forward-planning note (do not confuse with the answer)

The same GOV.UK rates table already shows the **April 2027** row: £13.21 (21+), £11.27 (18–20), £8.31 (16–17 and apprentice). Treat these as published forward figures for multi-year budgeting only; the rates that answer this request, and the only rates legally in force from 1 April 2026, are **£12.71** and **£10.85**.

## 7. What these figures are not

- They are **not** the voluntary "Real Living Wage" published by the Living Wage Foundation, which is set independently of Government, is higher, and is not a statutory minimum. No figure for it is stated here; verify separately if it is needed for accreditation or supplier policy.
- They are **not** London-weighted — there is no statutory regional or London rate.
- They are **not** net pay, and take no account of tax, National Insurance or employer-specific enhancements.
- They are **not** the rate for 16–17 year olds, apprentices, or the accommodation offset, each of which is listed separately above.

question: M11
answer:
Governing provision: 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1), the FMCSA short-haul exception to the record-of-duty-status requirement (current eCFR text; the 2020 HOS final rule expanded the exception from 100 air miles/12 hours to 150 air miles/14 hours).

Answer 1 — Radius: The driver must operate within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location. The regulation states this as "150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles)." The regulatory unit is air miles; 150 air miles is approximately 172.6 statute miles, not 150 statute miles.

Answer 2 — Release from work: The driver must return to the work reporting location and be released from work within 14 consecutive hours. The 14-hour period runs consecutively from the time the driver comes on duty following the required off-duty period; it is not cumulative on-duty time summed across shifts.

Supporting conditions in 395.1(e)(1):
- The driver must operate within the 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location.
- Except for a driver-salesperson, the driver must return to the work reporting location and be released from work within 14 consecutive hours.
- A property-carrying CMV driver must have at least 10 consecutive hours off duty separating each 14 hours on duty.
- A passenger-carrying CMV driver must have at least 8 consecutive hours off duty separating each 14 hours on duty.
- The motor carrier must maintain and retain for 6 months accurate time records showing the time the driver reports for duty each day, total hours on duty each day, time released from duty each day, and, for drivers used for the first time or intermittently, total time for the preceding 7 days under 395.8(j)(2).

Both the property-carrying and passenger-carrying versions of 395.1(e)(1) use the same 150-air-mile radius and the same 14-consecutive-hour return-and-release deadline. The difference between the two versions is the off-duty minimum: 10 consecutive hours for property-carrying drivers and 8 consecutive hours for passenger-carrying drivers.

The exception relieves the driver of the RODS and ELD requirements of 395.8 and 395.11; it does not relieve the driver of all hours-of-service obligations. If the driver exceeds the 150-air-mile radius or is not returned and released within 14 consecutive hours, the exception is unavailable for that day and a record of duty status is required.

Note on the separate non-CDL property-carrying exception: 49 CFR 395.1(e)(2) also uses a 150 air-mile radius, but its hour structure is not a single 14-hour release rule. It prohibits driving after the 14th hour after coming on duty on 5 days of any period of 7 consecutive days and after the 16th hour after coming on duty on 2 days of any period of 7 consecutive days, with return to the normal work reporting location at the end of each duty tour. The two answers above address the 395.1(e)(1) short-haul exception described in the question.
